post_owner.name: Catarina Oliveira
text:
You should really be eating warm food. 
In Traditional Chinese Medicine this is non negotiable, and there’s also research backing it up.

There’s a study in Appetite (2021, ID 105069) showing that simply serving food warm increases fullness and helps people make better food choices. Literally just the temperature changes how satisfied you feel.

Another study in the British Journal of Nutrition, compared Asian and Western eating habits and found something interesting. People who regularly eat warm meals have fewer digestive issues and fewer “cold stomach” symptoms after eating.

And  this is exactly what TCM has been saying forever. Your stomach works like a warm little pot. If you keep cooling it down with iced drinks or cold raw foods, you weaken the fire that drives your digestion. Your Spleen Qi drops, dampness will build up, and you start to feel heavy, bloated, puffy, and sluggish.

When digestion slows, your skin feels it too. Sagging, dullness, puffiness, slow metabolism,  it’s all connected.

So try choosing warm, cooked meals. Soups, porridges, stews, steamed vegetables. Even room temperature water (as long as the room is warm not frigid) is kinder to your system than anything iced. Give it a week and your digestion, energy, and blood will improve.

text:
Every woman carries an elemental blueprint — a pattern the ancient physicians of Chinese Medicine used to understand personality, health, emotions, beauty, and even the way a woman moves through the world. 

The Five Elements aren’t “mystical labels”; they’re a physiological-energetic model of how life expresses itself through you. Wood gives you direction. Fire gives you charisma. Earth gives you stability. Metal gives you refinement. Water gives you depth.

When your primary element is balanced, life feels aligned: your hormones respond better, your digestion is smoother, your mind is clearer, and your relationships feel easier. 

When that element slips out of balance, the body starts whispering — sometimes as PMS, bloating, burnout, skin changes, irritability, anxiety, or sudden waves of fatigue. TCM has always taught that before symptoms appear in the body, they first appear in the element.

You might see yourself in more than one. Most women do. Elements shift through seasons, hormones, motherhood, stress levels, and age. The goal isn’t to “pick one.” The goal is to understand the patterns that guide your health, your emotions, and your feminine energy.

Tell me in the comments: which element feels most like you right now? 🔥💧🌱🪨🪙

text:
Asthma is a chronic condition characterised by recurrent attacks of wheezing, breathlessness, coughing, and chest tightness. These episodes may vary in severity and can be triggered by allergens, stress, or environmental changes. From a general medical perspective, asthma arises from inflammation and narrowing of the airways that restrict airflow. Some patients experience worsening symptoms in hot weather, during respiratory infections, or after consuming spicy and greasy foods. They often report coughing with thick yellow phlegm, a feeling of heat in the chest, thirst, and restlessness. This presentation corresponds to the heat-wheezing syndrome in Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), where internal heat and phlegm obstruct the Lung, making it difficult for Qi to descend and causing laboured breathing.

From a TCM viewpoint, heat wheezing occurs when phlegm heat congests the Lung, leading to rebellion of Lung Qi. This may result from external invasion of wind heat or from internal accumulation of heat due to improper diet, emotional stress, or chronic illness. The heat causes body fluids to dry and condense into thick phlegm, which then blocks the airways. Patients often experience loud wheezing, shortness of breath, chest oppression, coughing of yellow and sticky sputum that is hard to expectorate, and sometimes fever or thirst. TCM treatment principles focus on clearing heat, resolving phlegm, diffusing the Lung, and stopping wheezing.

Commonly used herbal formulas include Ding Chuan Tang and Ma Xing Shi Gan Tang. For acupuncture therapy, points such as Chi Ze (LU5) and Nei Ting (ST44) help clear heat from the Lung and Stomach channels. Cupping on the upper back may assist in clearing phlegm heat and improving lung ventilation. 

It is advisable to avoid spicy, fried or oily foods that generate internal heat, and instead include cooling foods such as pear, lotus root and mung bean soup. Staying hydrated and maintaining a calm emotional state also help prevent heat accumulation. Gentle exercises like Tai Chi, Qi Gong, or breathing meditation can enhance Lung function and balance internal Qi.

How Common: ⚠️ Mostly known culturally; rarely enforced in modern households.

Gynostemma pentaphyllum (Jiaogulan) aka Southern Ginseng) = Stellar Adaptogen = helps us adapt to stress. 

Joe Hollis, of Mountain Gardens (NC), introduced me to this plant on May 1, 2023. I was honored to tour his gardens with him on that day. He passed away some months later.

Joe said that G. pentaphyllum (he liked to call it southern ginseng), was one of the most important Chinese medicinal plants he introduced (in 1990) to cultivation in the US. 

He extolled its virtues: "It has extraordinary health benefits: more ginsenosides (active components of ginseng) than any other plant, including ginseng itself.
In TCM, considered a qi tonic, entering lung channel. Lowers blood pressure & cholesterol, used for prevention & treatment of cancer & tumors, anti-aging. Also in demand by race-horse owners."

I planted it in my gardens (May, 2023). He had both sweet & bitter tasting plants (same species, labeled G. pentaphyllum, sweet and G. pentaphyllum, bitter); we planted both.

We've nibbled fresh leaves (1 a day) and I like the centered, full energy it brings on. It's not very aggressive in our wild gardens here in USDA zone 5b, and will def. keep my eye on this. 

It's just starting to establish (2 years later), and so I've been gingerly harvesting tender tips (to eat right on spot). I dried small amount for tea this winter.

More from Joe's site:
"An herbaceous, perennial vine, hardy to at least 0°. The slender stems bear 1-2″, 5-parted leaves, tendrils (Cucurbit: squash family), and tiny greenish flowers (male and female on separate plants). 

Of all the tonic/adaptogenic herbs, this is the easiest to grow and use: since it is the entire plant that is active, you can harvest the vine, there is no need to dig. Just make a cup of tea from the easily dried herb to enjoy its extraordinary health benefits.

text:
[Recipe] In TCM, Daikon radish has a cooling nature that balances the accumulated heat in the body, which is believed to be a root cause of indigestion symptoms like irritability, bad breath, and headaches. It can help to alleviate the discomfort from bloating and food stagnation in the central part of the body (中焦), and is also particularly useful for digesting fatty food or meat.

If you are suffering from indigestion, give this recipe a try!

The soup is naturally sweet from the use of daikon and very appetizing in my opinion!

Ingredients
1/2 a small to medium sized daikon / radish
3 seedless red dates
3 to 4 slices of ginger
Moderate amount of goji berries
800ml of water

1) Remove the skin from daikon. I usually peel off 3 layers of skin as the outer layers may be bitter. Chop the daikon into small and thin slices.

2) Add all the above ingredients, except goji berries, into a pot. Bring the water to a boil, then simmer under medium low heat for 20 minutes.

3) Add goji berries and cook for another minute.

Enjoy!

Are you currently prepping to take your first ever practical cybersecurity certification exam? Below are some pointers to help you come out on top. We're rooting for you over here!

Our certifications are currently 20% off all month long! Check them out here: https://www.tcm.rocks/certs-igs-2025 

Survival Strategy 1 - 𝗥𝗲𝗮𝗱 𝗔𝗟𝗟 𝗗𝗼𝗰𝘂𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀. Seriously, don’t skip a 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘨. The documents will give you everything you need to know: the rules of engagement, the tools involved, how often you can use those tools, and so on. Don’t take any shortcuts either; review everything so you don’t miss any critical details.

Survival Strategy 2 - 𝗨𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗬𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗧𝗼𝗼𝗹𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗧𝗲𝗰𝗵𝗻𝗶𝗾𝘂𝗲𝘀. Make sure you have a thorough knowledge of all the skills and tools you will need to utilize during your exam. If there’s anything you feel inadequate with, dedicate time to improving in that area. Practice is the only way to get better.

Survival Strategy 3 - 𝗦𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗘𝗮𝘀𝘆 𝗪𝗶𝗻𝘀 𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗬𝗼𝘂 𝗖𝗮𝗻. In practical exams, you usually have options for scoring “easy wins” - that is, lower-level vulnerabilities that are easier to exploit. Use these to collect points AND boost your confidence, so that when the bigger challenges present themselves, you’ll be ready.

Survival Strategy 4 - 𝗗𝗶𝗱 𝗪𝗲 𝗠𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗦𝘁𝘂𝗱𝘆 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗣𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗲? On top of study sessions, you’ll want to dedicate at least one session to simulating what the exam experience will be like. Do this by setting up a time-limited scenario meant to mimic the real thing. TryHackMe or HackTheBox can help out with this. Ideally, you’ll want to do this a few times.

Survival Strategy 5 - 𝗘𝘅𝗮𝗺𝘀 𝗔𝗿𝗲 𝗔𝗹𝘄𝗮𝘆𝘀 𝗘𝗮𝘀𝗶𝗲𝗿 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗱 𝗧𝗶𝗺𝗲. If you need to do a retake (which we offer for free with each cert exam purchase), don’t sweat it. In fact, view your first attempt as a “practice run,” and use it to get comfortable with the format. And when you retake it, you are much likelier to ace it having prior knowledge.

text:
Evening Hours of the TCM Organ Clock

As daylight fades, the body turns inward, shifting from activity to restoration.
In Traditional Chinese Medicine, the evening hours are guided by the Kidney, Pericardium, and San Jiao meridians. This period supports nourishment, emotional connection, and preparation for rest.

🕯 5–7 PM | Kidney
The Kidney governs Jing, essence, and vitality. This is a time to replenish what has been used throughout the day, both physically and energetically. Gentle movement, a warm meal, or a mineral-rich bath support this hour. Choose foods that nourish Yin and Blood, such as root vegetables, black sesame, or seaweed, and allow yourself to slow down and ground.

🌹 7–9 PM | Pericardium
The Pericardium protects the Heart and supports emotional connection. These hours favor intimacy, laughter, and warmth. Enjoy light conversation, tea, journaling, or a soothing ritual that opens the Heart and calms the spirit.

🌙 9–11 PM | San Jiao (Triple Burner)
The San Jiao regulates circulation and internal harmony. As the night deepens, this system redistributes warmth and prepares the body for sleep. Dim the lights, hydrate, and allow your nervous system to unwind.
Aim to be asleep by the end of this phase, around 10:30 or 11 PM, so the body can enter the Gallbladder and Liver hours in a state of true restoration.

text:
Inside a TCM hospital in China this August, I saw techniques most people wouldn’t believe. One of them was needle knife, a therapy between acupuncture and micro surgery.

It’s tiny, flat, and very sharp! I watched a woman walk in with one leg waaay shorter than the other, her gait was unbalanced and painful. After a couple of minutes she was standing upstraighter, walked evenly, and left with both legs aligned.

Another patient came in with severe carpal tunnel, barely able to move her hand without pain. After 5 mins she flexed her fingers, smiled ear to ear! and said she could finally feel relief for the first time in months.

And then there was the woman struggling to breathe, because of sm back tightness and pain. The treatment released the tension right away. You could see her shoulders drop and her chest finally expand.

Needle knife, or Dao needle therapy, was developed in the 1970s as a bridge between classical acupuncture and modern orthopedics. Only a few thousand doctors practice it, because precision and deep anatomical knowledge are everything.

The doctor I studied under trained first as a Western medicine surgeon. But after facing lots of health issues he could never resolve, he turned to Dao needle. That shift changed his life and career, and now he helps so many in a couple of minutes. Like he said to me “before it used to take me months to help, now I can do it within 60 seconds”.

Months later I’m still in awe. But one thing is certain: this is not a DIY technique. Don’t try this at home.

Why your tongue is the window to your overall health tongue 👅 

If you’ve worked with me 1:1, you know one of the first things I ask for is a photo of your tongue. When I ask for a picture of your tongue, it’s not just about what I see that day — it helps me track changes in your digestion and overall balance over time. It’s one of the simplest ways to see how your body is responding to the changes we’re making together.

In Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), the tongue reflects the health of your internal organs and digestion. The color, shape, and coating all offer clues about your energy, hydration, and how well your body is processing food and fluids.

One thing I often see is a white coating on the tongue.
In TCM, this can point to what’s called “dampness” — meaning your body might be holding on to excess fluid or struggling to fully digest and transform what you’re taking in.

You might notice symptoms like:
- Feeling heavy or bloated after eating
- Low energy or fatigue
- Sinus congestion or mucus buildup
- Loose stools or sluggish digestion

These are signs your system could use some support in moving and clearing things out.

Along with the tips in the video above, I recommend using a copper tongue scraper daily as a simple, quick habit that removes that coating (which can include bacteria, debris, and buildup from overnight) and gives your digestion a cleaner start each morning. Plus — it’s great for fresh breath. Along with that, eat more antioxidant/vitamin C rich foods, chew your food really well until mush, eat without distractions and include more bitter foods to your diet. 

*My client didn’t fully remove dairy or smoothies, she reduced them from her diet so if you fully remove you may see changes sooner. Even just reducing it made a huge difference though! It can take 3ish months for these inflammatory markers to rid your body so 3 months is my recommendation to start then slowly start adding in again if you like but you will likely see changes quite quickly if you fully remove them*

text:
Potassium is one of the most under-discussed minerals in maternal health. It’s not flashy, it’s not a high tech biohacking supplement but it is SO critical and it’s the reason so many mothers I work with are feeling burnt out and “stuck.”

Most critically, studies show us that almost all women fall short of the recommended intake (which is already far below ✨optimal✨ intake).

Then you have a baby and suddenly there’s no time to think about your nutrition or prep all the foods you need to eat. 

This is a crisis! This is why I am so passionate about teaching women, their partners and their villages how to nourish mother bodies through matrescence. I truly believe focusing here will fundamentally shift how our health is expressing across the collective. 

Every cell in your body has a Na/K pump. Without enough potassium, nutrients and hormones struggle to get into the cells and waste products struggle to get out. Our bowels slow. In TCM they call it “stagnation” and it’s a real mineral-driven physiological state. 

Pregnancy, birth, breastfeeding, and ongoing stress each draw heavily on potassium stores. Over time, this can leave mothers feeling fatigued, tense, and depleted even when bloodwork appears normal. It’s the number one pattern that comes back when a woman tells me “my doctor says my bloodwork is fine but I feel off.”

Your bloodwork IS fine! But all that good stuff circulating is not being delivered into the cells themselves. You aren’t medically sick, you are undernourished. You don’t need a doctor, you need a nutritionist!

Focus on whole food sources that naturally restore mineral balance. I am not a fan of potassium supplements for many reasons. Potatoes, dairy, avocado, coconut water, and leafy greens all make a meaningful difference when eaten consistently. Bananas get more credit than they deserve in this department lol.

The reason I love using tissue mineral analysis (HTMA) for postpartum women is this more nuanced testing helps reveal deeper cellular patterns. I’ve got a waitlist going and I am working through it. If you’d like some support this winter, please add yourself to that list.

Winters are harsh on our bodies, all organ systems but winters are especially hard on kidneys. With kidneys more cold also impacts the spleen, stomach, intestines and triple burner. 
In TCM, winter is considered a time for rest, conservation, and introspection, aligning with nature's tendency to go inward and store energy. It is associated with the 👉Water element and the Kidneys👈, which are seen as the body's storage for vital energy, or Jing. Harsh winters Cold is pathological for our organ systems.

2. More hot stews, broths and stocks instead of hot or cold caffeinated drinks

text:
For those who saw my stories, thank you for all the kind messages, advice and food deliveries. You guys really made my day.

Honestly, at first I thought the spots were from the TCM herbs I was taking for my leg injury. When I went to the doctor, I still insisted, “I don’t have fever lah.” He looked at me, took my temperature, 38 degrees. Then he said, “99.9% chickenpox.”

I was like… huh? At my age? I’ve been vaccinated what!

Had to cancel all my shows and media events. I was very down of course, because I’ve been so looking forward to work with such wonderful dancers, choreographer and managers and coordinators on an event. But I’m super grateful for their understanding and how they immediately told me to rest and recover.

Super sian, but maybe it’s God’s way of forcing me to rest and heal my leg properly. I didn’t listen earlier, now kena double combo rest.

For anyone above 40, please don’t think you confirm safe just because you took the vaccine long ago. Adults can still get it, though usually milder if you were vaccinated before. Mine not the big blisters kind thankfully, but still not fun. Head damn heavy, body weak and itchy.

Chickenpox spreads before the spots even show, so really don’t know who I caught it from. Doctor said usually two weeks after exposure then it comes out.

My family is okay. Andy and Yaya already had before and Fami is vaccinated. So no need to worry too much.

Lesson learned:

🐥Don’t ignore any weird rashes or fever, even mild ones

🐥Adults tend to have stronger symptoms, so rest well and stay home

🐥Don’t scratch (I already scratched one or two early ones and might get scar)

🐥Hydrate, sleep and keep clean

Trying to see this positively, at least now I’ve got the “chickenpox license” haha. Next time immune already.

And for anyone planning to see me soon, don’t worry lah, I’ll be fine in a week. Virus gone by then. Can still come my Christmas party, I promise won’t spread snowflakes of chickenpox 😂

Appreciate all the love and care from friends. You all made recovery easier.

text:
Asthma is a chronic respiratory condition characterised by repeated episodes of wheezing, breathlessness, chest tightness, and coughing. The severity and duration of attacks can vary, and they are often triggered by environmental factors such as allergens, cold air, or emotional stress. From a general medical point of view, asthma occurs due to airway inflammation and narrowing that make breathing difficult. Among the various presentations, some patients experience symptoms that worsen in cold weather or after exposure to cold air. These patients often report coughing with clear, thin phlegm, a sensation of cold in the chest, and difficulty breathing that improves with warmth. This pattern is commonly referred to as cold-wheezing syndrome in Traditional Chinese Medicine.

In TCM, cold wheezing syndrome is mainly caused by the invasion of wind-cold pathogens that obstruct the Lung’s ability to disperse and descend qi, leading to retention of cold-phlegm in the airways. When cold enters the body, it constricts the Lung and causes body fluids to accumulate, forming phlegm that blocks the qi movement and triggers wheezing. Typical symptoms include shortness of breath, coughing with thin white sputum, chest tightness, chills without sweating, and a preference for warmth. TCM treatment focuses on dispersing wind cold, warming the Lung, transforming phlegm, and calming wheezing.

Herbs such as Xiao Qing Long Tang or Ma Huang Tang are commonly prescribed by qualified practitioners for this pattern. Acupoints like Ding Chuan (EX-B1) and Fei Shu (BL13) can be stimulated to relieve wheezing and open the chest. For cold-related asthma, moxibustion therapy using gentle heat over the back or chest can warm the meridians and ease breathing. From a lifestyle perspective, it is important to keep warm, avoid cold air exposure, and limit intake of raw, cold, or dairy foods that promote phlegm formation. 

Warm soups with ginger or cinnamon can support Lung function and dispel internal cold. Gentle exercises like Tai Chi and Qi Gong help regulate breathing and strengthen the body.

Each autumn, families gather to pick the season’s olives. ☀️ The air smells of earth and fruit; baskets fill, presses hum in old stone tafones, and tables overflow with bread, wine, pa amb oli, and laughter under the November sun.

💛 Every bottle of Mallorcan olive oil is more than a condiment - it’s the story of generations: of terraces and fincas, of patient work and shared harvests.

When golden oil glints on your plate, you’re tasting Mallorca’s past and present at once.

Cold vs. Flu in TCM (quick guide)

In Chinese medicine, many colds come from “wind-cold” at the body’s surface, while flus are stronger, often linked to 戾气 (lì qì)—a virulent, epidemic-type pathogen. Our aim isn’t to crush the fever outright but to support the body’s response and “release the exterior.”

For wind-cold patterns (chills > fever, clear mucus, body aches), we use warming, acrid herbs like fresh ginger (生姜) and cinnamon twig (桂枝) to gently promote a light sweat—helping the pathogen vent through the pores so the heat settles naturally.

This is different from directly suppressing fever.

Notes: If signs point to wind-heat (sore throat, yellow mucus, thirst) or if you’re depleted/dehydrated, warming and sweating aren’t suitable—please see a TCM practitioner for a personalized plan. Seek urgent care for persistent high fever, chest pain, or breathing difficulty.

post_owner.name: inner code cycle synced teas
text:
If you always feel tired or groggy after your period — you need this cozy Asian seafood stew.
It helps you rebuild blood and minerals, so you feel nourished again at the start of your new cycle 🥣

Because your period isn’t just the end of something — it’s your body’s reset.
And what you eat after it ends sets the tone for your next cycle.

✨ Ingredients:
1/4 cup mixed grain rice
2 cups miso dashi broth
1 small potatoes, chopped
½ onion, sliced
A handful of bok choy
A handful of dried seaweed (wakame)
A few shrimp, oysters, and clams (fresh or frozen)
1 tsp tamari
1 tsp brown rice vinegar
1 tsp mirin
White pepper powder, s&p
Sesame seeds + chopped green onions to garnish

🫕 Instructions:

1. Cook your multigrain rice and set aside.
2. In a pot, bring miso dashi broth to a gentle boil.
3. Add potatoes and onions — cook until soft.
4. Add bok choy, seaweed, and your seafood mix.
5. Add your seasonings.
6 Simmer for 8–10 minutes, then top with toasted sesame seeds and green onions.
7. Serve with your rice and let your body recharge.

This isn’t just a stew — it’s a rebuild ritual for the days after your period, when your body needs nourishment the most.

text:
Every vitamin, mineral, and amino acid absorbed through your digestive tract is more than biochemistry — it’s the raw material for your Blood and Qi

In Western physiology, the small intestine meticulously extracts nutrients:
🌀The duodenum takes in minerals like iron, magnesium, and calcium — essential for hemoglobin and enzyme activation
🌀 The jejunum absorbs amino acids, lipids, and most vitamins — the building blocks for proteins, hormones, and cellular energy
🌀 The ileum finishes the job, reclaiming B12 and bile acids — key for red blood cell formation and fat metabolism
🌀 Finally, the large intestine reabsorbs water and electrolytes while beneficial bacteria produce vitamin K and biotin, closing the nutrient cycle

From a TCM perspective, this whole process is the dance between Spleen Qi and Stomach Fire — the alchemical forge where food transforms into Gu Qi (nutrient essence) which becomes Blood

When digestion is weak — due to overthinking, irregular eating, cold/raw foods, or excessive stress — this transformation falters. Nutrients may be present, but the body fails to extract and convert them efficiently. 

This is the root of Blood Deficiency in Chinese Medicine:
✨ Pale lips and complexion
✨ Dizziness or fatigue
✨ Dry skin, hair, and nails
✨ Insomnia or vivid dreams
✨ Scant or delayed menstruation

The modern translation? Malabsorption, low iron, poor protein synthesis, or chronic stress diverting digestive energy

To nourish Blood, both medicine systems agree:
✔️ Support digestion with warmth, rest, and mindful meals
✔️ Strengthen the Spleen with cooked, grounding foods (millet, rice, beets, dates)
✔️ Restore the microbiome — your “Earth element” allies
✔️ Breathe deeply; oxygen is the yang partner to Blood’s yin

You don’t just digest food — you transform life into vitality

post_owner.name: The Broad Place
text:
When I was very young my brother was born severely disabled, and wasn’t supposed to survive. It torpedoed our family into a cycle of emergency ward visits, pediatric wards for weeks and months, brutal operations including his skull being sawn in two. A few weeks after he was born I had my first asthma attack and was also endlessly in hospital, collapsed lungs, pneumonias and bronchitis - the lungs are the grief centre and this all makes sense to me after working extensively with TCM doctors, acupuncturists, Ayurvedic doctors and healers over the years. A different hospital across the city from my brothers specialist hospital. I don’t know how my parents survived. Hospitals for me were about rigidity, patterns, and safety. The nurses in squeaky shoes seemed to know what was going on, stern doctors also - as long as I was there everything was under control. So I learned that control = safety which also hinged on my survival. Understanding this more about why I have such a deep seated need for control, a fervor for my little plans, a suffocating need to know what’s happening, has bought about an incredible sense of compassion towards my self. None of us that are anxious and controlling became that way through our own personal design, but through conditioning, through circumstance. 
And I want freedom, like I’m sure you do. But we can’t have freedom AND control. We can’t have grace and surrender AND our little plans adhered to always. And life will often give us multiple crossroads where we get to see all of it for what it is. And they’re often on our knees dark night of the soul moments, that shake us from a daze. And in hindsight we will be grateful but we can also be humbled and grateful immediately. We can use these moments to start to move more clearly, and boldly in the direction of what our soul wants. Which is always freedom, expansion, and love. 

What are your thoughts? ❤️

This ancient method of making tea resin was a lost art until very recently. These 4 acupressure points DU 24, Yin Tang, DU 26, and CV 24 are known in Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) for their powerful effect on calming the nervous system, releasing stress, and clearing mental fog.

Located between the upper lip and the nose, this point helps revive alertness, improve focus, and relieve mental fatigue. It’s often used to bring clarity during emotional or physical exhaustion making it perfect for when you feel drained or overwhelmed.

✨ 4️⃣ CV 24 (Chengjiang)
This point lies in the groove between your lower lip and chin. It helps release tension around the jaw and mouth, harmonizes emotional energy, and can even improve speech flow and facial relaxation.

Use your fingertips to gently massage each point for 30–60 seconds, applying steady pressure. Combine this with slow, mindful breathing inhale calm, exhale tension.

post_owner.name: My Mum's Flavour
text:
[Recipe] If it’s turning colder where you are, this healthy and warming apple ginger tea will definitely be a lovely treat for you!

In TCM, a hot apple drink, especially when made with warming herbs like ginger, can strengthen the lungs, spleen and stomach, aiding digestion and helping to relieve dryness and coughs.

In this recipe, I included fresh lemon juice, which further enhances the health benefits of this beverage. According to Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), the combination of lemon juice and ginger creates a balanced remedy that targets several bodily systems, particularly digestive health and immunity. The two ingredients work synergistically: the warming, pungent nature of ginger complements the cooling, sour properties of lemon to restore harmony and balance to the body.

Without further ado, check out the recipe -

Ingredients
1 medium sized apple
6 to 8 slices of ginger
5 to 6 jujube / red dates
Juice from half a lemon (can adjust based on preference)
1000ml of water
Pure or Raw honey (optional)

1) Add all the ingredients, except lemon juice, into a health pot. Cook using “Tea” function.

2) After the cooking is done, wait till the beverage cools down to between 60 to 70 before adding fresh lemon juice. The health pot I used will indicate the temperature on its monitor.

3) Add honey if desired.

4) If you do not have a health pot, add the ingredients into a regular pot. Bring the water to a boil, then simmer for 15 minutes. Wait till the temperature cools down (when the beverage is warm, not hot) before adding lemon juice and honey.

Enjoy!

It was the deadliest act of airline sabotage to date, and marked a major turning point for courtroom media access, forensic science, and air travel safety.

text:
Gout occurs when urate crystals build up in the joints, causing sudden pain, swelling, and inflammation.

These crystals form when there are high levels of uric acid in the blood — a substance produced when the body breaks down purines, which are found in the body and in foods like red meat, organ meats, and certain seafood (e.g. sardines, mussels, tuna). Alcohol (especially beer) and fructose-sweetened drinks can also raise uric acid levels. Normally, uric acid is filtered by the kidneys and excreted in urine. But if too much is produced or too little is excreted, it accumulates and forms sharp crystals in the joints, triggering a gout attack.

In Traditional Chinese Medicine, gout is seen as more than just a buildup of uric acid — it reflects a deeper imbalance in the body’s internal systems. Gout is classified under “Bi Syndrome” (痹症), which means “obstruction syndrome.” This occurs when external factors such as Wind, Damp, Cold, or Heat invade the joints and block the normal flow of Qi and Blood. At the same time, internal weaknesses such as Spleen deficiency, Liver Qi stagnation, or Kidney deficiency make the body more susceptible to these external influences. 

A weak Spleen fails to properly transform and transport fluids, leading to the accumulation of dampness. text:
Wow — what a tremendous life. Such a tender loss for me. Yesterday, my Grandma, Maria Riva, peacefully departed this world at 100 while watching Fred Astaire in Top Hat. 

After my dad passed, my friendship with my grandmother deepened in such a special way. What a luxury it was to have her when I needed a bit of “Dad wisdom,” or simply someone to bounce ideas off of — whether it was about work or just to quickly ask how much kirsch to add to the fondue.

I will miss our conversations, phonecalls, postcards — some of the best I ever received — alive with her wit, honesty, and experience until the end. I’ll absolutely miss her direct and fearless critique of my work. Boy, she would never let anything slide. And flat out tell me if she didn’t like something.  And I can’t thank her enough for it.

What an incredible educator and mentor she was — a living, breathing Rosetta Stone of history and heart. Each moment with her mattered. Yet our time never felt fleeting. We could sit for hours — sometimes in silence — perfectly content watching TCM. There was never any need to fill the air. Beneath everything was a profound mutual respect that made small talk unnecessary. 

But at her age she was ready— something she and I spoke about from time to time. It weighed on her that so many of the people, pets, and loved ones she’d grown up with were gone. Though hard to hear, I understood and respected it. And I think that helped her maintain a sense of humor about it, at least with me. She used to tell me that once she passed, she’d let me know soon after if she was at peace… by “haunting” me in some loving yet comical way. I’d always laugh and say, “Yeah, great. Can’t wait.

Early this morning, a ridiculous amount of crows, a MURDER of crows, if you will, descend into my backyard, straight out of Hitchcock’s frame. Loud, chaotic, and strangely purposeful, out of nowhere. They stayed for a good half hour, tormenting the quiet morning. I woke up disheveled but smiling. I grabbed my phone and documented the tail end of it.  Another gift. I’m comforted she’s united with my Dad and the rest of the lot. A century of stories, strength, love and butter. What a legacy. Love you.

post_owner.name: Sophie Duncan | Skin Radiance in Motherhood
text:
I used to rely on my morning caffeine hit to wake up… until I noticed what it was doing to my skin.

I switched from coffee to matcha, but drinking it daily started to feel depleting and drying. While matcha is trendy, in Ayurveda and TCM it’s cooling and stimulating ~ which can aggravate vata, the dosha most mothers unknowingly imbalance through “one-size-fits-all” wellness trends.

Letting go of daily coffee/ matcha has helped me feel more plump, radiant and grounded. These days, I consume a little caffeine mostly as chai ~ warmer, gentler and more skin friendly for my constitution.

Ayurveda isn’t about rules or perfection. It’s about understanding the qualities of what we consume so we can make choices that truly support our unique beauty.

Here’s what Ayurveda has taught me about caffeine and a mother’s skin:

☕ Caffeine is drying, heating, and stimulating. For many mothers ~ whose nervous systems are already wired ~ that daily hit can tip the balance.

High vata can push pitta to rise, burning through the fluids that keep us youthful, which may lead to dryness, hair fall or premature greying.

If you’re feeling dry, depleted, anxious or prematurely aged, easing up (or taking a break) can be incredibly supportive.

Here’s how I enjoy caffeine in a more skin-loving way:

✓ With a touch of ghee & fresh almond or cow’s milk (not carton)

✓ Half chai, half rooibos ~ warming and comforting, with 50% less stimulation

✓ 1- 2 hrs after food ~ never on an empty stomach

✓ With a pinch of cardamom, nutmeg or @oneelevenhealth Bliss to soften stimulation

✓ Regular breaks to avoid dependence

✓ Cultivating more sattva in motherhood ~ peace and balance ~ so caffeine feels less necessary

So, beauties, do you drink caffeine? Have you noticed its effect on your skin?

post_owner.name: Elizabeth Marundé // Holistic Homesteading
text:
Save this post if you’re nursing or send to your nursing friend. 🤱🏻

Unlike white sesame seeds (which are typically hulled and milder), black sesame seeds retain their outer coating, making them richer in antioxidants, calcium, fiber, calcium, and iron. Black sesame seeds are valued in Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) for their restorative properties, especially in postpartum care. 

Foods like sesame seeds that offer concentrated nutrition in small amounts can help support your overall energy and milk production.

What you’ll need:
• 1 cup raw cashews
• 1 cup medjool dates (pitted)
• 13.5 oz can full-fat coconut milk 
• 2 teaspoons vanilla extract 
• ¼ cup maple syrup
• ½ cup black tahini
• 2 pinches salt

What you’ll do:
• Add raw cashews to a bowl and cover with 2 cups of hot water and let soak for at least 30 minutes.
• Drain the soaked cashews, then add to a high-speed blender along with the (room temperature, pitted) dates, coconut milk, vanilla extract, maple syrup, black tahini, and salt. Blend until everything is fully incorporated.
• No-churn method: Pour into a freezer-safe container and freeze to enjoy the next day.

🌅 Morning Boost: Yellow Ginger Wine Offal Soup 🌅

· The "Yang" Boost: In Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), this soup is considered highly "yang" – meaning it is warming and energizing. The ginger and wine are "hot" ingredients that are believed to dispel cold, dampness, and wind from the body.
· Metabolic Kickstart: The combination of protein from the offal and the warming effect of ginger can raise your metabolic rate and core body temperature, which can be very invigorating on a cold morning and help you feel more alert.

This traditional soup isn't your average breakfast! 

But it packed with lots of great benefits:
🔥Warms the Body - Ginger & wine kickstart circulation.
💪Powerhouse of Nutrients - Offal is loaded with Iron & B12.
🍳Protein-Packed - Keeps you full & fueled all morning.
🤢Settles Your Stomach - Ginger aids digestion.

· Offal is a Nutritional Powerhouse: Organ meats are some of the most concentrated sources of vitamins and minerals.
 · Iron (Heme Iron): Liver is incredibly rich in heme iron, which is easily absorbed by the body. This is excellent for preventing and treating iron-deficiency anemia, which can cause fatigue.
 · Vitamin B12: Crucial for nerve function and red blood cell formation. Offal is one of the best sources.
 · Vitamin A (Retinol): Essential for vision, immune function, and skin health (primarily from liver).
 · Zinc and Selenium: Important for immune support and thyroid function.

Heads up: It's rich in cholesterol & contains alcohol, so it's not for everyone! A powerful, traditional meal best enjoyed wisely.

You should avoid it or consume it very sparingly if you:

· Have high cholesterol, heart disease, or gout.
· Are pregnant or breastfeeding (due to alcohol and Vitamin A risk).
· Have kidney or liver conditions.
· Need to be sharp and alert for mental tasks (due to the alcohol).
· Simply have a sensitive stomach.

Some of the Asteraceae like to flower late in the year, a habit that is good for the bees and the herbalist in us. Bo-ju-hua (Chrysanthemum morifolium) is one of them. Even a handful of flowers, slowly dried indoors, can bring great comfort should cold weather dampen the spirit. The flower blossoms once on the bush, and once again in the teacup. 
We do get consistent raves about our potted ju-hua--it seems to perform well for everyone--a robust plant with a delicate flower--may we all be like that. 
(Link in profile)

The photos show how it appears right now. Here's a bit more info.

Bo-ju-hua (Chrysanthemum morifolium)
Family: Aster (Asteraceae)
Hardy to Zones 6 to 10
(Autumn Chrysanthemum, Bo-ju-hua) Evergreen subshrub native to China, an ancient cultigen that cannot be propagated by seed. This is a choice cultivar, flowering to 3 feet tall and equally as wide, with single-petaled flowers of cream, between 1 and 2 inches in size. Main harvest occurs around Halloween (Oct 31). This cultivar flowers earlier than Gong-ju-hua. Taste sweet, considered to be a superior flower for making Chrysanthemum tea. Traditional uses (TCM): one of the Chinese herbs that releases the exterior, used in treating common cold, flu, fever and heatstroke; high blood pressure, heart pain, atherosclerosis; dizziness, hearing loss, tinnitus, headache and migraine; red and swollen eyes, blurry vision; liver inflammation and toxicity; infections including staphylococcus, streptococcus and blood spirochetes. Plant prefers sun and well-drained garden soil, frequent watering. Space plants 2 feet apart.

text:
📍 Comment DIGEST and I will send you the links to my Liver Recharge and Spleen Rescue+. These two tinctures to combat each side of the coin of the body and mind, helping you stay mentally sound and digest well.

In TCM, the Spleen and Stomach are the center of digestion, but they are also deeply affected by our emotional world. Worry, rumination, and mental overactivity weaken the Spleen, making it harder to break down food, absorb nutrients, and create energy and Blood.

On the other hand, the Liver— the organ that keeps Qi flowing smoothly— reacts to stress, frustration, irritability, and emotional stagnation. When the Liver is tight, it attacks the Stomach and Spleen, leading to bloating, nausea, cravings, fatigue, or digestive upset.

Absolutely what you eat matters, but how you feel when you eat matters just as much.

How can we nourish our mind and our digestion?

- Take your meals seriously: meals are important times of the day and food should not be mixed with work, reading, or watching television. 
- Avoid snacking/ overeating: overeating results in an overworked Spleen and food stagnation. The digestion does not have sufficient time to empty the Stomach before your next meal, causing you to feel bloated and fatigued.
- Don't speak or think negatively while eating: engaging in gossip or negative talk sours your mind and your food. Notice if you are upset it's hard to eat?
- Chew well!: Chewing your food thoroughly reduces the workload for your digestive system and food gets absorbed more easily. This also allows a longer time for your meals, letting you realize the feeling of fullness and prevent overeating.
- Avoid cold or chilled beverages: too much "cold" lowers the digestive temperature and the body needs to use more Qi to warm it up before it gets digested.

post_owner.name: The Eastern Philosophy
text:
The tiniest pills in traditional Chinese medicine, this is a 40+ year old vessel 🌿 Liuying Wan (六应丸) is a discreet powerhouse of classical Chinese herbal medicine—long revered for its effectiveness in treating tonsillitis, sore throats, and early-stage glandular swellings. Often prescribed for “clearing heat” in the throat and lymphatic regions, the formula works by rapidly reducing inflammation.

What makes Liuying Wan especially striking is its size. Traditionally, these were packaged in thumb-sized glass vials—barely larger than a fingertip—containing dozens of tiny, pearl-like pills, each no bigger than a grain of millet. But the size is not incidental. In fact, it reflects a key tenet of Chinese medical formulation: potency through precision.

The micro-dosage allows for several things:
➤ Sublingual or buccal absorption, targeting the upper respiratory and throat tissues directly
➤ Ease of titration, enabling practitioners to scale doses according to the patient’s constitution and stage of illness
➤ Minimal digestive burden, making it especially suitable for children or those with GI issues.

Historically, these miniature forms were also easier to preserve and transport, often carried in silk pouches or scholar’s kits. Each tiny sphere was hand-rolled, then covered with medicinal glazes or plant resins to preserve freshness. Many of the Chinese medicine formulas we carry continue to use traditional tiny pills, known as “tea pills,” which are easier than tablets or pills to dissolve in the stomach and digest.

This artifact is a testament that in traditional Chinese medicine, efficacy doesn’t always come in large doses. Sometimes, it’s the smallest pills that carry the most refined thought ☯️

From the collection of Chinese medicine practitioner <redacted_mention>, who gifted us his beautiful collection of 1980s Chinese medicine 🙏🏻

Rehmannia (Sheng-di-huang) (Rehmannia glutinosa)

Family: Figwort (Scrophulariaceae)

Hardy to Zones 7 to 10

(Chinese Foxglove, Lit. "Cooked Earth Yellow") Herbaceous perennial native to China. Honored by a 400 year history of cultivation, the plant is quite showy, with foxglove-like (no digitalis alkaloids, though) flaring, dark red flowers on a short, wide plant. The leaves are also showy and tend toward red. The root is rubbery, orange, and covered with propagative buds. Rehmannia is extremely rare in the US. We are delighted to again have this important Chinese herb available for serious growers. Traditional uses (TCM): processed root replenishes vitality, strengthen liver and kidney, also heart, treating diabetes, constipation, anemia, urinary tract problems, dizziness and menstrual woes. Plant prefers sun and very fast-draining soil. A very good choice for potted culture, the plant tends to do better in pots than anywhere else. Traditionally grown on well-drained terraces and sometimes found growing on old, crumbling walls. Space 1 to 2 feet apart.

text:
Your Kitchen Pharmacy for Coughs

In Chinese Medicine we often say the kitchen is your first pharmacy. When it comes to coughs, some of the most powerful allies are simple everyday foods.

🍐 Pears (Yin nourishing)
Pears are cooling and Yin nourishing in Chinese Medicine. They help moisten dryness, making them perfect for dry coughs, sore throat and even constipation. Modern research also shows pears contain polyphenols with anti inflammatory and antioxidant properties that can support upper respiratory health. Kiwi fruits and Papaya are another pantry staple for coughs! 

🌱 Spring Onion (Cong Bai)
This humble kitchen staple is a traditional remedy for the early stages of colds. In TCM, cong bai helps release the exterior. It promotes a light sweat, clears phlegm and can ease nasal congestion. Studies highlight that spring onions have antimicrobial compounds such as allicin, which may help fight respiratory infections.

🧣 Protect Your Neck
One of the simplest yet most overlooked practices in Chinese Medicine is wearing a scarf on windy days. Wind is seen as an invasive pathogen that can trigger coughs, colds, stiff necks and chills. Exposure to sudden cold and wind can impair mucosal immunity, making us more vulnerable to viral infections.

✨ Takeaway
Before reaching for pharmacy shelves, look to your kitchen pharmacy and simple rituals. These everyday practices, rooted in ancient wisdom help strengthen your body’s natural defences.

text:
"先天之本在腎，後天之本在脾" translates as "The foundation of congenital vitality lies in the Kidneys, while the foundation of postnatal vitality lies in the Spleen." This concept reflects the importance of both the Kidneys and Spleen in overall health and vitality. The Spleen is understood quite differently in TCM and Western medicine: Traditional Chinese Medicine views the Spleen as a vital organ in overall health, encompassing digestion, energy and mental clarity, while Western medicine focuses on its role in blood filtration and immune function.

1. Kidneys and Congenital Vitality (先天之本在腎):
The Kidneys are considered the source of "Essence" (精, Jing), which is fundamental for growth, development, and reproduction. This Essence is inherited from one's parents and forms the basis of a person's congenital vitality or constitution. The Kidneys are thought to store the Essence, which influences one's overall health, longevity, and physical and mental development throughout life. This congenital vitality is crucial for the body's ability to resist diseases and maintain its functions.

2. Spleen and Postnatal Vitality (後天之本在脾):
After birth, the Spleen plays a vital role in the transformation and transportation of food and drink into Qi (energy) and Blood. This process is essential for maintaining postnatal vitality. The Spleen is responsible for the digestion and absorption of nutrients, which are then used to produce Qi and Blood. This postnatal vitality supports the body's daily functions and overall health. A well-functioning Spleen ensures that the body has adequate energy and nourishment to sustain health and vitality after birth.

In summary, the Kidneys are crucial for the foundational, inherited aspect of vitality, while the Spleen is key to maintaining health through the postnatal process of digestion and nourishment. Both organs are integral to maintaining a balanced and healthy life, with the Kidneys supporting long-term health through congenital Essence, and the Spleen managing daily vitality and energy through postnatal nourishment.💕

post_owner.name: My Mum's Flavour
text:
[Recipe] If you have cravings for milk tea like I do, go for this much healthier version! Personally, I think it tastes  better than what you can get at milk tea stores, without the use of white sugar or sugar syrup. This Chinese Style milk tea is sweetened with healthy ingredients like red dates, longan and Chinese Brown Sugar, which are regarded as super food in Traditional Chinese Medicine. 

Without further ado, this is the recipe -

Ingredients
4 large red dates (with seeds removed)
6 dried longans
1 tsp of goji berries
10 pieces of dried rose buds
8g of Chinese Brown Sugar
200ml of water
300ml of hot milk (can replace with plant based milk if preferred)

1) Add red dates, longans, Chinese Brown Sugar and water into a health pot. Cook using “Tea” Function.

2) Add hot milk, goji berries and rose into the health pot when the boiling is almost done (the health pot I used will give a 5 minutes countdown before the cooking stops). Then cover and let the ingredients steep inside the pot for 10 minutes or till ready to drink.

3) If you do not have a health pot, add the ingredients in point 1 into a regular pot. Bring the liquid to a boil, then simmer for about 10 minutes.

After 10 minutes, add the rest of the ingredients in point 2. Bring the milk to a light boil, then off the heat. Cover and steep the ingredients for a few minutes before drinking.

Enjoy!

text:
Recently, I received acupuncture therapy from Dr. Shrilaxmi at @srivasahealthcare__udupi , Parkala, Udupi, for stress management. Honestly, after the first session, I felt a positive impact — my stress was relieved, I felt calm, and I slept peacefully without any disturbance. I’m sharing this post in case you’d like to explore & learn this traditional practice yourself.
⸻
🌿 What is Acupuncture Therapy?

Acupuncture involves the insertion of very thin, sterile needles into specific points on the body called acupoints.According to traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), these points lie along pathways called meridians, through which life energy or “Qi” (Chi) flows.The idea is that when Qi becomes blocked or unbalanced, illness can result — and acupuncture helps restore balance and flow.

In modern medical terms, acupuncture is thought to work by:
	•	Stimulating nerves, muscles, and connective tissue
	•	Boosting the body’s natural painkillers (endorphins)
	•	Improving blood circulation and reducing inflammation

🪡 How is Acupuncture Done?
	1.	Assessment:
The acupuncturist asks about your symptoms, lifestyle, and health history.
	2.	Point Selection:
Based on the diagnosis, specific acupoints are chosen.
	3.	Needle Insertion:
Ultra thin, high density metal needles which are next to hair size and wont leave any marks on the skin.
	•	Depth varies (a few millimeters to 1–2 cm).
	•	You may feel mild tingling, warmth, or pressure — not sharp pain.
	4.	Retention:
Needles are left in place for 15–30 minutes.
	5.	Removal:
Needles are carefully removed, and you can resume normal activities afterward.

Sometimes mild electrical stimulation (electro-acupuncture) or heat therapy (moxibustion) is added for better results.

💪 Benefits of Acupuncture

	•	Chronic back or neck pain
	•	Osteoarthritis, knee pain
	•	Migraine and tension headaches
	•	Shoulder, elbow, or wrist pain
	•	Sciatica, fibromyalgia
	•	Anxiety, depression
 . Diabetes, hypertension, thyroid problems 

⚕️ Who Performs It

Always see a licensed acupuncturist or medical doctor trained in acupuncture. Proper hygiene and sterile needles are essential to avoid infections or injury.

We live in a world that praises logic and dismisses intuition. That medicates symptoms before asking where they came from. That treats the body like a machine instead of a memory bank of everything we’ve lived through.

Modern medicine is exceptional in many ways, acute trauma care, surgical interventions, life-saving diagnostics. But when it comes to understanding the human experience, it’s systemically disconnected. 

Disconnected from the wisdom of the body, the cycles of nature, and the emotional and energetic roots of disease.

Western science separated the body from the soul. It mapped the organs, measured the hormones, and learned how to manipulate the biochemistry. 

But it forgot to ask why the liver holds anger, or why thyroid disorders are overwhelmingly common in women who’ve spent a lifetime swallowing their voices.

Meanwhile, traditional healing systems like Ayurveda, Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), and Indigenous practices never made that separation. 

They didn’t view your organs as isolated mechanical parts, but as dynamic expressions of your emotional, spiritual, and energetic reality.

Ayurveda teaches that trauma can live in your tissues. That digestion isn’t just about food, but also about how well you “digest” your life, your relationships, your boundaries, your stress. 

TCM teaches that unresolved grief will weaken the lungs, that repressed anger will stagnate the liver, and that fear will deplete the kidneys, affecting your entire hormonal axis. 

Indigenous medicine, in all its global expressions, holds a sacred understanding that healing is not about eliminating symptoms, it’s about restoring wholeness.

But we don’t live in that world anymore. We live in a world of blue-lit screens, 10-minute GP appointments, rushed prescriptions, and emotional bypassing. 

We cannot separate the physical from the emotional. The energetic from the biological. The past from the present. To do so is to miss the entire point of healing.

When your body feels tired, pale, dizzy, or “running on empty,” it may be a sign of blood deficiency. 

In TCM, we don’t “add blood”—we support the five organs so your body can build Qi & Blood by itself.

Today’s practice focuses on Spleen 9 (Yinlingquan) because the Spleen & Stomach are the source of Qi and Blood（气血生化之源）. 

Gently pressing and kneading this point can help ease stagnation, improve flow, and leave you feeling steadier and more nourished.

How to try it:

• Find SP9: slide your thumb up the inner shin to the soft hollow near the knee.

• Press/kn ead 1–2 min each side, breathe slowly.

• Do it daily for 7 days. If it was sore at first and becomes less sore, that’s a good sign—flow is improving.

Be kind to yourself—small, gentle steps count.

Please know that If you’re pregnant, have a medical condition, or feel sharp pain/skin irritation, please check with a professional before acupressure.🥰🙏

How to Make Dried Ginger at Home | Easy TCM Method for Soups & Teas

Did you know the best dried ginger comes from older ginger? 🫚 In this video, I’ll show you exactly how to make your own dried ginger and ginger peel at home — the way I prepare it for soups, teas, and herbal tonics.

You’ll learn how to:
1️⃣ Choose the right type of ginger (older, shriveled, more pungent)
2️⃣ Peel ginger easily with a spoon — the cleanest, safest method
3️⃣ Slice ginger thinly for faster air-drying
4️⃣ Dry it naturally for 2–3 days at room temperature
5️⃣ Store your homemade dried ginger properly for long-term use

🌿 Why it matters:
Old ginger is stronger, hotter, and more aromatic — like dense wood that burns longer. Fresh ginger is warm and dispersing, while dried ginger is hot, deep, and restorative — perfect for warming the middle burner, improving digestion, and soothing cold-type conditions in Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM).

✨ Ingredients & Tools
Old ginger root (mature rhizome)
Small spoon for peeling
Knife or mandolin
Paper towel or drying rack

Store your finished slices in a dry, airtight container. Use them in soups, teas, or herbal blends anytime you need that deep, warming energy.

Early Afternoon Hours of the TCM Organ Clock

The early afternoon marks a shift in the body’s rhythm, moving from outward activity toward nourishment and integration. In Traditional Chinese Medicine, these hours are guided by the Heart, Small Intestine, and Bladder meridians.

❤️ 11 AM – 1 PM | Heart
The Heart governs circulation, joy, and connection. This is an ideal time to share a meal or conversation, enjoy warmth and laughter, and engage the senses. Light, colorful foods like fresh fruit or tea support the Heart’s vitality.

🍵 1 – 3 PM | Small Intestine
The Small Intestine separates the pure from the impure, both physically and emotionally. It is a time for discernment, to process what you have taken in and determine what to keep or release. Support digestion and focus with herbal tea, gentle movement, or a nutrient-rich lunch. Tasks that require clarity and organization, such as replying to emails, tidying your workspace, or planning the rest of the day, fit the energy of this hour.

💧 3 – 5 PM | Bladder
The Bladder governs fluid metabolism and release. Movement and hydration help this system flow, so take time to stretch, walk, or drink mineral-rich water. Journaling or spending time outdoors supports reflection and replenishment before the evening hours.

Many women don’t realize that an incomplete abortion can sometimes lead to infertility. In my 20s I had an abortion to escape an abusive partner. I never went for the follow-up scan to make sure my uterus was clear because I wasn’t educated about the risks back then. I buried myself in work and didn’t take care of my body.

After a miscarriage, birth, or abortion, any tissue left in the uterus can cause inflammation, infection, and scarring - leading to a thin or damaged uterine lining. Even if your hormones and ovulation are normal, a scarred uterus can’t support embryo implantation. It’s like trying to plant seeds on cement instead of soil.

I’m sharing my story because no one told me. Go for your follow-up 7–14 days after. Do the ultrasound, hysteroscopy, or saline sonogram to make sure your uterus is clear. If anything remains, it can usually be treated easily with medication or a minor procedure. By the time I found out it was years later and the scarring was too severe to reverse.

post_owner.name: Dynasty Harmon
text:
In Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), the body & emotions are deeply interconnected. Each major organ is linked to a specific emotion & when that emotion is suppressed or out of balance, the body often speaks through physical symptoms.

The lungs are associated with grief & sadness. Unprocessed emotions from heartbreak, loss, or long-standing disappointment tend to settle here. This may manifest as shallow breathing, a chronic cough, asthma, or even skin issues, as the lungs also govern the skin in TCM. People who have experienced deep loss often report respiratory problems shortly after, like bronchitis. That’s grief, showing up through the breath.

The heart holds the Shen (the spirit) & is connected to joy. Not joy as excitement, but a deeper sense of inner peace. When the heart is out of balance, symptoms like insomnia, anxiety, palpitations, or even inappropriate laughter can arise. A person who’s mentally overwhelmed & unable to sleep may not just be stressed their heart energy could be disturbed from emotional overload.

The liver governs the smooth flow of qi, blood & emotion. It’s most closely tied to anger & frustration. When emotions get stuck, liver qi stagnates, showing up as PMS, headaches (especially behind the eyes), muscle tension, or sudden mood swings. Suppressed emotions can build silently, until they erupt in what feels like uncontrollable rage.

The spleen & stomach are related to worry and overthinking. These organs help digest both food & thoughts. Excessive mental activity weakens them, leading to fatigue, bloating, poor appetite & brain fog. People who are always planning, analyzing, or stuck in their heads may find themselves drained, craving sweets, or struggling with digestion.

Finally, the kidneys are linked to fear and survival instincts. They store our deepest energy reserves. When depleted, we may feel exhausted, experience lower back pain, hair loss, or fearfulness. Long-term stress can burn out this “battery” leaving us feeling unsafe or deeply fatigued.

So when the body hurts, it may be saying what the heart cannot. In TCM, symptoms aren’t mistakes, they’re messages. We just have to learn how to listen.

#holistic #health

Negative self-talk has been linked to a variety of negative consequences, including increased stress, anxiety, depression, decreased self-esteem and impaired cognitive performance.

A study published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology found that participants who engaged in negative self-talk during a stress-inducing task had higher cortisol levels (a hormone associated with stress) than participants who engaged in positive self-talk. Study published in the Journal of Cognitive Psychotherapy found that negative self-talk was significantly related to symptoms of anxiety and depression. A study published in the Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology found that negative self-talk was correlated with decreased self-esteem and a study published in the Journal of Applied Sport Psychology found that negative self-talk was associated with decreased cognitive performance.

⚖️ How to help stress hormones with TCM? Comment BALANCE and I will send you the best herbs to help support this.

- Support the Liver Qi: Practice daily movement like tai chi, qigong, or gentle yoga to keep energy flowing smoothly. Stretch the body as the Liver governs the tendons. Energy can get stuck and cause emotional stagnation, too.
- Honor Kidney Yin & Yang: Go to bed before 10 PM to preserve Jing (essence) and prevent adrenal (Kidney) depletion and allow the Liver to detox.
- Strengthen the Spleen & Stomach: Eat warm, cooked meals at regular times; avoid cold/raw foods and excessive sugar.
- Flow with nature: Align activities with the seasons (e.g., conserve energy in the Fall and Winter and move more in Spring).
- Acupressure: Stimulate points like LV3 (Liver 3), LI4 (Large Intestine 4), and Yintang to calm stress and regulate Qi. Google for their location.
-Prioritize yourself: Avoid overwork and overstimulation; schedule breaks and moments of stillness throughout the day
- Stay hydrated: Sip warm water or teas (try my Mei Cha tea or place drops of my Chrysanthemum, Red Dates and Goji Extract) to nourish Yin and prevent dryness.
- Express emotions: Journaling, art, or talking with loved ones helps prevent Liver Qi stagnation (the root of stress).

By stimulating specific acupuncture points, acupuncture activates the parasympathetic nervous system - shifting you from survival mode into “rest & digest.” This helps your body calm down, reduce tension, and recover from stress more effectively.

Research shows acupuncture increases serotonin + dopamine - key neurotransmitters for mood and emotional balance - while reducing cortisol (your main stress hormone). It also influences endorphins, your body’s natural feel-good chemicals, helping you feel more grounded and at ease.

3️⃣ Regulates your stress system (HPA axis).
Acupuncture helps modulate the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, your body’s central stress circuit. Studies show it can lower cortisol levels and rebalance how your body responds to ongoing stress.

4️⃣ Improves sleep quality.
Poor sleep keeps your nervous system in overdrive. Acupuncture supports deeper, more restorative sleep by regulating serotonin, GABA, and melatonin - all crucial for relaxation and stress resilience.

5️⃣ Creates a calming “acu-nap” reset.
Beyond the science, the session itself is deeply restorative. Lying still, with minimal stimulation, allows your body and mind to slow down- reinforcing the physiological calm acupuncture creates. ✨

🍂 What I’m Doing Now to Keep Well Through Autumn & Winter 

As the seasons change, I always come back to simple rituals that help me feel grounded, nourished, and in rhythm with nature.

✨ Warm Drinks Only
From now on, it’s warm drinks all the way. I always feel the cold, and as the temperature drops, my body needs all the warmth it can get. Drinking cold (or even ice-cold!) drinks forces the body to work harder to stay warm - and I’d rather support it, not fight against it.

😴 Early Nights
I aim to be in bed before 11pm. In TCM, after 11 is when the body’s organs begin their cleansing and restorative work. My sleep routine matters more in winter - this is the time to conserve energy and build inner reserves.

🥣 Hearty, Slow-Cooked Meals
Warming, slow cooker meals like soups, stews, and casseroles help support digestion. I lean into grounding flavours that strengthen my centre.

🌬 Breathwork & the Metal Element
We’re in the time of Metal, connected to the Lungs and Large Intestine. I focus on breathing deeply and fully - it strengthens the lungs, helps release emotional stagnation, and prevents dampness from taking hold.

🌿 Skin Rituals
The skin mirrors the health of the lungs and large intestine, so I dry brush, gua sha and moisturise with warming sesame oil regularly. I support my skin from within too, with omega-3-rich foods and nourishing oils.

💗 Lifting My Shen (Spirit)
Winter is a more introspective season - time when emotions rise to the surface. I prioritise self-care and time with friends. Community and connection are medicine for the heart and Shen.

text:
Sometimes we love acupuncture too much. Because not every patient wants needles. But they all want help with their problem.

I had a teacher once who said "when a patient refuses acupuncture they're tying one hand behind my back. But my other hand has herbs."

"What if they don't want herbs?"

"Then I'll headbutt them with self care!"

Lol. In reality we have to find the balance between patients' goals and how much they want to micromanage the methods used to achieve those goals.

And we must respect their choices. And have alternatives available.

Sometimes those alternatives are simply to refer them out, but if you'd like to help as many people as possible then it pays to beef up your skill set and come to the table with a variety of tools.

Dynamic, adaptive, flexible solutions.

Now check this out:

Instead of giving a big spiky hug, what if we realize that some of the most important healing will happen when the patient has a shift in consciousness?

I'm not talking about chakra fluffiness either. A shift in consciousness involves seeing a new perspective (the larger picture of how their lifestyle choices are influencing the problems they're asking you to solve) combined with an identity upgrade so they they *become the kind of person* who starts making decisions more aligned with their goals.

You don't have to put down the needles and become a health coach. We can have it all.

Growing in this way helps you evolve up from technician-delivering-a-service to physician-as-leader/teacher.

Solving cash flow means getting out of the time for money model.

Streamlining your clinic means getting out of the time for money model.

Going online and having location and time freedom (if you're bold enough) means getting out of the time for money model.

Developing deeper relationships with the people you help? You guessed it.

post_owner.name: Jeremy Cornish
text:
Sometimes ''liver qi stagnation" is the only thing holding someone together. Consider...

You've had a rough night of little sleep. You're depleted, exhausted and feel empty and vulnerable inside. Your kids demand breakfast (again!), your spouse asks you to take care of something later that day, and your inbox is full of things you need to deal with...

All of these things take energy you don't have. And you become grumpy.

Grumpiness, here, is a defense mechanism. It's a way to gently repel other people when you don't have the bandwidth to deal with them. Because inside you're depleted.

In TCM terms we're looking at Liver Qi Stagnation. Which isn't pathological in this case. It's protective.

So we need to understand this for our patients. Just because we see it, doesn't mean we treat it. 

We have to look deeper.

Is there depletion driving the agitation?

And if there is, where is that depletion coming from?

Because it's not enough to tonify the person. 

This is a personalized medicine, which means we need to understand primary patterns, the causal web, and the highest leverage areas where we can intervene without making things worse.

Sometimes "pathologies" are a shield.

GLOBAL PALATES: The Ancient Science of Hot & Cold Foods 

Did you know the idea of "hot" and "cold" foods isn't just one culture's belief? It's a fascinating, worldwide phenomenon in traditional medicine!

From Ancient Greece & Persia's Humoral Theory (think Unani medicine with its Safra and Balgham) to Traditional Chinese Medicine's (TCM) Yin & Yang energies, and Ayurveda's Hot (Ushna) & Cold (Sheeta) Virya – cultures across the globe have classified foods by their perceived energetic effects on the body. Even Mesoamerican folk medicine uses a caliente/frío system!

Traditional "Hot" foods might include spices, red meat, or certain stimulating herbs. Traditional "Cold" foods often involve cooling vegetables, dairy, or hydrating fruits.

But here's the modern twist: While these systems provided valuable frameworks for health for centuries, modern science offers new insights! What was once attributed to "hotness" (like pimples from sweets) we now understand as insulin spikes. And what seemed like a "cold" food issue might actually be a specific food allergy!

This global tradition highlights how humans have always sought to understand the connection between food and well-being. It's a beautiful blend of cultural wisdom meeting contemporary science!

Addressing Dampness in Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) 🌧️✨

If you’ve been feeling tired, bloated, heavy, or sluggish, it might not just be “fatigue.” In TCM, this often points to dampness — a kind of internal heaviness that slows your Qi and affects digestion, focus, and energy.

There are 4 types of dampness:

💨 External Damp — comes from the environment (cold, rain, humidity).
Feels like: stiff joints, heavy limbs, sore muscles.
👉 Try: Fresh ginger + scallion whites + miso soup (optionally add in seaweed)

💧 Internal Damp — from weak digestion or overconsumption of cold foods.
Feels like: bloating, fatigue, nausea, loose stools.
👉 Try: Fu Ling (Poria) + dried red dates + dried ginger tea

🔥 Damp-Heat — when dampness combines with internal heat.
Feels like: acne, irritability, bitter taste, yellow discharge.
👉 Try: Green radish + mung beans + pork bone soup (optionally add barley, carrots, or corn)

❄️ Damp-Cold — when dampness meets coldness.
Feels like: cold limbs, low energy, loose stool, tummy pain relieved by warmth.
👉 Try: Chicken + ginger + scallion congee (optionally add in white pepper)

These soups and teas help the body clear excess dampness and restore balance naturally.

🫖 Remember: Dampness doesn’t clear overnight. Consistency, warmth, and mindful eating make a big difference! Food is medicine.

text:
🌺 Spring Glow up Marshmallows with Hibiscus, Rose & Sea Buckthorn 🌺

Spring is the season of renewal, when everything begins to move & grow again • These marshmallows aren’t just a treat, the grass-fed gelatin makes them soothing for your gut & nourishing for your skin whilst gently supporting the Liver’s Qi & Blood • 
	• Hibiscus moves Liver Qi, cools gentle heat, promotes detoxification
	• Rose soothes emotional tension, opens the Heart, harmonises Liver Qi
	• Goji berries replenish Liver Blood, support vitality & vision
	• Sea buckthorn berries nourish Yin, support skin health & restore the glow of spring
	• Ginger adds warmth & balance, harmonising digestion

Herbal Infusion Base:
	•	1 cup filtered water
	•	1 tbsp hibiscus petals
	•	1 tbsp rose petals
	•	1 tbsp goji berries
	•	1 tbsp dried sea buckthorn berries 
	•	2 thin slice fresh ginger
	•	¼ tsp lemon zest 

Marshmallow Base:
	•	3 tbsp grass-fed gelatin
	•	1 cup maple syrup or raw honey 
	•	¼ tsp sea salt
	•	½ tsp vanilla extract

🫖 Instructions
	1.	Make the herbal infusion: Combine hibiscus, rose, goji, sea buckthorn, ginger & lemon zest with 1 cup boiling water 
	2.	Bloom the gelatin: Pour ½ cup of the warm herbal infusion into a large mixing bowl • Sprinkle gelatin evenly over the top & let it bloom for 5–10 minutes 
	3.	Make the syrup: In a small saucepan, combine the remaining ¼ cup of herbal infusion, maple syrup, vanilla & sea salt 
Bring to a steady simmer & heat until it reaches 240°F 
	4.	Whip into marshmallow fluff: slowly drizzle the hot syrup into the gelatin mixture whilst slowly whipping • Increase speed to high & whip for 8–10 minutes, until glossy, pale & fluffy
	5.	Set & cure: Pour into a lined 8×8-inch pan, smooth the surface & let set for 4–6 hours at room temperature.
	6.	Cut and finish: Dust with coconut flour, cut into squares & store in an airtight container for up to 5 days

post_owner.name: American Wild Horse Conservation
text:
Before the government shutdown, Representative Don Beyer (D-VA-8) reintroduced the Ejiao Act, which aims to ban the United State's role in the donkey hide skin trade. ✊ 

⚠️ Every year, millions of donkeys are slaughtered for their skin to produce ejiao, a gelatin that is used in traditional Chinese medicine and beauty products. The United States is currently one of the top importers, helping to fuel the global demand.❗ 

🚨 In under a decade, donkey populations in several countries have been slashed in half. 🚨 In many cases, donkeys are stolen from rural communities, leaving families without transportation for food, water, and goods. 

Ejiao products can be easily replaced with synthetic or plant-based alternatives. 🌿 

The Ejiao Act of 2025 calls to: 
👉 Ban the import, export, sale, and transport of ejiao and donkey skins in the U.S.

Metal season arrives when the air turns crisp and the light sharpens — a time of refinement, structure, and release. 🍂

In Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), autumn corresponds to the Metal Element, which governs the lungs and large intestine — the organs responsible for what we take in and what we let go of. Physically, this is a season of exchange and purification. The lungs draw in oxygen and release carbon dioxide, regulating our Qi (vital energy) and influencing the tone of our skin, voice, and immune defenses. The large intestine mirrors this process by helping the body eliminate what is no longer needed.

From a scientific perspective, the lungs are not just passive organs of respiration — they are rhythmic conductors of the autonomic nervous system. Every conscious breath we take signals the vagus nerve, helping to regulate heart rate, digestion, and emotional balance. In this sense, breathwork isn’t just spiritual — it’s neurological hygiene. Similarly, the colon, often called our “second brain,” communicates with the gut microbiome, which in turn affects mood, clarity, and energy.

Spiritually, Metal is the alchemist of the elements. It teaches discernment — the ability to separate the precious from the unnecessary. Just as the trees release their leaves, we too are asked to shed old layers: outdated beliefs, emotional residue, habits that dull our radiance. In TCM, this process is tied to the emotion of grief — not as something to suppress, but as a sacred cleansing force that makes space for new inspiration to enter.

When the Metal Element is balanced, we feel focused, clear, and inspired — able to articulate our truth with grace. When it’s out of balance, we may feel constricted in breath, rigid in thinking, or unable to let go.

To nourish your Metal energy this season:
— Practice deep, slow breathing to strengthen lung Qi.
— Eat white, pungent foods like daikon, garlic, and pear to moisten and clear the lungs.
— Engage in gentle movement and fascia release to expand the chest and support lymphatic flow.
— Create ritual around letting go — journal, tidy, or simply breathe with awareness of release.

Ever notice how you sometimes sneeze right after a meal, especially if it’s big, cold, or heavy?
In Western medicine, it’s often brushed off as a harmless “gustatory reflex.”
But in Chinese medicine, sneezing after eating is a sign that your Spleen Qi is weak and your body is struggling to transform food into energy.

Here’s what’s really happening 👇

In TCM, the Spleen and Stomach are the center of digestion - your “digestive fire.”
When Spleen Qi is strong, it moves food downward and converts it into usable Qi.
When it’s weak, digestion becomes sluggish, and instead of Qi flowing down, it rebels upward - which can trigger sneezing, hiccups, or even reflux.

It’s also a sign that external Wind (from cold foods, AC, or drafts) can easily invade the body because your defensive Wei Qi isn’t anchored.
Basically, your system is saying:

“I can’t handle this much, I’m overwhelmed.”

🧠 Common triggers:
- Eating too quickly or when stressed
- Consuming cold or raw foods
- Overeating or snacking constantly
- Drinking iced beverages with meals

🌿 Try instead:
- Eat warm, cooked foods, not cold smoothies or salads
- Chew slowly and avoid multitasking
- Add a little ginger or cinnamon to meals to warm digestion

So next time you sneeze after a meal, it’s not “just allergies.”
Your body might be asking you to strengthen your Spleen and slow down.

🦶 Quick Tip: Keep your feet warm and dry. Wear socks  or soft footwear indoors, avoid walking barefoot on cold floors, and try a warm foot soak in the evening to restore circulation and balance.

🔥 Conditions Commonly Linked to “Cold Feet” in Eastern Medicine:
	1.	Kidney Yang Deficiency – fatigue, cold lower back, low libido, frequent urination, feeling cold all over.

	5.	Cold Damp Invasion – cold heavy legs, swelling, sluggishness, joint pain worse in damp weather.

🦶 Why You Should Keep the Bottom of Your Feet Warm (Especially in Winter)

In Traditional (Eastern) Medicine, the feet are seen as the “roots” of the body — where vital energy (Qi) and blood circulate upward to nourish every organ. The soles of your feet contain key acupuncture points connected to the kidneys, liver, and spine — meaning cold feet can affect your whole system, not just your toes!

When your feet get cold, your body pulls warmth and circulation away from your extremities to protect vital organs, often leading to fatigue, poor sleep, or even pain elsewhere in the body. Keeping your feet warm helps maintain healthy blood flow, supports energy, and prevents the deeper penetration of cold — one of the most common causes of illness in winter.
