text:
Perimenopause marks a gradual transition, shaped by shifting hormones and changing rhythms of the body. In Traditional Chinese Medicine, this passage reflects the natural decline of Kidney Jing, which governs reproductive essence, vitality, and the body’s reserves of Yin and Yang.

As Yin begins to wane with age, the cooling, anchoring fluids of the body slowly diminish. Without sufficient Yin to ground it, Yang becomes relatively excessive, what TCM describes as “false heat.” This imbalance gives rise to symptoms like hot flashes, night sweats, irritability, and restlessness. Rather than fighting these changes, the focus is on replenishing Yin so the body can regain its natural equilibrium.

The body’s needs shift as these patterns emerge. Cooling foods such as cucumber, watermelon, tofu, and mint help temper internal heat and restore Yin fluids. Yin-nourishing and cooling herbs like Tremella or Pearl can further anchor fluids and ease internal heat.
Grounding evening meals with slow-digesting carbohydrates, magnesium-rich foods, and calming herbs like chamomile, lemon balm, reishi, or rose support the Shen, calm the mind, and encourage deeper sleep.
Iron- and mineral-rich foods like eggs, beef, black sesame, nettles, and dark leafy greens help replenish after heavy bleeding, rebuilding Blood and fortifying Qi, supported by Blood-building herbs such as He Shou Wu or Nurture Blend.

Perimenopause often brings several of these presentations at once, such as Yin deficiency with heat, Blood deficiency with fatigue, or Shen disturbance with anxiety and insomnia. Each calls for its own form of nourishment. In TCM, food and herbs are chosen not for restriction, but for restoration. They rebuild what time and stress have drawn from the body, encouraging balance rather than suppression.

Perimenopause is not a problem to be solved but a passage to be supported. When Yin is replenished, Yang naturally returns to harmony, and the body finds its equilibrium once more. 🌀

text:
Did you know this about @TCM ?
Turner Classic Movies (TCM) has preserved old movies primarily through partnerships with organizations like The Film Foundation and the UCLA Film & Television Archive. It also directly supports restoration efforts, showcases restored films, and provides a platform for airing films in their original format, often without commercials. This includes funding restoration projects, highlighting films with newly commissioned soundtracks, and presenting widescreen versions of movies. 

Partnerships and funding

You can wa

The Film Foundation: TCM has a long-standing relationship with The Film Foundation, which includes a partnership with Warner Bros. for the WB100 centennial celebration. This collaboration involved restoring 10 films from the Warner Bros. library to highlight during the celebration.

UCLA Film & Television Archive: TCM has also partnered with the UCLA Film & Television Archive on various restoration projects. This includes supporting the restoration of films like the Laurel & Hardy short, "The Battle of the Century".

Film Noir Foundation: Through its "Noir Alley" program, TCM has supported the Film Noir Foundation, which has helped restore previously "lost" films like Woman on the Run. 

Restored films: TCM regularly showcases restored versions of classic films, such as the 4K restoration of Giant.

Widescreen presentations: The channel presents many films in their original widescreen formats, which are often unavailable on home video.

Silent films: TCM sometimes features restored silent films with newly commissioned musical scores.

Commercial-free broadcasts: TCM provides a commercial-free viewing experience, which is rare and important for allowing audiences to engage with the films without interruption. 

Contextualizing film history

Public dialogue: TCM's programming and educational initiatives provide a platform for discussion and dialogue around classic films, which is crucial for contextualizing their historical and cultural significance.

Cultural preservation: By presenting films as a form of culture, TCM helps preserve "the best American selves" and reminds audiences of historical and societal narratives.

text:
🪴Rhubarb & Blueberry Galette 🫐

A rustic galette made with rhubarb (slightly sour, supports Liver Qi flow in TCM) & blueberries (sweet, antioxidant-rich, nourish Blood & Yin) 

For the crust:
• 1 ½ cups spelt flour
• ¼ tsp sea salt
• 1 tsp cinnamon powder 
• 1 tbsp coconut sugar 
• ½ cup cold organic butter
• 3–4 tbsp ice-cold water (if needed)

For the filling:
• 1 ½ cups blueberries 
• 1 ½ cups chopped rhubarb 
• 2–3 tbsp maple syrup or raw honey, to taste
• 1 tsp vanilla extract 

Optional for brushing 
• 1 beaten egg, or a little melted butter/coconut oil

🥣 Instructions
Make the crust by whisking together spelt flour, salt, cinnamon & sugar • Cut in the cold butter using your fingers or a pastry cutter until crumbly • Add cold water one tablespoon at a time until the dough just holds together • Form into a disc & chill for 30–60 minutes

• Preheat oven to 180°C • Roll out the dough on lightly floured parchment into a rough circle • Spoon blueberries, rhubarb, maple syrup & vanilla into centre of dough • Toss gently leaving a 2-inch border • Fold edges over the filling & brush the crust with egg or butter/oil if desired • Bake for 35–40 minutes, until the crust is golden & the filling bubbly • Cool slightly before slicing & enjoy! 😋

post_owner.name: My Mum's Flavour
text:
[Recipe] Morel mushrooms can help to nourish and strengthen the body by improving immunity, support antioxidant activity / fight free radicals, as well as aiding in digestion, resolving phlegm and regulating “Qi” (vital energy). It is also used to nourish the kidneys and strengthen “Yang”, enhance brain health and improve mental clarity. Being rich in polysaccharides, polyphenols, protein and a variety of essential amino acids and minerals, etc., morel mushrooms have many benefits to health.

Apart from its many benefits, morel mushrooms are especially delicious when used in Chinese style soups! This Morel Mushroom Pork Rib Soup is super flavourful with a natural sweetness from the ingredients. Check out the recipe -

Ingredients
10 pieces of morel mushrooms
500g of pork ribs
Few slices of ginger
1/2 to 1 stick of Iron Rod Yam (another superfood!)
1200ml water (including morel mushrooms’ soaking water)

1) Rinse morel mushrooms and soak them in warm water for 20 minutes or till softened.

2) Remove the skin of Iron Rod Yam and chop into bite-sizes. Recommend to wear gloves when handling Iron Rod Yam as it may caused skin itchiness.

3) Blanch pork ribs. Add a little cooking wine or ginger slices during the blanching process (optional). After blanching, rinse the pork ribs under running water.

4) Add pork ribs, morel mushrooms + its soaking liquid and hot water into a Dutch oven or soup pot. Bring the water to a boil, then cover and simmer for 30 minutes.

5) Add Iron Rod Yam and continue to simmer for another 20 to 30 minutes.

6) Add salt to taste.

Enjoy!

text:
Sardines are one of the most nutrient dense foods in the world.

In TCM, sardines tonify Qi and Yin. This means that they are able to strengthen our vital energy as well as nourish our bodily fluids— lubricating the body and combating dry conditions. This also includes strengthening our Blood. They are able to regulate water circulation, helping both the Kidney and Spleen organ systems.

All about sardines:

- Sardines contain the most beneficial and easily absorbed fatty acids, which help both our physical and mental health and boost brain function. Their anti-inflammatory properties protect against Heart disease.
- Sardines have an excellent source of vitamin b-12 which is essential for so many vital functions of the body. It keeps the body’s nerves and Blood cells healthy and helps make DNA, the genetic material in all cells, helps against anemia that makes people tired and weak. It is especially great for those who are pregnant or elderly.
- Sardines contain essential minerals like selenium, niacin, iron, potassium, magnesium, zinc and phosphorus. Because it is hard to get adequate minerals from our soil and food, this is a great source. 
- Sardines are imperative for bone health because they are one of the few foods containing calcium, phosphorus and vitamin D— which regulate bone metabolism, a process in which mature bone tissue is removed to allow for the formation of new bone tissue.

If you are lucky enough to have access to fresh sardines, make sure they smell fresh, have shiny skin, bright eyes with a firm texture. Because they are highly perishable, they are often canned in oil or water. You can grill them, bake them or eat them as is. I love to add lemon and oregano!

The menstrual cycle unfolds in four phases: menstrual, follicular, ovulatory, and luteal. Each is marked by distinct physiological shifts, and in Traditional Chinese Medicine these stages are also understood through changes in Blood, Yin, Yang, Qi, and Shen.

This dual lens shows us something essential: the body’s needs are not static. What nourishes in one phase may not be what supports in the next.

Rather than the casual notion of a ‘girl dinner’ made of snacks, this is nourishment that actively engages with the cycle — iron and mineral-rich foods during menstruation, fluid-building proteins and fruits in the follicular phase, cooling and antioxidant support around ovulation, and warming, stabilizing meals in the luteal phase.

In TCM, animal foods are not incidental but central, they are recognized for their ability to restore Blood, strengthen Qi, and carry the body through transitions.

‘Girl dinner’ reimagined as food that doesn’t just fill, but fortifies. 🍲🥚🐟🍇

"Here is an insight 🌈
Ancestral medicine, across various cultures, didn't use the term "perimenopause" as we do today, but many traditional systems recognized the transitional phase in women’s lives before menopause, often viewing it as a natural and significant life stage. 

Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) associated this phase with a decline in Kidney essence (Jing), which governs reproduction and aging. Symptoms like hot flashes, irregular periods, and mood changes were seen as imbalances in Yin and Yang, particularly Kidney Yin deficiency. 

Treatments included acupuncture, herbal formulas like Liu Wei Di Huang Wan, and dietary adjustments to nourish Yin, such as black sesame, goji berries, or bone broth.

In Ayurveda (Indian Medicine), perimenopause aligns with the transition from Pitta (midlife) to Vata (later life) dominance. Symptoms like irritability, insomnia, or irregular bleeding were attributed to Vata imbalances or Pitta heat excess. 

Remedies included cooling herbs like shatavari, ashwagandha for stress, and lifestyle practices like meditation and oil massages to balance Vata.

Indigenous and Native American Traditions and cultures viewed this phase as a spiritual transition, where women gained wisdom and power as they moved toward elder status. Physical symptoms were often addressed with herbal remedies, such as black cohosh for hot flashes or sage for hormonal balance, alongside rituals to honor the shift. 

Community support and storytelling were key.

In Ancient Greek and European humoral #medicine, perimenopause-like symptoms were linked to an imbalance of bodily humors, often excess heat or drying of fluids. 

Herbal teas, like chamomile or licorice root, and bloodletting or dietary changes were used to restore balance. Women were often seen as transitioning to a phase of greater intellectual or spiritual clarity.

In African Traditional Medicine healing systems, this life stage was often revered, with symptoms managed through herbal concoctions (e.g., moringa or rooibos) and rituals to honor the body’s changes. Healers emphasized community, diet, and #spiritual alignment to ease the transition.

As a Medical Doctor & Chinese medicine expert, I lived 3 years in China. These 3 learnings really had an impact on how I saw health and the body:

1️⃣ Health begins in the gut
In Chinese Medicine, digestion is seen as the root of our energy and vitality.
It’s not only what you eat, but how well your body transforms it into Qi and Blood.
Warm, cooked meals nourish your system, while too much cold or raw food can weaken it.
 
2️⃣ Your body give signals 
Before illness develops, the body gives subtle signals — through your tongue, your skin, your sleep, your energy levels.
In China I learned to observe these signs as messages, not annoyances.
A pale tongue, dark circles, bloating, restless nights… all are clues.
This awareness taught me that prevention is not a luxury, it’s the foundation of true health.
 
3️⃣ Balance matters more than perfection
Western culture often pushes us to optimize, perfect, control every detail.
Chinese Medicine showed me something softer: that harmony is more powerful than perfection.
Your body is meant to move with the seasons, your hormones with your cycle, your energy with your life stage.
Health isn’t about strict rules — it’s about being in rhythm with yourself and with nature.

The Mid Autumn festival has always been one of my favourite times of the year. It’s about reunion, reflection, and the small rituals that bring everyone closer. Families share mooncakes, admire the full moon, and give thanks for the harvest.

In Traditional Chinese Medicine, autumn belongs to the metal element. It rules the lungs and the skin, reminding us to slow down, breathe deeply, and hold on to moisture as the air turns crisp.

As a kid, I loved going with my family to pick out mooncakes. The bakeries smelled sweet and nutty, and choosing the box felt like a ceremony. If you can, find an Asian store and get yourself a mooncake—it’s part of the magic. Mooncakes aren’t just dessert, they’re symbols of togetherness. I like cutting a small wedge, sipping warm tea, and eating slowly. Oolong or Pu’er are classics, but chrysanthemum with pear is my favourite for a lighter finish.

Autumn is a drying season in TCM, so the lungs and skin need moisture and protection. My routine stays simple: Face Nectar for a juicy base, Face Oil to lock it in at night, and Barrier Cream as daily comfort. Kidney failure is quite common in cats, especially as they get older, and dogs can be affected, too. One of the problems with kidney disease is that by the time you can pick up increases in blood urea nitrogen or creatinine in blood tests, up to 75% of the kidney's function or capacity has already been lost!

In cats, dry food is a significant risk factor, because it makes your cats chronically dehydrated.

Morning EFT Practice — Regulating the Mind and Body

I had a rough night in the dream world and woke with worries for my family and the world sitting heavily in my mind. Before heading into clinic, I decided to reset my energy so my thoughts could guide my day with steadiness and clarity. Maybe you could try this if you wake with a heavy heart.

I began with a 35-minute Joe Dispenza morning meditation on YouTube, then settled into a few gentle rounds of EFT (Emotional Freedom Technique), also known as tapping.

EFT is a simple technique that combines tapping on acupuncture points with mindful awareness of what we’re feeling. It helps calm the nervous system, soften stress responses, and restore a sense of safety and flow.

Here’s how you can try it:

Notice what you feel right now.
Ask yourself: what’s weighing on me or holding me back?
“Face the dirt on the dish before you clean it.”
Say it out loud.
“Even although I feel trapped / angry / sad / afraid / lonely…”
Add affirmations.
“I trust myself.”
“I’m OK.”
“I can hold this.”
“I know what I need.”
“I have boundaries.”
“I am on my way.”

Tap gently on each point:

Side of hand (near pinky knuckle)
Top of head
Inner eyebrow
Outer eyebrow
Under eye
Under nose
Under bottom lip
Under clavicle
Side of ribs
Heart centre (both hands)

Do 2–3 rounds, repeating your feeling first, then your affirmations.

This simple practice helps release what’s held inside and brings you back to yourself, steady, grounded, and able to trust your own rhythm.

In Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), fall is the season of Metal—refinement, release, and return to essence. The air becomes dry, the light sharpens, and nature begins the elegant art of letting go.

Element & Organs: Metal governs the Lungs and Large Intestine, the systems responsible for intake and release. The Lungs draw in heavenly Qi (air, inspiration, clarity), while the Large Intestine eliminates what no longer serves. Together they teach the rhythm of breathing and the wisdom of surrender—both physically and emotionally.

Emotion & Spirit: The emotion of Metal is grief, which, when transformed, becomes gratitude. Grief arises from loss—of summer’s warmth, of youth, of people or dreams. But fall invites us to honor what once was, extract its essence, and exhale the rest.

The predominant energy is dryness, which affects the Lungs, skin, throat, and mucous membranes. You might notice cough, dry skin, constipation, or sadness surfacing—signals to moisten body and soul.

The pungent (spicy) flavor opens the Lungs; the sweet and moistening tones balance the dryness. Think of pears, apples, sesame, almonds, honey, tofu, daikon, pumpkin, and white foods that resonate with the Metal element. Avoid excessive heat or drying foods like coffee, fried dishes, and alcohol.

Slow down. Breathe deeply. Practice Qigong that opens the chest and expands the lungs. Reflect on your year—what needs to be kept as wisdom and what can be released as weight. Create space for what’s next by clearing both clutter and resentment.

Autumn is the great exhalation of the year—nature teaches that letting go is not loss, but preparation for renewal

(Link in profile)

Szechuan Pepper (Zanthoxylum simulans) The shiny black orbs are the seeds used for planting. The red portion is the part used in Szechuan cooking. This is the seed husk, or pericarp, an appetite stimulant and flavor enhancer that prepares the palate for spicy hot foods. Add the powdered herb at the last minute for best effect! At the spice market in Kunming I observed workers separating husk from seed. They offered me the husks, and were quite surprised that I wished to obtain the seed instead! Years later we have the newly harvested seed available to growers in the US. In TCM, the herb is used to warm the middle burner, a treatment for acute abdominal pain, vomiting, and watery diarrhea. Zanthoxylum promotes blood circulation and is often included in formulas to help move other herbs throughout the body and to the outer extremities. It is an ingredient in the famous "five spice powder."

Szechuan Pepper (Zanthoxylum simulans)
Family:Citrus (Rutaceae)
Hardy to Zones 5 to 9
(Hua-jiao, Sichuan Pepper, Szechwan Pepper, Flatspine Prickly Ash, Chinese Prickly Ash) Dioecious shrub to 6 feet tall. Native to E . China and Taiwan. Handsome prickly landscape plant that yields the famous tongue-tingling spice that characterizes Sichuan cuisine. The shrub does best in moist, rich soil in the sun to part shade. They are dioecious (male and female flowers on separate plants) but lacking an available male, female plants will become hermaphroditic and self-pollinating. I know this sounds like an oxymoron but it is relatively common in nature. Sow seed in the fall for germination in the spring. Alternatively, give 90 days cold, moist refrigeration (put seed in moist medium in a plastic bag and refrigerate, not freeze) and then plant in warm conditions. Germination can take from 30 to 90 days, although we find them to be pretty reliable germinators. Individuate seedlings to pots and grow on for a year or two before planting to landscape. For hedging, plant 2 feet apart. Otherwise, give at least 10 foot spacing between shrubs.

text:
[Recipe] Euryale seeds (Qian Shi) and red beans, when combined in soup, offer benefits in Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) by tonifying the spleen and kidneys. This can help to alleviate symptoms such as diarrhoea, strengthen the lower back and knees as well as reduce fluid retention (i.e Euryale seeds are known to specifically drain dampness, and red beans help to promote the transport of fluids, reducing overall fluid retention and edema). Red beans are also rich in fiber and minerals that support digestive and cardiovascular health. 

Highly recommended to add some Osmanthus to this sweet soup too as it adds a lovely floral fragrance to the overall flavour. In addition, osmanthus is believed to benefit the digestive and respiratory systems, alleviate menstrual pain, and promote healthy skin in TCM.
Without further ado, check out the recipe -
Ingredients
115g of red beans
40g of fresh Euryale seeds (芡实）
12 to 15g yellow rock sugar
1 tsp of Osmanthus
Moderate amount of hot/boiling water (approximately 800ml + add more if needed)
1) Pre-soak red beans in boiling water for 1 hour or more. Drain the water and store the red beans in the refrigerator overnight.
2) Add red beans into a pot with adequate amount of hot / boiling water and rock sugar. Bring the water to a boil, then cover and simmer for 1 hour, or till the beans have softened to your liking. If the liquid has reduced too much during the cooking process, add more hot water.
Mashed some of the red beans if you like the texture of the soup to be thicker, when the cooking is almost done.
3) Cook fresh Euryale seeds in boiling water for 3 to 4 minutes.
4) Add Euryale seeds and Osmanthus into the red bean soup. Mix the ingredients before eating.
Enjoy!

Patients frequently report that their symptoms worsen during periods of frustration, anger, or tension, and may be accompanied by belching, nausea, or appetite changes.

Because the Liver is responsible for free flow of qi, its stagnation easily overacts on the Stomach, disrupting its harmony and impairing digestion. This leads to rebellious Stomach qi, resulting in discomfort and irregular digestion. Clinical manifestations include distending epigastric pain or fullness, pain that fluctuates with emotions, frequent belching, acid regurgitation, nausea, poor appetite, and sometimes sighing or irritability.

Key acupoints for soothing the Liver and harmonising the Stomach include LR3 Tai Chong (太冲) and ST36 Zu San Li (足三里). Tai Chong is the principal point to regulate Liver qi, disperse stagnation, and relieve stress-induced tension. Zu San Li strengthens the Stomach, regulates qi, and improves digestion. text:
The Autumn Moon Festival or Mid-Autumn Festival is on October 6th this year and is a really important date in the Chinese Calendar. This a harvest celebration on the 15th day of the 8th lunar month, when the full moon symbolises reunion, abundance, and harmony.

In China this is one of the year’s “big three” festivals and is a really important time for family and gratitude. This marks the perfect time to continue your Autumn declutter, replacing let it go with gratitude before Winter at the beginning of November. An amazing fact I learnt recently is that when you take the time to notice what you’re grateful for, your brain releases dopamine and serotonin. The two neurotransmitters related to happiness and wellbeing.

To prepare for the moon I recommend
Eating a lighter dinner like a soup, stew or steamed vegetables.
Declutter one small thing in your house like a drawer, bag or your inbox to model letting go.
Picking round food and setting out a notebook ready to journal. Round food is really significant today as it symbolises the moon.

Happy Autumn Moon Festival! I’ll be talking lots about this over on The Health Club Facebook group so please do join me there.

INTERSTITIAL CYSTITIS - ENDOMETRIOSIS - WOMEN’s HEALTH: A TCM APPROACH

From a holistic and Chinese medicine perspective, interstitial cystitis, chronic UTIs, endometriosis, and chronic painful periods share a common root: imbalance within the pelvic region, often linked to stagnation of Qi and Blood, as well as underlying inflammation and depletion of vital energy. In Chinese medicine, pain and inflammation occur when there is obstruction—when Qi (energy) and Blood cannot flow freely through the lower abdomen. Factors such as chronic stress, unresolved emotions, poor digestion, and overwork can weaken the body’s core systems (Kidney, Liver, and Spleen), leading to congestion, heat, and stagnation in the pelvic organs. This stagnation can manifest as pain, urinary frequency, burning, or cyclical flares that worsen with hormonal shifts.

The Role of Organ Systems and Energetics

The Liver plays a central role in regulating the smooth flow of Qi and menstrual cycles. When Liver Qi becomes constrained—often from stress or emotional repression—it can generate internal heat and cause Blood stagnation, leading to painful periods and conditions such as endometriosis. The Kidney system governs the reproductive organs and stores the body’s deepest energy reserves; when deficient, tissues lose resilience and repair capacity, predisposing to chronic inflammation and bladder pain syndromes like interstitial cystitis. Meanwhile, the Spleen system, responsible for digestion and transformation, influences dampness and phlegm accumulation in the pelvis—contributing to inflammation, cyst formation, and bacterial imbalances. Together, these patterns reflect a disharmony that extends beyond isolated symptoms, illustrating how pelvic pain and urinary issues often stem from deeper energetic and systemic imbalances.

According to Traditional Chinese Medicine, this practice doesn’t just move the body — it opens the gates of life itself, letting energy pour through you like fresh water at sunrise. 🌞🌿

The “gates of life” are found in the lower back, where the kidneys rest. In TCM, this area is seen as a reservoir of vitality — your batteries for stamina, clarity, and resilience. When you wake it up, you don’t just stretch the body, you switch on the flow of life force itself.

Best done in the morning.

text:
While working in TCM clinic & hospital we see so many cases of sudden facial paralysis. The face reflects what’s happening inside, and when movement disappears on one side, it usually means the flow of Qi and Blood has been blocked.

Why it happens
Wind invasion – the classic cause. Often after sleeping near wind, exposing the face and neck to a lot of spontaneous wind or going out after sweating. Wind enters through open pores and blocks facial meridians.
Qi and blood deficiency – after illness, childbirth or exhaustion, the face isn’t nourished properly and becomes more vulnerable.
Liver and kidney weakness – shows up in lingering cases normally. These organs are tied to nerves and sinews, so if they’re weak, recovery slows down.
Emotional stress – frustration or stress blocks liver Qi, creating stagnation on one side of the face.
Phlegm and dampness – common in people with sluggish digestion, slow metabolism or sinus issues. They clog channels and make symptoms worse.

Interesting facts
Bell’s palsy vs stroke – in TCM, bell’s palsy is wind attacking the channels, not the organs. It’s usually less serious and often reversible with early treatment.
The side matters – right is often linked to Lung and Spleen patterns, left to Liver.
Seasonal spikes – more common in spring and autumn when wind and temperature shifts are stronger.
Early acupuncture works best – ideally within the first week, using points like ST4, ST6, LI4 and GB14.
Facial paralysis is a mix of external factors, internal states and emotions all intersecting at once. TCM’s strength is catching these patterns early and restoring flow before symptoms linger.

Digestives warmth. TCM emphasizes the importance of warm and cooked foods for optimal digestion. Raw foods are considered cold and fam in nature which can impair the digestive function properly.  The impairment can lead to deficiency in spleen qi which is essential for overall fertility.

Dampness is where fluids accumulate and stagnate which can lead to phlegm and fluid retention. Nutrient absorption. Cooking foods  help break down cell walls and makes nutrients more bioavailable. For fertility patients maximizing nutrient absorption is crucial.

Warm and cooked foods
Balanced diet
Avoid excess cold foods.

Postpartum is not a time to bounce back, it is an initiation into the first 40 days that set the foundation for the next 40 years (TCM saying).

In Traditional Chinese Medicine, this saying reflects a truth we also see in clinical nutrition: the way you replenish blood, yin, warmth, and minerals in those first weeks not only affect recovery, but it shapes hormonal resilience, emotional steadiness, future fertility, and even how your body transitions into later life stages like perimenopause.

Birth empties reserves. The way you replenish determines how your body heals tissues, lactates, and stabilizes mood.

Skip it, and depletion lingers as fatigue, hair loss, low milk supply, cycle disruptions, postpartum anxiety, or prolapse. Honor it, and you lay reserves that last decades.

Restorative foods for the postpartum window:
⚘ Blood-builders: soups, congees, liver pate, beets, broths, black sesame, jujube dates, goji berries, molasses.
⚘ Warmth + circulation: stews, ginger, garlic, long-simmered grains, root veg.
⚘ Mineral tonics: bone broth, seaweed, soaked seeds, egg yolks, nettles, herbal allies for your specific constitution + needs.
⚘ Yin-sweet tonics: figs, dates, sesame, jujube–goji teas, full-fat dairy if tolerated.
⚘ Warm drinks: decoctions, teas, and broths (never iced).

This is the wisdom of the forty-day window: keep it warm, slow, and restorative.
Not cold salads, iced drinks, or depletion dressed up as discipline, but grounding nourishment that rebuild what birth emptied.

Postpartum is not a time to restrict or “bounce back.” It’s a time to be rebuilt.

text:
Should I Be Worried About a Cold Uterus?

When I first came across the concept of a “cold uterus” in Traditional Chinese Medicine, it finally explained many things I had experienced. In TCM, a cold uterus isn’t just about temperature—it reflects poor circulation and energy flow in the reproductive system. When warmth and blood flow are insufficient, the uterus lining doesn’t nourish well, which can make implantation harder and increase the risk of miscarriage.

Looking back, I saw many of the classic TCM signs in myself—cold hands and feet, back pain during periods, fatigue, frequent urination, late ovulation, low libido, scanty periods, and dark or painful clots. These are all ways the body signals that energy (Qi) and blood are not flowing optimally to the uterus.

Lifestyle plays a big role. In TCM, the feet are seen as gateways to warming the body. Walking barefoot on cold floors, spending long hours in air-conditioned rooms, or sleeping in a cold environment all drain warmth and slow circulation. From a functional view, poor circulation and cold exposure affect the liver, kidneys, and digestion—all of which influence hormonal balance.

Simple practices help restore warmth: keeping the feet covered, using socks at night, warm compresses on the lower abdomen, and occasional hot water soaks through the feet.

Food is also medicine here. Warming foods and spices—like ginger water ( comment ginger tea for recipe ) —support digestion and blood flow. Too much raw, uncooked, or cold food can weaken digestive “fire,” making it harder for the body to generate warmth and energy for reproduction. Even something as small as avoiding cold drinks with meals can make a big difference.

Even if you’re not actively trying for pregnancy, maintaining uterine warmth improves overall vitality, hormone health, and long-term fertility. A “warm uterus” in TCM is really about strong circulation, balanced hormones, and a nourished body.

Breathing is a mirror of how Qi moves. In Traditional Chinese Medicine the rhythm, depth, and sound of the breath hint at the state of the Lungs, Kidneys, and the nervous system.

-If your breath is shallow and quick
Often points to Lung Qi weakness or stress that keeps Qi at the surface. You may feel tired yet wired, with a tight chest and frequent sighs.

-If you hold your breath or forget to exhale
Suggests Qi stagnation. Emotions feel stuck and the ribcage feels tense. Sighing brings brief relief because it moves Liver Qi.

-Frequent sighing
Sighing is your body’s way of moving stagnant Liver Qi. Occasional sighs are healthy, but frequent, unconscious sighing suggests emotional tension, frustration, or a sense of “stuckness.” In TCM, this often links to the Liver’s role in regulating the smooth flow of Qi.

-If you feel short of breath on stairs
Can reflect Spleen and Lung Qi deficiency. Low stamina, heavy limbs, brain fog, and craving for sweets are common companions.

-If you breathe through the mouth at rest
The Lungs prefer breathing through the nose. Mouth breathing dries fluids and can aggravate heat and irritability.

If you wake at 3 to 5 am
This is the Lung time on the body clock. Waking then with a busy mind can signal grief not yet processed or Lung Qi imbalance.

In Traditional Chinese Medicine and Ayurveda , birth is seen as a “cold” state — warmth is needed to restore balance, prevent fatigue, and support milk supply. Warm foods provide grounding energy and steady nourishment instead of shock to the system.

Cooking makes many nutrients more bioavailable — for example, minerals in bone broth, or carotenoids in cooked veggies. Soups, stews, porridges, and teas deliver vitamins, minerals, and hydration in the most digestible way possible.

text:
Fall is prime time for cold, cough, and fatigue. 

According to Traditional Chinese Medicine, the fall season is connected to the lungs. 
 
Which means we need foods that support immunity, calm coughs, and keep digestion steady.
Try this nourishing stew recipe for a strong immune system.
 
Ingredients:
 
1 can of great northern beans
1 cup Japanese sweet potato (chopped)
1 tin coconut milk
2 cups vegetable broth or chicken stock
1 cup zucchini (chopped)
1 cup leeks (chopped)
1 tsp grated ginger
½ tsp garlic powder
1 tsp garam masala (mine is from diaspora)
¼ cup lime juice
1 tsp olive oil
Salt + pepper to taste
 
Recipe:
 
Heat a stainless steel pot and add olive oil.
Sauté chopped leeks, sweet potato, and zucchini until softened.
Add garlic powder + garam masala, then pour in broth. Bring to a boil, then simmer 15 minutes.
Add coconut milk, ginger, and northern beans. Simmer on low for 5 minutes.
Finish with salt, pepper, and a squeeze of lime juice, then serve.

text:
Are you feeling super irritated?

🥲 Comment RELIEF and I will send you Liver and total body supporting herbal formulas to help smooth the flow of your emotions along with the physical symptoms that manifest alongside of them.

In Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), our emotions give us clues to our physical state and vice versa. Certain times of year make us more susceptible to more environments, both physically and mentally. Turning into Autumn, we may find ourselves more irritable, more anxious and feeling melancholy. This has to do with our Liver, as the Liver governs our emotions, and are Lung and Large Intestine system which is the organ system that correlates to Autumn.

Our Liver system is in charge of keeping our Qi moving smoothly— especially our emotional energy. When the seasons shift from the moist warmth of late Summer into the cool, dry, boundary-setting energy of Autumn, the Liver Qi can get stuck. That stagnation shows up as irritability, tension in the neck and shoulders, headaches, even feeling emotionally short-fused.

The Lungs and Large Intestine are the organs that help us release and let go. If the Large Intestine isn’t functioning optimally— think sluggish bowels, bloating, or trouble physically “letting go”— it can trap that stagnant Liver energy. This creates both physical and emotional congestion.

A smooth transition through the seasons means supporting both systems: helping the Liver move freely and making sure the Large Intestine is eliminating well. Think warm, cooked foods, extra hydration, gentle stretching or twisting, deep breathing, and consistent meal times to keep the Qi flowing.

text:
Wishing the irreplaceable, Julie Andrews, a very Happy 90th Birthday today! 💐💐💖 In honor of this special day, let’s revisit the great story of two fair ladies! 

The 1956 Broadway production of ‘My Fair Lady’ was a notable critical and popular success, winning six Tony Awards, including Best Musical. Rex Harrison and Julie Andrews starred in the  production, which set a record for the longest run of any musical on Broadway up to that time.

When it came time to cast for the 1964 feature film, lyricist Alan Jay Lerner had his eye on Andrews for the hit Broadway show’s film adaptation. “I so wanted you to do it, Julie, but they wanted a name”, Lerner shared. The head of Warner Brothers, Jack Warner, had vetoed the decision and cast Audrey Hepburn instead. 

‘My Fair Lady’ was coincidentally released the same year as ‘Mary Poppins’ in which Andrews starred in. This resulted in some competition at the award shows between the two films. Andrews took home Best Actress for ‘Mary Poppins’. And though Hepburn wasn’t nominated for ‘My Fair Lady’, the overall film won the Academy Award for Best Picture.

When Andrews scooped the Golden Globe for her ‘Mary Poppins’ performance, she used the opportunity to shade Jack Warner by sarcastically thanking him for blocking her from joining the cast of ‘My Fair Lady’ once more. She said: “My thanks to a man who made a wonderful movie and who made all this possible in the first place, Mr. Jack Warner.” 

When Rex Harrison accepted his 1965 Best Actor Oscar for starring alongside Audrey Hepburn in the film, he thanked his “two fair ladies”—a nod to his long run alongside Julie Andrews in the original Broadway production.

💫 DEMYSTIFYING ACUPUNCTURE 💫 

In The Spark in the Machine, Dr. Daniel Keown explains acupuncture through the lens of both traditional Chinese medicine and modern embryology. He describes how the human body develops along energetic lines that are laid down during embryogenesis, which later correspond to the acupuncture meridians. These meridians aren’t “imaginary” channels but are rooted in the body’s developmental blueprint, guiding communication and coordination between tissues. In this way, acupuncture taps into the same organizing forces that first shaped us in the womb, reactivating the body’s innate intelligence to restore balance and healing.

Keown emphasizes that acupuncture works by influencing the fascia—the connective tissue network that runs throughout the body. Fascia is highly responsive to mechanical stimulation, such as the insertion and manipulation of a fine needle. When an acupuncturist stimulates a point, it sets off a chain of responses in the fascia and the underlying tissues, creating a ripple effect that travels along the pathways of least resistance. These pathways correspond closely to the classical meridians, allowing acupuncture to regulate circulation, reduce inflammation, and influence the nervous and endocrine systems.

Finally, Dr. Keown frames acupuncture as a method of restoring flow where energy or communication has become blocked. Illness and pain, in this view, arise when the body’s electrical and biochemical signals are interrupted or stuck. By needling precise points, acupuncture can unblock these areas, restoring normal signaling and promoting self-healing. This helps explain why acupuncture can influence such a wide range of conditions—from musculoskeletal pain to digestive issues to hormonal imbalances—because it works not on isolated symptoms but on the body’s underlying regulatory systems.

text:
Gastric pain and discomfort, often described as burning in nature and accompanied by acid regurgitation or heartburn, can arise from a variety of causes in modern medicine. Biomedically, excessive stomach acid, gastritis, peptic ulcers, or reflux disease are common contributors. Risk factors include frequent consumption of spicy, greasy, or fried foods, alcohol, smoking, and certain medications such as NSAIDs. Stress and irregular meal habits may further aggravate the stomach lining, leading to inflammation and increased acid production. Patients may experience symptoms such as epigastric burning pain, sour regurgitation, thirst, bad breath, and sometimes nausea or even minor bleeding, which reflect irritation of the gastric mucosa.

From the perspective of Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), this presentation corresponds to the pattern of Stomach Heat (胃热). In this syndrome, excessive internal heat accumulates in the Stomach, disturbing its normal function of receiving and digesting food. The condition may be triggered by overeating spicy or greasy foods, alcohol consumption, emotional stress that transforms into heat, or constitutional yang excess. Clinical manifestations typically include burning epigastric pain, a strong preference for cold drinks, acid reflux, foul breath, irritability, gum swelling or bleeding, constipation with dry stools, and excessive hunger.

Key acupoints for clearing Stomach Heat and relieving pain include ST44 Nei Ting (内庭) and CV12 Zhong Wan (中脘). Nei Ting, a fire-clearing point on the Stomach channel, strongly reduces excess heat, alleviates pain, and harmonizes digestion. Zhong Wan regulates the Stomach Qi, calms epigastric discomfort, and supports digestion. In herbal medicine, the classic approach involves formulas that clear heat from the Stomach, descend rebellious qi, and protect the gastric lining. One such prescription is Qing Wei San (清胃散), This formula is particularly suited for Stomach heat manifesting with toothache, gum inflammation, or bad breath.

text:
Here are 6 habits that have made a real difference in my energy, mood, and overall wellbeing in my 40s:

1. A daily check-in (just 2 minutes can shift everything)
Even on the busiest days, I take a moment to reconnect: journaling, a quick voice note, or simply talking to myself.
That tiny pause brings clarity after chaos. It helps me reset and return to myself.

2. Warm, real food, no cold drinks
My Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) doctor taught me that cold drinks can weaken digestion and reproductive health, especially for women in our 40s.
Since switching to warm, nourishing meals, I feel more grounded and supported from within.

3. Emotional healing = hormonal support
Whether it’s therapy, breathwork, or energy healing, I clear what I can’t carry.
Because emotions don’t disappear ,they settle in the body.
Making space for that work has changed my sleep, mood, and hormone health.

4. Time in nature , even 10 minutes helps
Earthing (yes, it’s a thing) has been shown to lower cortisol, calm the nervous system, and reduce inflammation.
Even in the city, I pause in the park, take off my shoes, and just breathe.

5. Rest as rhythm, not reward
Most workout advice is designed for men.
In my 40s, I’ve learned to move with my own rhythms: gentle workouts, deeper sleep, slower mornings.
It’s not about doing less. It’s about choosing what truly supports me.

6. Self-love : the habit that holds it all together
Not the aesthetic kind.
The kind where you choose what truly supports you, even when it’s not convenient.
You say yes to what nourishes you, no to what drains you, and trust that how you feel matters.
That’s what makes these habits stick , and why they actually work.

text:
Taught a yoga class this Saturday and introduced fall and Traditional Chinese medicine tips for the season. 
I've been studying TCM principles for yoga practice for a moment now and I love to always have them in mind for my daily life and yoga practice. 

Fall is an interesting time. It's a good one to build, or go back to a certain structure, routine or discipline in life. Having one really helps to stay focus on what's important and allows us to shed the rest away. Like trees have their leaves falling, they don't need dead leaves anymore. 

Right timing to drop what no longer serves us, have a  structure, cultivate essentialism and find clarity. 

The element for fall is the metal. Another metaphor for strength and structure. But metal can also be totally reshaped. Again, the idea of shedding and changing. 

The emotional characteristics of metal element is its capacity to process grief and move forward. Like being able to discern what has value and what doesn’t, to keep what nourishes us and let go of the rest.
When we are able to focus on the important, we get that sense of inner strength, clarity, and integrity. 

We may feel a lot of melancholy but all good, it's normal. It's part of the process of welcoming better. It's time to accept to slow down, to release, and to be more inward. 

The lungs and large intestines are the main organs in fall. Here too we can see how it all makes sense : 

The lungs are directly tied to the breath, which is the constant cycle of taking in and letting go. When we hold on to grief, the breath becomes shallow and the chest tight. When we breathe deeply and consciously, we give space for emotions to move and be released.

The large intestines is about letting go of waste, not only physically, but also symbolically, releasing old stories, guilt, attachments.

I could go on. I find this fascinating and the new class I shared on At-home today is about opening space for the lungs 🫁 and twists for a good intestines care.

post_owner.name: Dr. Lily Choi ☯︎ D. Ac, L. Ac
text:
In our modern world and in Western practices, we are taught to look at food in terms of its calories and nutrients. In fact, general practice is that if you stick to a certain amount of calories a day you will lose weight. And that usually is true! Is that best for the long term? There’s this assumption that everyone’s bodies are the same.

In Chinese medicine, food is viewed by its energetic properties. Whether or not a food is beneficial for you depends on your body’s constitution, situation and the qualities of that food. If that food has qualities that nurture your specific body situation, then it is healthy for you. 

One guiding principle that is universal in Chinese medicine as well as most Asian cultures around the world are that warm, cooked foods are the guiding principle. The way TCM views digestion is like a cooking pot. Our body needs food to be at the body’s temperature in order for the most efficient digestion. When the food is too cold, then the body needs to divert energy from other parts of the body to warm that food up in order to digest it. It tends to pull from the bottom half of the body, like from the reproductive organs first. This can lead to symptoms like painful periods, irregular body temperature, infertility, and weight imbalances. Cooked foods, even lightly cooked, can be thought of as partially already digested, so it takes less energy for the Spleen and Stomach to digest, making it easier on the entire body.

|| There’s growing clinical research that acupuncture around the time of embryo transfer can improve outcomes; gently, safely, naturally. 

I’ve see this first hand in clinic and have also been involved in a clinical trial in 2012/2013 where I supported women going through IVF with acupuncture. 

What the Studies Show 🔬 
•	A large meta-analysis of 20 trials (5,130 women) found that acupuncture as an adjunct to embryo transfer increased clinical pregnancy rates and live births compared to no adjunct treatment. 
•	Another recent updated meta-analysis confirmed that acupuncture improves clinical & ongoing pregnancy rates when paired with IVF-ET, though the effect on live birth rate is more modest. 
•	In women who’ve had repeated implantation failure, a randomized controlled trial using acupuncture + moxibustion before and after embryo transfer showed a clinical pregnancy rate of 35.7% (versus ~7-10% in control groups). 

How Acupuncture Supports Implantation (through a TCM lens) ☯️
•	Helps relax the uterus and reduce contractions so the embryo can implant more smoothly
•	Improves blood flow, micro-circulation and Qi to the womb lining (endometrium) → making it more receptive
•	Reduces stress and anxiety → lowering cortisol and supporting hormonal balance
•	Helps modulate immune responses locally so the embryo isn’t rejected

What This Means for our IVF warriors:❤️‍🔥
•	Acupuncture before and after ET appears most beneficial
•	Even if you’ve had failed transfers, acupuncture + moxa may offer added support
•	It’s not a guarantee, but data is promising, and many find it helpful emotionally & physically.

“You are only as young as your spine” is used in yoga, massage therapy, chiropractic, and other healing arts. The beauty of this message is noted below and why we say this … it just might be why I thoroughly love working the neck and back. 

Let’s start with 👇
1. Physical Youthfulness
	-The spine is the central support structure for the whole body. If it stays flexible, strong, and aligned, movement stays easy and pain-free.
	-Mobility & posture: A supple spine keeps joints lubricated, muscles balanced, and posture upright — all markers of vitality.
 - Circulation & breath: Movement of the spine encourages circulation of blood, lymph, and cerebrospinal fluid, which keeps tissues nourished.

2. Nervous System & Energy
	-The spine houses the spinal cord, the main communication highway of the nervous system.
	-When the spine is healthy, nerve signals travel freely, supporting organ function, reflexes, and overall vitality.
	-In yoga and Chinese medicine, the spine is seen as the channel for life force (prana / qi), so spinal blockages = reduced vitality.

There’s that word again… VITALITY!💪

3. Symbolic & Psychological Dimension
	-A flexible spine symbolizes adaptability and resilience. Rigidity in the spine often reflects rigidity in life….read that again !
	•	A bent or stiff spine (hunched posture, immobility) is culturally and physiologically associated with aging.
	•	In contrast, the upright, open spine of a child or healthy adult radiates energy, confidence, and youth.

4. Traditions that Emphasize This
	•	Yoga: “You are as young as your spine is flexible.” Backbends, twists, and forward folds are designed to keep the spine supple.
	•	Massage & Bodywork: Many techniques (Swedish, Rolfing, Thai massage) focus on freeing restrictions in the spine to restore vitality.
	•	Ayurveda & TCM: The spine is a channel for energy; keeping it open is key to maintaining youth and health.

In a superficial world, one’s true youth is said to be “in the spine” because the spine’s health determines mobility, nerve flow, energy, and posture…all of which are hallmarks of being young, vital, and resilient. Now go live your best life !💪#livebright

Male menopause is often referred to as andropause or late-onset hypogonadism. Unlike female menopause, which is a clear and rapid transition, male menopause happens gradually as testosterone levels decline with age.

⸻

🌟 What is Male Menopause (Andropause)?
	•	A collection of physical, emotional, and hormonal changes in men, usually between ages 40–60.
	•	Related to a steady decline in testosterone production (~1% per year after age 30).
	•	Not every man experiences noticeable symptoms, and the severity varies.

⸻

🌟 Common Symptoms
	•	Physical:
	•	Low energy & fatigue
	•	Decreased muscle mass, strength, and endurance
	•	Increased body fat, sometimes around the abdomen
	•	Reduced libido & sexual performance issues
	•	Hot flashes or night sweats (less common but possible)
	•	Emotional & Cognitive:
	•	Mood swings, irritability, or depression
	•	Reduced motivation & confidence
	•	Difficulty concentrating or memory problems
	•	Sleep disturbances

⸻

🌟 Health Considerations
	•	Increased risk of osteoporosis (weak bones)
	•	Higher chance of metabolic syndrome (diabetes, hypertension, obesity)
	•	Possible cardiovascular risks if unmanaged

⸻

🌟 Ways to Manage

Lifestyle & Natural Support
	•	Regular exercise (strength + cardio) to maintain testosterone and muscle mass
	•	Balanced diet: rich in protein, zinc, magnesium, healthy fats (nuts, seeds, fish)
	•	Adequate sleep & stress management

Medical Options
	•	Testosterone Replacement Therapy (TRT) – can help but must be closely monitored by a doctor
	•	Medications for specific symptoms (ED, depression, insomnia)

Holistic Approaches
	•	Yoga & meditation for stress and hormonal balance
	•	Ayurveda: Ashwagandha, Shilajit, Safed Musli
	•	TCM/Sujok: points for kidney and adrenal energy systems

⸻

✨ Male menopause isn’t an abrupt “end,” but a gradual shift into a new life phase. With healthy lifestyle, holistic support, and medical care when needed, men can stay strong, vibrant, and emotionally balanced.

Premenopause is the stage in a woman’s life that leads up to menopause. It refers to the entire reproductive life before menopause, including the years when periods are regular and fertility is present, but it is often used to describe the early changes that begin several years before menopause when hormone levels start to fluctuate.

⸻

🌸 Key Features of Premenopause
	•	Regular Menstrual Cycles: Periods may still be consistent, though sometimes lighter or heavier.
	•	Hormonal Shifts: Gradual decline and fluctuations in estrogen and progesterone.
	•	Subtle Symptoms: Some women may notice early changes like mild hot flashes, mood swings, or sleep disturbances, while others don’t feel much difference.
	•	Fertility Still Possible: Pregnancy can still occur, though fertility slowly declines.

⸻

🌸 Common Symptoms
	•	Irregular or changing menstrual flow
	•	Breast tenderness or bloating
	•	Mood changes, irritability, or anxiety
	•	Mild hot flashes or night sweats
	•	Vaginal dryness (in some women)
	•	Trouble sleeping or fatigue

⸻

🌸 Supporting the Body in Premenopause
	•	Nutrition: Balanced diet rich in calcium, magnesium, vitamin D, and healthy fats
	•	Lifestyle: Regular exercise, yoga, pranayama, and meditation
	•	Herbal & Natural Support:
	•	Ayurveda: Shatavari, Ashwagandha, Triphala
	•	Western Herbs: Black cohosh, red clover, evening primrose
	•	Sujok/TCM: Focus on balancing hormones, liver, kidney, and spleen energy systems
	•	Self-Care: Adequate rest, stress reduction, creative outlets

⸻

✨ In simple terms, premenopause is the transitionary stage before menopause where the body begins to signal hormonal changes. It can last anywhere from 2 to 10 years before actual menopause sets in. 🌺

post_owner.name: Vandana Kohli
text:
Menopause is a natural biological process that marks the end of a woman’s menstrual cycles. It is officially diagnosed after 12 consecutive months without a period, usually between the ages of 45 and 55, though it can occur earlier or later.

⸻

🌸 Causes
	•	Natural decline of estrogen and progesterone as the ovaries age
	•	Surgical removal of ovaries (surgical menopause)
	•	Some medical treatments like chemotherapy or radiation

⸻

🌸 Common Symptoms
	•	Hot flashes & night sweats
	•	Irregular or skipped periods (before they stop fully)
	•	Vaginal dryness & discomfort during intimacy
	•	Mood swings, irritability, anxiety, or depression
	•	Sleep disturbances & fatigue
	•	Weight gain, slowed metabolism, or hair thinning
	•	Memory lapses (“brain fog”)

⸻

🌸 Health Considerations
	•	Increased risk of osteoporosis (weaker bones)
	•	Higher chance of cardiovascular issues (due to lower estrogen)
	•	Urogenital changes (bladder or urinary issues)

⸻

🌸 Ways to Manage

Lifestyle & Natural Support
	•	Balanced diet rich in calcium, vitamin D, and phytoestrogens (soy, flaxseed)
	•	Regular exercise (yoga, walking, strength training for bone health)
	•	Stress management (meditation, pranayama, mindfulness)
	•	Adequate hydration & sleep hygiene

Medical Options
	•	Hormone Replacement Therapy (HRT) – effective but must be discussed with a doctor due to risks/benefits
	•	Non-hormonal medications for hot flashes, mood, or bone health
	•	Vaginal moisturizers & lubricants

Holistic & Alternative Therapies
	•	Ayurveda: herbs like Shatavari, Ashwagandha
	•	TCM/Sujok: points for hormonal balance & emotional regulation
	•	Reiki, meditation, crystal healing (moonstone, rose quartz, amethyst)

⸻

✨ Menopause is not an illness—it’s a transition into a new phase of life. Many women find it as a time of empowerment, self-discovery, and spiritual growth. 🌺

How to make tea, Gong Fu style, in a mini tea pot! 🍃🫖 Gong Fu brewing is a traditional Chinese method of making tea that puts emphasis on the quality and quantity of tea and water used, temperature of water, length of steeping, and material of teaware. I’m using this mini tea set—with a tea pot that fits in the palm of my hand (the small size made it a bit difficult for pouring but this was a fun experience)!

While in the West, people often refer to it as “tea ceremony,” this translation is not an accurate way to think of Gong Fu style tea, as there are usually no religious or ceremonial aspects. Instead, Gong Fu style tea is most often done among friends or family and with the primary goal of enjoying quality tea together. It can also be done when having tea alone!

While some tea drinkers may be fussier than others, tea drinking in China is usually thought of as a casual activity, with no aspect considered off-limits for “outside groups” and few techniques considered absolutes. Therefore, there is no need to ever feel daunted or intimidated by tea—the main goal should always be the tasting and enjoyment of the tea itself!

We now have a wide selection of sticky rice Pu’er teas sourced directly from Yunnan 🍚 Note: we’ve had a lot of questions about our sticky rice Pu’er. These tea cakes are naturally sticky rice flavored using a plant indigenous to the Southern Yunnan rainforests near Laos called Semnostachya Menglaensis. This is a local plant in the Xishuangbanna Autonomous Prefecture, one of the most species-rich forest ecosystems in China—it’s home to the most wild elephants in China! There are no actual carbs or rice in this tea.

Because the tea cakes I’m using are highly compressed, a 30 second steep is necessary. Loose Pu’er or less compressed Pu’er usually only needs 10-15 seconds of steeping.

Have you tried tea Gong Fu style? Would you ever try making tea in such a small tea pot? 🫖🍵

text:
I’ll be honest, I like a cold drink every now and then too. They’re refreshing, especially on a hot day. But from a Traditional Chinese Medicine perspective, our digestion doesn’t love it quite as much.

The Spleen and Stomach are thought of as the “engine” of digestion, and that engine runs on warmth. When we constantly introduce iced or very cold drinks, that Yang energy is forced to work overtime just to warm things up before transformation can even happen. Over time this can look like slower digestion, bloating, fatigue, loose stools, or Dampness that shows up as heaviness and congestion in the body.
That doesn’t mean you need to avoid iced drinks forever. It’s about balance and awareness. 

If you’re craving something cold, notice how your body responds. Try sipping slowly rather than gulping, pair it with a warm meal, or offset with warming spices like ginger or cinnamon. Save the iced drinks for hotter days when your body naturally craves cooling.

In TCM, protecting your Yang energy is foundational for long-term vitality. But joy matters too, and sometimes part of balance is allowing the occasional iced matcha or smoothie while knowing how to support yourself when you do. ❄️

Type 2 diabetes is often understood as a problem of high blood sugar and insulin resistance, yet both recent clinical research and Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) suggest a more empowering picture. 

In TCM, diabetes is closely linked with spleen qi deficiency (including the stomach and pancreas). When spleen qi is weak, food is not properly converted into energy, dampness accumulates, and the pancreas struggles to regulate blood sugar. This mirrors what Western science describes when insulin production and glucose metabolism begin to fail.

Recent studies confirm that people with type 2 diabetes are more likely to have low levels of essential minerals. Magnesium deficiency is common, and supplementation has been shown to improve blood sugar and reduce inflammation in clinical trials (Frontiers in Nutrition, 2022; JCEM, 2024). 

Potassium deficiency is also linked with higher risk of developing diabetes, and higher potassium intake is associated with fewer cardiovascular events in people with the condition (Nutrients, 2022; Cardiovascular Diabetology, 2024). 

Chromium has been studied extensively, with some trials showing modest benefits for glucose control, though results remain mixed (Environmental Geochemistry & Health, 2024).

From a natural healing perspective, this means that nourishing the spleen and pancreas with mineral-rich foods, restful lifestyle habits, and stress reduction can support the body’s own capacity to restore balance! Magnesium, in particular, is deeply healing to the spleen network, helping the body transform food into energy rather than dampness, and offering a bridge between ancient wisdom and modern science.

• Location of the pain?
• Onset? Duration? Acute or chronic?
• The nature of the pain: stabbing, aching or dull?
• Constant? Comes & goes?
• Better with cold or heat?
• Better or worse with massage?

Here's the TCM diagnosis for the quality of Pain: 
• Achy or dull pain: deficiency
• Constant pain: excess
• Stabbing pain, fixed local pain: Blood stasis

• Better with cold: excess Heat
• Better with heat: Excess Cold

✨ Acupressure & the Stomach Meridian: Unlocking Whole-Body Balance ✨

Acupressure isn’t just another “hands-on” technique—it’s a centuries-old healing art rooted in Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), and it’s transforming the way holistic animal professionals care for horses, dogs, and cats. Unlike massage or other bodywork that focus mainly on muscles and joints, acupressure works by stimulating energy pathways called meridians, which connect organs, emotions, and physical function.

By pressing or holding specific acupoints, we can influence digestion, calm anxiety, regulate immunity, and restore balance through the entire body. That’s why acupressure is becoming such a powerful tool in holistic practice—it bridges physical and energetic healing.

🌿 The Stomach Meridian
This is one of the longest and most influential meridians. It begins near the eye, runs down the face, neck, chest, and abdomen, then travels along the hind limbs to the hoof or paw. It governs digestion, appetite, muscle tone, and emotional grounding. Imbalances often show up as colic, ulcers, bloating, poor appetite, stiffness, or anxiety.

✨ 3 Key Points on the Stomach Meridian:

ST 36 (Zusanli – “Leg Three Miles”): Below the stifle, just forward of the tibia. Boosts digestion, immunity, energy, and vitality.

ST 25 (Tianshu – “Heaven’s Pivot”): About 2–3 finger widths from the umbilicus. Regulates the intestines and eases digestive upset.

ST 45 (Lidui – “Strict Exchange”):
• Horses – lateral side of the coronet band, away from the midline.
• Dogs & Cats – lateral side of the nail bed on the second hind toe.
Calms anxiety, clears excess heat, and soothes stress-related digestion issues.

When these points are stimulated, their effects ripple through the entire system—improving gut health, emotional balance, and overall vitality.

text:
It's staggering to me how much society has normalized medicating our problems. 
 
And then medicating the side effects of those medications... 
 
Now before the mob shows up in the comments section, let me say that yes obviously western medicine has saved some lives and been useful. For some people it's the only thing keeping them alive. 
 
I get it. 
 
And it's particularly effective in an immediate crisis. 
 
The problem is when we try to take crisis medicine and stretch it into a medium or long term patch... 
 
The good news is if you practice Eastern Medicine or a similar modality that works *with* rather than *against* the body then there is an astounding number of people you can help. 
 
Most practitioners are worried about having enough patients when the reality is once people know what you can do and how elegant your solutions are you'll wish you could clone yourself to handle the flood. 
 
Take a moment to consider your mission to make the world a healthier more vibrant place. 
 
And let's acknowledge that if you can help someone manage the side effects of their meds (or, gasp, wean off them entirely!) you're not only helping one person have more quality of life.. 
 
You're helping their family get them back. 
 
Clinical Clarity means being able to navigate a mess of patterns and complexity in a streamlined, systematic way. 
 
So that you're not guessing which formula to use next. Rather bringing your patients through a systematic process of getting healthier. 
 
With milestones they understand and can feel so that they know it's working. And you know when to pivot or stay the course. 
 
The confidence that comes from this is palpable, and the patients can feel it. Which is important because if they've been heavily indoctrinated into industrialized medicine it may be difficult for them to open up to new ways. 
 
Your confidence can inspire. 
 
But you can't fake it.

Coconut Milk Chai Latte

Want a discount for chai from @thenaturalmkt comment TEA below and I can send you one!

The Recipe - makes 2 cups 
1 cup organic coconut milk from a carton( if you can go organic, some coconut milk has additives. If you use a tin of coconut milk use half a cup and froth it)
½ cup water
1–2 organic chai teabags (or equivalent loose tea)
Extra cinnamon to taste
Gently heat coconut milk and water, add teabags, and simmer 5–7 minutes. Do not boil the tea. Remove the tea, whisk or froth, and finish with a dusting of cinnamon.
 
Why It’s Perfect for This Season (TCM Insight)
Autumn in Traditional Chinese Medicine relates to the Lungs and is prone to dryness.
Coconut milk nourishes Yin and moistens the lungs and skin.
Warming spices (chai blend + cinnamon) support digestion, boost circulation, and protect against the cool, dry air.
 
Who Might Skip or Modify
Caffeine-sensitive? Choose a rooibos-based chai.
Digestive weakness or “dampness” (loose stools, heavy feeling)? Use less coconut milk or dilute with more water.
Blood-sugar concerns? Keep it unsweetened as I did.

The menstrual cycle unfolds in four phases: menstrual, follicular, ovulatory, and luteal. Each is marked by distinct physiological shifts, and in Traditional Chinese Medicine these stages are also understood through changes in Blood, Yin, Yang, Qi, and Shen.
-
By @rootandbones 

This dual lens shows us something essential: the body’s needs are not static. What nourishes in one phase may not be what supports in the next.

Rather than the casual notion of a ‘girl dinner’ made of snacks, this is nourishment that actively engages with the cycle — iron and mineral-rich foods during menstruation, fluid-building proteins and fruits in the follicular phase, cooling and antioxidant support around ovulation, and warming, stabilizing meals in the luteal phase.

In TCM, animal foods are not incidental but central, they are recognized for their ability to restore Blood, strengthen Qi, and carry the body through transitions.

‘Girl dinner’ reimagined as food that doesn’t just fill, but fortifies. 🍲🥚🐟🍇

So, what's a  tongue diagnosis?

In TCM, tongue diagnosis is a diagnostic method that involves observing the tongue's shape, color, texture, and coating to gain insights into the health of the body's internal organs and overall energy status. TCM theory suggests that different parts of the tongue correspond to specific organs, so practitioners look for clues in areas like the tongue's tip (heart and lungs) or center (stomach and digestive system).

 What is observed?
TCM practitioners examine several aspects of the tongue: 

Tongue Colour:The colour of the tongue body can indicate the overall condition of the body, with red often signaling heat or inflammation, and pale indicating a deficiency. 

Tongue Coating:The thickness, color, and distribution of the coating are noted. A thick coating can suggest a buildup of fluid or pathogens, while a thick white coating might point to a cold, damp condition. A lack of coating can suggest Yin deficiency. 

Tongue Shape and Texture:The tongue's size and shape can reveal imbalances. For example, teeth marks on the sides of the tongue can indicate digestive system weakness or an accumulation of dampness. 

Moisture:The degree of moisture in the tongue is also assessed; a very dry tongue might signal a lack of fluids, while a very wet one could indicate excess dampness, according to Thomson Medical. 

Cracks and Spots:The presence of cracks, red dots, or "strawberry" dots can signify stagnation or inflammation in the body. 

How is it used?

Internal Organ Health:By using a "tongue map," practitioners can link specific areas of the tongue to corresponding organs, such as the stomach, heart, or liver. 

Understanding Disease:The tongue provides clues about the nature of a disease, the state of the vital energy (qi) and blood, and the progression of illness. 

Guiding Treatment:Based on these observations, a TCM practitioner can determine a patient's TCM syndrome and develop a personalised treatment plan.

post_owner.name: Vandana Kohli
text:
In Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), emotions are not seen as separate from the body—they are an integral part of health. Each of the Five Zang (organ systems) is associated with a specific emotion, and when emotions are excessive, repressed, or unbalanced, they can damage the organ and disrupt Qi (energy) flow.

Here’s the classic Five Emotions (Wu Zhi, 五志) framework:

⸻

🌿 The Five Emotions in TCM
	1.	Liver – Anger (怒, Nù)
	•	Related emotions: frustration, resentment, irritability.
	•	Balanced: gives courage, assertiveness, ability to plan.
	•	Imbalanced: causes Qi to rise, leading to headaches, dizziness, high blood pressure, menstrual issues.
	2.	Heart – Joy (喜, Xǐ)
	•	Related emotions: excitement, agitation, overexuberance.
	•	Balanced: warmth, love, inspiration, good communication.
	•	Imbalanced: too much joy or over-stimulation scatters Shen (spirit), causing insomnia, anxiety, palpitations.
	3.	Spleen – Worry/Overthinking (思, Sī)
	•	Related emotions: pensiveness, obsessive thoughts, rumination.
	•	Balanced: promotes clear thinking, studying, intention.
	•	Imbalanced: damages digestion, leading to bloating, fatigue, poor concentration.
	4.	Lungs – Grief/Sadness (悲, Bēi)
	•	Related emotions: sorrow, melancholy, longing.
	•	Balanced: ability to process loss, let go, show compassion.
	•	Imbalanced: weakens Qi, causing shortness of breath, low immunity, fatigue, skin issues.
	5.	Kidneys – Fear (恐, Kǒng)
	•	Related emotions: fright, chronic insecurity, phobias.
	•	Balanced: caution, willpower, survival instinct.
	•	Imbalanced: depletes Kidney Qi/Essence, leading to urinary problems, infertility, premature aging.

⸻

⚖️ TCM Perspective
	•	Excess of an emotion → injures its organ.
	•	Weakness in an organ → makes a person prone to that emotion.
	•	Balance is maintained through moderation, expression, and free flow of Qi.

⸻

✨ Bonus:
TCM also considers shock/trauma (惊, Jīng) as an emotion, mainly affecting the Heart and Kidneys.

- Very cooling, clears heat & dampness.

In Traditional Chinese Medicine, the back of the neck is called the Wind Gate (Feng Men)🌬️. It’s considered one of the most vulnerable entry points for external pathogens like “Wind,” which often carries cold or heat. When the Wind Gate is left unprotected — especially during the fall and winter months — it can allow these external factors to penetrate, leading to symptoms like chills, sore throat, stiff neck, headaches, or the onset of a cold or flu.

Covering the Wind Gate 🧣 is one of the simplest and most effective preventative practices. A scarf isn’t just a cozy accessory — it’s a protective layer that helps maintain your body’s defensive Qi (Wei Qi). In TCM, Wei Qi is your outermost shield, circulating at the surface of the body to protect you against illness. When Wei Qi is strong and the Wind Gate is guarded, you’re less likely to “catch” what’s going around. 🍂

This is why, as acupuncturists, we’re constantly reminding people to wear scarves as soon as the weather shifts. Prevention is central to Chinese medicine: supporting the body before it’s under attack. Something as small as keeping your neck warm and covered can make a meaningful difference in how resilient you feel throughout the season. 🍂

First day of fall is today, make this to transition from summer heat to autumn dryness. 

🥣 Autumn Elixir Recipe (4 servings)
* adjust to your liking, I usually make 2 servings. 
Ingredients I use can be found in my amazon under TCM.

Ingredients
- 20g dried snow fungus (soaked until soft, tough center removed)
- 30g lotus seeds
- 10g dried lily bulb
- 20g Chinese yam (dried slices)
- 30g pearl barley (Job’s tears, rinse well)
- 1 apple, sliced
- 6–7 cups water

Instructions
1. Rinse all dried herbs and soak snow fungus in warm water until softened (about 30 minutes). Trim and tear into small florets (can be done before or after it’s all boiled).
2. In a large pot, add all ingredients & water. Bring to a boil.
3. Lower to a simmer and cook for 30+ minutes.
4. Boil until everything is tender and soup turns slightly thick and silky.

✨ Best enjoyed a few times per week as the seasons change — a grounding ritual to keep your digestion strong, skin hydrated, and spirit calm as autumn settles in.

In Traditional Chinese Medicine, the Metal element represents clarity, structure, and refinement. It is linked to the autumn season, a time of harvest, release, and preparation for winter. Just as metal can be shaped yet retains its strength, this element symbolizes resilience, discipline, and the ability to let go. In the human body, Metal corresponds to the Lungs and Large Intestine, which govern breathing, elimination, and the exchange of energy with the environment. On a deeper level, Metal reflects the capacity to find value, honor boundaries, and connect with a sense of purity or higher purpose.

The Lungs, regarded as the “delicate organ” in TCM, are central to the Metal element. They control respiration, regulate qi, and distribute defensive qi that protects the body from external pathogens. The Large Intestine, Metal’s paired organ, governs elimination, symbolizing the ability to release waste both physically and emotionally. A balanced Metal element manifests as strong immunity, clear skin, a steady breath, and a healthy sense of detachment and order. When Metal is out of balance, however, symptoms such as coughs, asthma, constipation, or skin conditions may appear. Emotionally, imbalance often reveals itself as grief, rigidity, or difficulty letting go of the past.

Nurturing the Metal element involves practices that support the lungs, strengthen immunity, and cultivate acceptance. Breathing exercises, qigong, or spending time in fresh air are particularly beneficial for Metal’s energy. Foods that are pungent in flavour, such as onions, garlic, and radish, are said to aid lung qi, while warm soups and cooked grains prepare the body for the cooler season of autumn. Acupuncture and herbal formulas can help regulate lung function, resolve phlegm, and support the Large Intestine. Ultimately, the Metal element teaches the value of clarity, integrity, and release. Just as autumn trees shed their leaves, a balanced Metal energy allows us to let go of what no longer serves us while holding onto what is essential, leading to resilience, purity, and inner strength.💕

text:
The ultimate gut-friendly fall breakfast? Stewed apples 🍎 🥣 

As the seasons change, I swap my juicer for my slow cooker and salads for soups and stews. It’s important to adjust your diet as the days become shorter and air becomes cooler to avoid falling sick. When I was going through health issues my TCM doctor told me my body was damp and cold and that most North American women need to swap out the iced drinks, smoothies and salads for teas, soups and warming foods. This simple swap made all the difference in my health! 

Here’s why they seriously deserve a spot in your morning routine:

🍎 Reduce bloating: Cooking apples breaks down the fiber, making them easier to digest — perfect if your gut is feeling sensitive.
🍎 Feed your good gut bacteria: Apples are rich in pectin, a prebiotic fiber that acts like food for your microbiome.
🍎 Support regular digestion: Warm foods are easier on your system, especially in cooler months when your digestive fire naturally slows down. 
🍎 Balance blood sugar: The natural sweetness of stewed apples helps curb cravings, without spiking your glucose.
🍎 Packed with antioxidants: Especially in the peel — cinnamon and cloves add even more anti-inflammatory magic.

Recipe. Chop 8-10 apples and add to pot on medium-low heat with about 1/3 cup water and fresh chopped ginger. Cover and let cook for 5ish minutes until apples become soft. Drizzle with a little coconut oil and lots of spices: nutmeg, clove + cinnamon until cooked through.

I like always warm them back up on the stove and top with the grass-fed Greek yogurt! For the pumpkin pie crumble, blend 1/2 cup walnuts, 1/2 cup pumpkin seeds, 1:2 cup pecans, 1/2 cup hemp hearts, 2 Tbsp pumpkin pie spice and a pinch of pinch of sea salt. 

This is best made the night before because when the apples are refrigerated the fibre becomes much higher in prebiotics, meaning much easier to digest and essentially feed the good bacteria in our gut to help them thrive.

The menstrual cycle unfolds in four phases: menstrual, follicular, ovulatory, and luteal. Each is marked by distinct physiological shifts, and in Traditional Chinese Medicine these stages are also understood through changes in Blood, Yin, Yang, Qi, and Shen.

This dual lens shows us something essential: the body’s needs are not static. What nourishes in one phase may not be what supports in the next.

Rather than the casual notion of a ‘girl dinner’ made of snacks, this is nourishment that actively engages with the cycle — iron and mineral-rich foods during menstruation, fluid-building proteins and fruits in the follicular phase, cooling and antioxidant support around ovulation, and warming, stabilizing meals in the luteal phase.

In TCM, animal foods are not incidental but central, they are recognized for their ability to restore Blood, strengthen Qi, and carry the body through transitions.

‘Girl dinner’ reimagined as food that doesn’t just fill, but fortifies. 🍲🥚🐟🍇
