I was so skeptical at 1st, but when I noticed the 2 teeth I had root canals done on are linked to migraines, I simply had to look deeper.
Your teeth are not just for chewing — they can have a direct and significant impact on your overall health. Here’s a breakdown of how specific teeth (or their problems) can influence different systems in the body:

🦷 1. Molars (especially wisdom teeth)
Location: Back of the mouth
Role in Body Health:
Impacted molars can cause chronic inflammation, infections, and even headaches or jaw tension.
According to some cranial nerve mapping and acupuncture theories, upper molars are connected to the sinuses, and infected or decayed upper molars can contribute to chronic sinus issues.

🦷 2. Incisors (front teeth)
Location: Front center (top and bottom)
Role in Body Health:
Connected to the urinary tract, kidneys, and ears (according to certain traditional Eastern medicine and meridian theories).
Cracks or trauma here can sometimes lead to nerve sensitivity, which may result in referred pain in the jaw or even the neck.

🦷 3. Canines (cuspids)
Location: Pointed teeth next to the incisors
Role in Body Health:
Associated with the liver and gallbladder in meridian charts.
Often tied to emotional expression (e.g., anger and assertiveness in some psychological/energetic models).
Problems here could reflect digestive or hormonal issues in holistic traditions.

🦷 4. Premolars (bicuspids)
Location: Between canines and molars
Role in Body Health:
Linked to the lungs and large intestine in acupuncture/TCM mapping.
Sensitivity in these teeth may correspond with respiratory problems, allergies, or gut inflammation.

🧠 Neuro-Muscular Connection:
Each tooth sits near cranial and facial nerves (especially the trigeminal nerve).
An infection or abscess in a tooth can irritate these nerves, sometimes causing:

Facial pain or numbness

Migraine-like headaches

Referred neck or shoulder pain

❤️ Systemic Health Links:
Gum disease (often starting around molars) is strongly linked to:

Heart disease

Diabetes

Stroke

Infections in upper teeth can spread to the brain in rare but serious cases.

🔥Having a hard time sleeping in this heat?  A major heatwave is gripping most of the country. It’s not just the temperature. Humidity is rising too, and that makes it harder for your body to cool down at night.

This is due in part to evapotranspiration, a process where moisture is released from plants into the air. This increases humidity and makes it harder for the body to cool down through sweat.

High humidity blocks your body’s natural cooling mechanism. When sweat can’t evaporate, internal heat builds up. This raises the risk for heat exhaustion and heat stroke, especially in vulnerable groups:
• children
• elderly
• pregnant women
• individuals with asthma, allergies, or heart conditions

If your sleep has been off, your nervous system may be stuck in overdrive from the heat.

Here’s a calming practice to try:

Press Heart 7, located on the inside of your wrist near the pinky side. This point calms the Shen, or spirit, and helps settle an overactive mind.
Then try Yintang, the point between your eyebrows. It helps release heat, reduce tension, and quiet the nervous system.

Pair this with deep breathing and a cool, dark room. These small steps can help your system reset when the weather is working against you.

text:
Turkey Rhubarb (Rheum palmatum) is grown for the root (pictured in cross-section), which when cured is an efficient laxative--evacuating, then astringing. It takes a couple of years and some applications of compost to get plants this large, but then the root production is prodigious. You can identify them by the palmate leaf, different from the entire leaf margin seen on the standard garden rhubarb (Rheum rhabarbarum), which is grown for the stalks. Seeds available online at Strictly Medicinal Seeds. An epic plant.
(Link in profile)

Turkey Rhubarb (Rheum palmatum)
Family: Buckwheat (Polygonaceae)
Hardy to Zones 6 to 9
(Da-huang; Turkey Rhubarb; Chinese Rhubarb; Rhubarb, Chinese) Herbaceous perennial. Native to China and Tibet. Rare. Plants boast red-tinged, handsomely palmate leaves, and are much appreciated in the ornamental garden for their shape, color, and colorful history. Traditional usage of dried, cured root (TWM, TCM): Laxative. Source of anthraquinones. Taste mild. It is amazing how quickly usable quantities of this herb can be grown--a reasonable harvest can be made in the fall of the first year's growth. Dig the roots, wash throughly, slice, pierce, and hang to dry and cure. Plant prefers part shade to full sun, well-drained soils of raised bed or hilliside. Best to sow in spring in flats and transplant out to field after the roots have grown sufficiently large to survive out-of doors. Leaves generally have an entire margin in the first year and demonstrate palmate structure in the second year. Sometimes, fast-growing and healthy individuals will start making palmate leaves in the first year. Average germination time 13 days. Space plants 2 to 3 feet apart.

In Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), timing your meals with the body’s organ clock is believed to support digestion, energy, and overall health. Here’s a quick breakdown of ideal meal times according to the TCM organ clock:

✦ Breakfast (7 AM – 9 AM)

Stomach time
This is considered the most important meal of the day. The stomach Qi is strongest during this window, making it the ideal time for a warm, nourishing breakfast—think congee, steamed veggies, soft eggs, or soups. Avoid cold smoothies or raw foods, which can weaken digestive fire.

✦ Lunch (11 AM – 1 PM)

Heart time
Qi and blood are flowing strongly. This is the best time to eat your main, most substantial meal. Ideally something cooked and balanced (grains, protein, veggies) to fuel the rest of the day.

✦ Dinner (5 PM – 7 PM)

Kidney time
The digestive system starts to wind down, so dinner should be lighter and earlier. A warm, easy-to-digest meal—like soups or stir-fried veggies—is ideal. Avoid heavy or late dinners, which can tax the Spleen and cause stagnation.

✦ Avoid eating heavily after 7 PM

After this, the body enters its rest and repair phase. Eating too late can interfere with the Liver and Gallbladder’s detox process (active from 11 PM – 3 AM), and disrupt sleep and digestion

TCM tip: Consistency is key. Eat meals around the same time daily to support Spleen Qi and digestion. Warm, cooked foods are almost always favored over cold, raw ones—especially in the morning and evening.

text:
Gout occurs when urate crystals build up in the joints, causing sudden pain, swelling, and inflammation.
These crystals form when there are high levels of uric acid in the blood — a substance produced when the body breaks down purines, which are found in the body and in foods like red meat, organ meats, and certain seafood (e.g. sardines, mussels, tuna). Alcohol (especially beer) and fructose-sweetened drinks can also raise uric acid levels. Normally, uric acid is filtered by the kidneys and excreted in urine. But if too much is produced or too little is excreted, it accumulates and forms sharp crystals in the joints, triggering a gout attack.

In Traditional Chinese Medicine, gout is seen as more than just a buildup of uric acid — it reflects a deeper imbalance in the body’s internal systems. Gout is classified under “Bi Syndrome” (痹症), which means “obstruction syndrome.” This occurs when external factors such as Wind, Damp, Cold, or Heat invade the joints and block the normal flow of Qi and Blood. At the same time, internal weaknesses such as Spleen deficiency, Liver Qi stagnation, or Kidney deficiency make the body more susceptible to these external influences. 

A weak Spleen fails to properly transform and transport fluids, leading to the accumulation of dampness. Over time, this dampness can combine with internal heat and stagnation, forming damp-heat that causes redness, swelling, and pain in the joints. If the Kidney essence is deficient, it cannot nourish the bones and joints adequately, resulting in chronic, recurrent gout attacks. TCM aims to treat both the symptoms and the root cause, restoring harmony and preventing flare-ups.

TCM doesn’t just chase the uric acid—it looks at the pattern behind your symptoms. Identifying your unique syndrome is the first step to long-lasting relief.

post_owner.name: Diana Wilson
text:
🍏stewed apples🍏 
a TCM remedy for weak digestion 

Ingredients: 
	• 2 organic unwaxed apples (I love green) 
	• 1 cup filtered water (or enough to just cover the apples)
	• 2–3 medjool dates (pitted) or 4 Chinese red dates (jujubes)
	• 2/3 thin slices fresh ginger (warming for digestion)
	• ½ tsp ground cinnamon / 1 cinnamon stick 
	• small pinch of nutmeg & cloves (for extra warmth)

Instructions:
	1. Prepare the apples: Wash, core & chop into chunks or slices (skin can be left on for extra fiber).
	2. Simmer: In a small saucepan, add the apples, water, dates & ginger • Bring to a gentle simmer.
	3. Add spices: Stir in the cinnamon & any other warming spices.
	4. Cook: Cover & simmer on low for 10–15 minutes, until apples are soft but not mush

Nutritional Benefits:
	• Vitamin C & antioxidants – support immunity
	• Natural fiber (pectin) – feeds good gut bacteria & balances blood sugar
	• Warming spices (ginger & cinnamon) – improve circulation & digestion
	• Medjool or Chinese red dates – boost qi & blood in TCM

Why the Juice is Good:
	• Nutrient leaching: Vitamin C, minerals (like potassium) & polyphenols naturally move from the apple into the cooking water 
	• Digestive benefits: The warm, lightly sweet liquid contains soluble fiber (pectin) & the essence of the ginger, dates & cinnamon you’ve added, this is gentle, nourishing & hydrating 
	• TCM perspective: The stewing liquid carries the “essence” (qi) of the apples & herbs, making it a warm, easily assimilated tonic for the spleen & stomach

@White peony and lotus, while both plants with cultural and medicinal significance, have distinct uses. The white peony (Paeonia lactiflora) is primarily used in traditional Chinese medicine for its potential anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and blood clotting-related properties. The lotus (Nelumbo nucifera) is widely cultivated for its edible seeds, and its various parts (flowers, petals, leaves, rhizomes) are used in religious offerings, culinary traditions, and even traditional medicine. 

White Peony (Paeonia lactiflora):

Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM): Used to address various ailments, including pain, swelling, and blood clotting issues. 

Potential Benefits: May have antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects. 

Parts Used: Primarily the roots. 

Lotus (Nelumbo nucifera):

Culinary Uses:

Seeds are widely eaten. 

Religious and Cultural Significance:

Symbolizes purity, enlightenment, and spiritual awakening in Hinduism, Buddhism, and other cultures. 

Traditional Medicine:

Parts of the plant, like rhizomes and leaves, are used in traditional medicine systems. 

Other Uses:

Flowers are used in floral crafts, and leaves can be used for packing and serving food. 

Key Differences:

Focus of Use:

post_owner.name: My Mum's Flavour
text:
[Recipe] Did you know that the hottest period of 2025 starts from 20 July to 18 August? It’s really important to replenish body fluids (known as “Jing” / 精 in Traditional Chinese Medicine or TCM) during this time for good health!

This recipe combines apple with a couple of well-known Chinese herbs to create a cooling beverage with the effect of moistening the body, especially the lungs and stomach. Recommend to have this drink twice a week during this period.

Here is a breakdown of the ingredients’ benefits:

Mai dong (Dwarf Lilyturf Root Tuber) - a traditional Chinese herb known for nourishing the “Yin”, promoting body fluid production, and moistening the lungs, stomach and intestines. In TCM, it is used to address conditions associated with “Yin” deficiency, like dry coughs and constipation. Mai dong can also help with insomnia by calming the mind.

Yu Zhu (Solomon’s Seal) - Like Mai dong, this herb is traditionally used to nourish the “Yin” and replenish fluids for the body. Often found in Chinese herbal soups, Yu Zhu is believed to have benefits for both the lungs and stomach,which are important for respiration, “Qi” production, and digestion. In TCM, it’s considered mildly cooling. By clearing heat in the lungs, it can be used to relieve dry coughs with little phlegm and soothe sore throats.

Dried figs - Believed to moisten the lungs, this ingredient is often recommended in TCM for dry coughs or cough accompanied by a scratchy throat. Dried figs can also help to promote healthy bowel movements, being a good source of fiber.

Cooked apple - In TCM, apples which are cooked are seen as nourishing, especially for the Spleen and Stomach, and can help with digestion and dryness. They are also considered cooling and can help to clear heat.

Check out the recipe below -

Ingredients
1 apple
10g of Mai dong (麦冬)
10g of Yu Zhu (玉竹)
4 dried figs
1200ml of water

Add all the ingredients into a pot. Bring the water to a boil, then cover and simmer for 20 minutes.

Enjoy!

When we feel angry, our body goes into a stress response, often referred to as “fight or flight.” This emotional response affects several organs, but the liver, heart, and nervous system are the most impacted

Liver especially in Traditional Chinese Medicine In Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), anger is closely associated with the liver. Anger is believed to cause liver qi (energy) stagnation, which can lead to:

•Headaches
•Digestive issues
•Menstrual problems
•Muscle tension
•The liver is also responsible for detoxifying hormones, including stress hormones.

Heart and Cardiovascular System. Anger causes a surge of adrenaline, increasing:
•Heart rate
Blood pressure
•Risk of heart palpitations or arrhythmias
Long-term anger and stress can increase the risk of:
•Heart attack
•Stroke
•Hypertension

Brain and Nervous System
•Anger activates the amygdala, the part of the brain involved in emotion.
•This triggers the hypothalamus-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, which:
•Releases cortisol (stress hormone
•Increases alertness
•Reduces rational thinking
•Chronic anger can lead to anxiety, poor sleep, and mental exhaustion.

Digestive System
•Anger may suppress digestion by diverting blood flow away from the gut.

•May cause:
Nausea
•Acid reflux
•Irritable bowel symptoms

Anger is a normal emotion, but holding it in can strain our body. Gentle movement, mindful breathing, and liver supportive habits can help bring balance.

text:
The Story of Wǔjiào – China's Midday Sleep Tradition

In many parts of China, there's a long-standing tradition known as 午觉 (wǔjiào), which literally means "noon nap" or "midday sleep." It’s not just a casual habit — it’s a cultural practice that dates back thousands of years and is believed to align with the natural rhythms of the body and traditional Chinese medicine.

According to Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), the body’s Yin and Yang energies shift throughout the day. The midday (around 11 a.m. to 1 p.m.) is considered a peak time for Yang energy, which governs activity and function. A short rest or nap during this period helps balance the body’s energy, promoting long-term health and mental clarity.

In ancient China, emperors and scholars alike were known to take a short wǔjiào after their midday meal to recharge. Even today, schools, companies, and households across China often support the practice — students might nap at their desks, and some workplaces dim the lights or allow a brief break after lunch.

While Western cultures often view midday napping as laziness, in China it’s seen as a smart and healthy ritual. Studies even back this up — short naps (10–30 minutes) have been shown to improve memory, mood, and cognitive performance.

Your pulse holds the story of your health.
In Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), pulse diagnosis is an ancient art that allows us to feel the subtle rhythms of the body — not just the heartbeat, but the quality of Qi (energy), blood flow, and organ balance. Each wrist is divided into three positions, each linked to an internal organ system, and we read the pulse at three depths (superficial, middle, deep) to gain insight into the body’s current state.

Left Wrist:
	•	Heart (Cun position): Reflects heart health, circulation, and emotional balance. A steady, harmonious pulse suggests a calm mind and balanced cardiovascular function.
	•	Liver (Guan position): Represents the Liver’s role in detoxification, stress regulation, and the smooth flow of Qi. A tense or wiry pulse here may show emotional stress or stagnation.
	•	Kidney Yin (Chi position): Indicates the health of Yin energy, fluids, and overall vitality. Weakness here can point to exhaustion or burnout.

Right Wrist:
	•	Lungs (Cun position): Shows the strength of respiration, immunity, and the flow of energy in the chest. A weak pulse here can indicate low energy or respiratory concerns.
	•	Spleen (Guan position): Reflects digestion, nutrient absorption, and blood production. A soft or soggy pulse may point to digestive weakness or dampness.
	•	Kidney Yang (Chi position): Linked to warmth, energy, and reproductive health. A deep, cold pulse may indicate depleted energy or adrenal fatigue.

Why this matters:
Your pulse can reveal imbalances before symptoms fully appear, offering a powerful way to create preventative and personalized treatments. In TCM, we don’t just treat the symptom — we find and balance the root cause.

post_owner.name: Michaela Magan
text:
Herbal medicine and natural remedies for horses gets a bad rap at the best of times.

Recently a client sent me a couple of links to  people calling themselves “master” herbalists. 
They are promoting their ability to heal horses with TCM ( Traditional Chinese Medicine). Maybe they can, I don’t know. 

In Australia, there is no specific qualification for Master Herbalist.

What you need to know is that there is very little research or evidence of herbs from TCM that are safe for horses. 

I’m an advocate of TCM for humans absolutely. I have used a Chinese herbalist for myself over the years.

Western Herbal Medicine has been the norm for hundreds of years. 
Lots of research has been done and documented, and I would advise all of you to be very careful about those who claim to heal horses with TCM.

While TCM has been shown to be safe in general for human consumption, there just isn’t enough known about TCM to put our faith in it for horses.

This is why people like me know the actions, phytochemical compounds and most importantly, contraindications of herbs.

This is the reason I have not studied TCM. 

Don’t get caught up with flashy websites and self proclaimed “mastery”.

☀️ Favor loose-fitting clothing – It allows Qi to circulate freely. Tight, restrictive garments can create heat, stagnation, and energetic blockages.

☀️ Choose natural fibers – Cotton, linen, and silk are breathable, temperature-regulating, and help maintain harmony between the body and environment. Synthetic fabrics tend to trap sweat and heat, disrupting both comfort and Qi flow.

text:
5 reasons why everyone should sauna (from a Chinese medicine perspective):

1. Moves qi and blood: Sauna helps move stagnant Qi and invigorate blood circulation, which is essential for pain relief, better energy flow, and preventing blockages in the channels.

2. Releases dampness: By promoting sweating, sauna helps the body expel internal Dampness—a root cause of fatigue, bloating, brain fog, and a heavy body sensation.

3. Warms the yang: The external heat supports the body’s Yang energy, especially for those with Cold patterns like cold hands and feet, low libido, slow digestion, or fatigue.

4. Opens the pores and detoxifies: Sauna opens the skin’s pores and allows the release of trapped Heat and toxins through sweat, supporting the Lung and skin systems.

5. Calms the shen: The deep warmth relaxes the nervous system and soothes the Heart spirit (Shen), reducing stress, anxiety, and promoting restful sleep.

How often you should sauna depends on your individual constitution and baseline. In TCM, someone with strong Yang may benefit from 3–4 times per week for 15-30 mins, while those with Yin or fluid deficiency may need shorter sessions or less frequent use. Always listen to your body, and if unsure, consult your practitioner.

text:
9 Things I Wish I Knew About Mental Health in Perimenopause and Menopause, According to Traditional Chinese Medicine

1️⃣ Hormonal Shifts Affect More Than Just Your Period
In TCM, declining Kidney Yin and Blood during menopause can lead to symptoms like anxiety, irritability, and insomnia—long before your period fully stops.

2️⃣ Your Liver Influences Your Mood
The Liver is responsible for the smooth flow of Qi and emotions. If Liver Qi stagnates (often from stress), it can trigger mood swings, anger, or depression.

3️⃣ Sleep Is Your First Medicine
Poor sleep depletes Heart Blood and disturbs the Shen (mind/spirit). Perimenopause often brings disrupted sleep, which amplifies emotional symptoms.

4️⃣ You’re Not Just ‘More Emotional’, Your Heart May Be Out of Balance
In TCM, the Heart houses the Shen. If the Heart is affected by Heat, Blood deficiency, or stagnation, it can manifest as anxiety, racing thoughts, or feeling unsettled.

5️⃣ Digestive Health Impacts Mental Health
A weakened Spleen leads to Dampness, which can cloud the mind and contribute to brain fog, fatigue, and low motivation.

6️⃣ Yin Nourishment Calms the Mind
Yin deficiency, common in menopause, can lead to restlessness, agitation, and night sweats that disturb sleep and mental clarity.

7️⃣ External Stress Hits Harder Now
Your resilience may feel lower. TCM sees this as a depletion of foundational energy (Kidney Jing), making recovery from stress slower and more emotionally draining.

8️⃣ You Might Feel Lonely or Untethered; and That’s a Spirit Imbalance
In Chinese medicine, feeling disconnected, isolated, or ungrounded can reflect a Heart or Kidney imbalance. It’s not just in your head, it’s in your Qi.

text:
The five notes in Chinese traditional music: Jue (角), Zheng (徵), Gong (宫), Shang (商), Yu (羽) are not only fundamental to the structure of Chinese melodies, but are also deeply woven into the philosophical and medical frameworks of Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM). Rooted in the Five Elements (Wood, Fire, Earth, Metal, Water) and corresponding to the Zang-Fu organ systems, these tones are more than musical. They resonate with the body’s internal rhythms and reflect the subtle interplay between emotion, health, and energy flow.

Yu (羽) is the note that embodies gentleness, inward movement, and reflection. It is closely associated with the element of Water, the season of winter, and the Kidneys, which in TCM are considered the storehouse of Essence (Jing) the vital substance that underlies growth, development, reproduction, and longevity. The Kidney system also governs willpower and is viewed as the foundation of both yin and yang in the body.

Winter is a time of rest, preservation, and stillness. In this context, the note Yu evokes a deep sense of introspection, still waters, and the energy of potential not yet expressed, but quietly gathering. Emotionally, Yu is linked with fear, and when the Kidney energy is imbalanced, this fear can become overwhelming or irrational. Conversely, when Kidney Qi is strong and balanced, it manifests as calm courage, resilience, and deep-rooted stability. 

The resonance of Yu in music is often soft, fluid, and soothing—much like the flow of water through hidden depths. By attuning oneself to the vibration of Yu, one can cultivate stillness, replenish inner resources, and restore strength at the core level. It reminds us of the need to retreat, reflect, and renew. Just as winter prepares the ground for spring’s rebirth, Yu fosters the inner quiet necessary for true transformation.

Each of the five musical tones reflects not just physical organs, but the emotional and energetic states that flow through our lives. When balanced, they create harmony internally and externally. Yu, as the most inward and contemplative of the five tones, invites us to pause, listen deeply, and reconnect with the wellspring of our being.💕

In Chinese medicine, sunning your back during San Fu Days (三伏天) is a deeply therapeutic practice because this time of year is when Yang energy in nature is at its peak — and the back, especially the Du (Governing) Channel, is the highway of Yang in the body.

Quick How-To:
* Expose your upper and lower back to early morning or late afternoon sun (10–20 minutes is enough)
* Have Ginger Power tea or ginger tea afterwards

Why is this Medicine? 
1. Opens the Yang Channels
The Du Channel runs along the spine and governs all the Yang meridians. When you expose your back to the sun, you’re directly tonifying Yang Qi, helping to boost immunity, warm the organs, and strengthen vitality.

 2. Expels Cold and Damp
Many people carry cold and damp pathogens lodged in the back — especially in the upper back and lower spine. The summer heat penetrates these areas, helping the body release stored pathogenic factors that cause chronic pain, stiffness, fatigue, and even menstrual issues.

3. Preventative Healing
In TCM, “treat winter diseases in the summer” (冬病夏治) is a core idea behind Chinese medicine during San Fu. By warming and opening the body now, we can prevent cold-related illness later, like asthma, joint pain, digestive issues, or lowered immunity in the fall/winter.

10 Things I Wish I Knew About Perimenopause & Menopause
According to Traditional Chinese Medicine. Menopause isn’t just about hot flashes and mood swings-it’s a complete shift in your body’s energy. In Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), this transition is deeply connected to the balance of Yin and Yang, especially in the Kidneys. Here’s what I wish I knew sooner:

1 It Starts Sooner Than You Think - Perimenopause can begin in your late 30s or early 40s as Kidney Yin declines, leading to sleep and energy issues.

2) Hot Flashes Are a Sign of Yin Deficiency - When Yin (cooling energy) weakens, Yang (heat) rises, causing sudden warmth, night sweats, and insomnia.
Strengthening Yin with foods like black sesame, bone broth, and cooked dark leafy greens can help.

3 Your Digestion Might Change
- As Yang weakens, digestion slows, leading to bloating and sluggish metabolism. Warming foods like ginger, cinnamon, and soups support digestion.

4 Sleep Disruptions Are
Common—And Treatable -Difficulty staying asleep is often due to Heart and Kidney disharmony. Acupuncture, herbs like Suan Zao Ren, and calming bedtime rituals can restore deep sleep.

5 Emotional Swings Are More Than Just Hormones - Liver Qi stagnation from stress can cause irritability, anxiety, or sadness. Movement, breathwork, and herbs like Chai Hu (Bupleurum) can ease emotional ups and downs.

6.Bone Health Begins Now -Kidney Essence declines with age, weakening bones.  Weight-bearing exercises, mineral-rich foods, and TCM herbs like Du Zhong (Eucommia bark) support bone strength. 

7. Brain Fog Isn’t Just in Your Head - TCM sees this as a Spleen and Kidney deficiency.
Eating warming, nourishing foods and practicing Qigong can clear the mind.

8 Vaginal Dryness is a Yin Deficiency Issue - Hydrating foods like pears, tremella mushroom, and seaweed, along with acupuncture, can help restore moisture.
9. Your body temperature can feel out of control. Alternating kidney yang can signify your body thermostat is wearing. Try adding warming spices and chi gong. 

10.Menopause is not an end but a beginning. In Traditional Chinese  Medicne it is a second spring. A time to focus on yourself and your wisdom .

🔥Having a hard time sleeping in this heat?  A major heatwave is gripping most of the country. It’s not just the temperature. Humidity is rising too, and that makes it harder for your body to cool down at night.

This is due in part to evapotranspiration, a process where moisture is released from plants into the air. This increases humidity and makes it harder for the body to cool down through sweat.

High humidity blocks your body’s natural cooling mechanism. When sweat can’t evaporate, internal heat builds up. This raises the risk for heat exhaustion and heat stroke, especially in vulnerable groups:
• children
• elderly
• pregnant women
• individuals with asthma, allergies, or heart conditions

If your sleep has been off, your nervous system may be stuck in overdrive from the heat.

Here’s a calming practice to try:

Press Heart 7, located on the inside of your wrist near the pinky side. This point calms the Shen, or spirit, and helps settle an overactive mind.
Then try Yintang, the point between your eyebrows. It helps release heat, reduce tension, and quiet the nervous system.

Pair this with deep breathing and a cool, dark room. These small steps can help your system reset when the weather is working against you.

text:
Not all Fa Wu are created equal. Just because it’s on the “avoid” list for someone else doesn’t mean it’s bad for you 🥹

In TCM, whether a food is “triggering” depends on you—your body, your condition, and your current phase in life.

It’s wild how the concept of trigger foods—known as 发物 (Fa Wu) in Traditional Chinese Medicine—can be traced all the way back to the Ming Dynasty. It’s recorded in the Compendium of Materia Medica 《本草纲目》: “凡服药，不可杂食肥猪、犬肉、油腻羹、腥臊陈臭诸物。凡服药，不可多食生蒜、胡荽、生葱、诸果、诸滑滞之物。”

Which basically highlights the types of foods to avoid while taking medicine—such as those that are greasy, strong-smelling, or hard to digest.

post_owner.name: 𝐂𝐇𝐑𝐈𝐒𝐓𝐈𝐍𝐀 | FERTILITY ACUPUNCTURIST + WOMEN’S HEALTH SPECIALIST
text:
1. Cycle Length
* A healthy cycle is 26–32 days long, consistently.
* In TCM, this reflects balanced Kidney and Liver function. Too short or long indicates Qi or Blood imbalance.

2. Blood Color
* Healthy menstrual blood is fresh red, like a cherry or hibiscus tea.
* Dark, purple, or very pale blood may signal Blood stagnation or deficiency.

3. Blood Consistency
* Flow should be smooth and fluid, not too thick or watery.
* Sludgy or thin blood can indicate Cold, Dampness, or Qi deficiency in TCM.

4. Amount of Blood Loss
* Around 50–80 ml per cycle (roughly 3–6 soaked pads/tampons a day).
* Too much = Heat or Qi deficiency; too little = Blood deficiency or Cold stagnation.

5. Cramping
* Mild cramping is okay, but pain-free periods are ideal.
* Severe cramps point to Qi/Blood stagnation, often from emotional stress or Cold in the uterus.

6. Clotting
* Small, occasional clots (pea-sized) are normal.
* Large or frequent clots mean Blood stagnation — especially if dark purple or accompanied by pain.

7. Cervical Mucus
* Around ovulation, you should notice clear, stretchy “egg-white” mucus.
* This indicates healthy Yin and Jing (essence) — crucial for fertility and moistening the uterus.

8. Bloating
* Mild or no bloating is a sign of good Spleen Qi and Liver Qi flow.
* Major bloating = Qi stagnation or Damp accumulation — usually worse with emotional stress or poor digestion.

text:
I’ve recently become obsessed with Traditional Chinese Medicine. 

Right now I’m working on boosting my Kidney Yang and Spleen Qi… which basically means warm foods, cozy drinks, and spices that heat you from the inside out.

So I asked ChatGPT to create a TCM-friendly ceremonial cacao with warming spices like ginger, cardamom, and cinnamon… and it’s pure magic in a cup. ✨☕

@msperception.co created the beautiful cacao ceremony experience for Mind Love Retreat last year, and @ido_grinberg sent me home with a jar. Now I’m just over here trying to act casual while making love to my mug.

📌 SAVE THIS for your next slow morning.

Yang Fire Warming Ceremonial Cacao (TCM Style)

🥛 1 cup raw milk (or half water + half milk)
🍫 1.5–2 tbsp ceremonial cacao (chopped or grated)
🧈 1 tsp cacao butter (optional)
🫚 ½ tsp fresh or ¼ tsp ground ginger
🌿 ¼ tsp cardamom
🌰 ¼ tsp cinnamon
🧂 Pinch of sea salt
🍯 1–2 tsp maple syrup or honey (add honey only after it cools slightly)

How to Make It:
1️⃣ Gently warm milk (don’t boil raw milk).
2️⃣ Add cacao and cacao butter, whisking until melted.
3️⃣ Stir in ginger, cardamom, cinnamon, and salt. Let steep for a minute.
4️⃣ Sweeten with maple syrup.
5️⃣ Froth or blend until creamy and smooth.

More Lazy Lymph here👇 Comment LAZY and I’ll DM you my exact facial dry brush & lymph tools 💕

I have struggled with a puffy face — I started doing nervous system regulation tools to get my nervous system into a rest-digest-draining state (like we learn to do in Beat the Burnout) and lymphatic drainage tools.

I will focus on my eye area, my chin, and full face with my gentle facial dry brush from @milliebeauty.official 

✨ How does dry brushing work?

Dry brushing involves gently brushing the skin in specific directions (toward lymphatic drainage pathways) using a natural-bristle brush. The brush gently gliding across the skin gently “tugs” the skin, and with that it stimulates:

▫️Superficial lymph (70% of our lymph is superficial) to help depuff and detox
▫️Circulation for more vibrant skin
▫️Exfoliation to create buttery smooth skin and improve skin texture
▫️Nervous system via light pressure, which can feel grounding and energizing

The pressure should be light…imagine using just enough to push a coin across a table. This helps support lymph flow, which lies just below the skin’s surface.

✨ Where did dry brushing originate?

Dry brushing is an ancient healing practice that has been used for centuries in Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM). It’s been applied alongside other holistic practices like gua sha to support detoxification, lymph and recently beauty benefits.

✨ For the past several months, I’ve noticed my cycle shortening—four, maybe five days. Some people say, “Oh, that’s just aging. Cycles get shorter.”

But I don’t quite buy that narrative.

I don’t really believe in menopause the way we define it in the West. In many tribal and traditional cultures, women don’t experience the same struggles or symptoms that are so common in modern life. I believe much of what we call menopause is the body responding to our culture of stress, disconnection, and unprocessed emotion.

This last cycle was different.

I bled for a full seven days. It wasn’t just fresh, new blood. There was old blood releasing. Stagnant. Waiting.

What’s fascinating is that this mirrored what was happening in me emotionally.

Over these last weeks, I had a massive internal shift. Letting go of old baggage. Forgiving things I’d held onto for years. Choosing to stop replaying the past in my mind. So much of it around my marriage, my expectations, my disappointments, my own hard edges.

As I released emotionally, my body released physically.

This is the wisdom our cycles carry.

Our womb is not separate from our psyche.
Our blood tells the story of what we’re holding, what we’re ready to let go of, what is asking to be cleansed.

🩸 This is why I’m so passionate about creating ritual around the moon cycle. It’s not just about periods—it’s about our connection to ourselves, our emotions, our healing.

I’m pouring this wisdom and my personal practices into my Moon Cycle Ritual Guide—a gentle invitation to treat your cycle as sacred, to listen, to honor what wants to be released.

text:
Systemic Lupus Erythematous (SLE) aka lupus, is a chronic autoimmune disease that happens when the immune system attacks the body, leading to inflammation and damage of the joints, skin, kidneys, heart, lungs, blood vessels, nervous system and other tissues. There is no cure for SLE but it can be managed. The symptoms vary with individuals, range from mild to life threatening. The initial disease often begins with fever and is then followed by symptoms: fatigue, butterfly shaped rash on the face, photosensitive, arthritis, joint pain, chest pain, hair loss, seizure, blood clotting and anemia. Some may have flares that comes once in a while, others may experience the flares more frequently throughout their life. 

Chinese Medicine is excellent in reducing the dependency on medications and preventing flare ups. The primary cause of SLE in Chinese Medicine is deficiency of Zang organs (Heart, Kidney, Spleen, Lungs or Liver), and the secondary cause is either excess heat, toxin, dampness or blood stasis. The common shared cause is Qi and Yin deficiency with heat. This can be translated into chronic inflammation and the symptoms include skin rash, joint pain, lack of strength, dry mouth and throat, always thirsty, less urination with yellow urine, red tongue with dry or less coating, the pulse is rapid and fine.

Treatments for SLE are customized Chinese herbs and acupuncture to tonify Qi, enrich Yin, remove internal heat, removing blood stasis and clear the toxin. This will ease the inflammation and all the symptoms, including side effects of medications. It is also good to get treatments to prevent remission and preventing the disease from progressing. 

Over the years, Chinese Medicine has made significant progress in the treatment of SLE. In China they are applying integrative therapies for lupus which typically combine herbal compounds with Western medicines such as corticosteroids and immunosuppressive agents. Clinical trials have compared patients with SLE treated with prednisone only to those treated both with steroids and herbs, and found that patients receiving TCM treatment as an adjunct fared better overall and were able to reduce their use of steroids.

text:
One of the integral principles of Chinese Medicine is that each part of us is contained within the whole; and the image of the whole is reflected within the confines of each part. This can relate to more modern findings of DNA— nearly every cell in a person’s body has the same DNA.

Our whole being contained on such a microscopic level. 

In Chinese medicine we diagnose patients based on their tongue, pulse, face; by touching certain acupressure points to see how tender they are, by mannerisms and one’s voice. This is because our bodies provide many maps. The tongue features a map, the pulse, the face— all parts make up the whole which correlate to our entirety, our physical, emotional and spiritual bodies.

These concepts are featured in my book “Heal Yourself with Traditional Chinese Medicine” - a cohesive and comprehensive guide for you to discover TCM on a deeper level while also learning recipes, teas, lifestyle tips and acupressure - all ways to take your life into your own hands.

📖🩵 Comment “book” below and I will message you a link to my book, available now worldwide. 

I invite you to see your body as part of a greater whole.

We treat someone’s symptoms through the root versus branch effect. Branch treatment provides temporary relief but does not create a chance for the problem to stop occurring. It’s like pruning branches of a diseased tree but not looking in the soil to find out why the branches are coming up sick. The branches are the visible manifestations of the problem, while the roots are what is going on deeper in the organ systems of the body. Only trimming and cleaning up the damaged branches won’t help when the roots are sick. The branches will keep growing back, diseased. The root cause treatment, however, would be to find out why the body is creating the unpleasant symptoms.

This concept spreads across many civilizations and defies time.

Every time I post a cooking video or photo like this—dressed up, full glam, cooking in my kitchen—someone says,
“Wow… who cooks like that?”
And yes, I do. But what you don’t see under the camera… are my slippers.
I’ve been a slipper girl my whole life.
Growing up in China with my grandparents, the rule was simple: the second you walk in the door—you change your shoes.
If I ever walked in with dirty street shoes, I’d get the look. You know the one.
So now, even with a Qi Pao, red lips, and two cleavers in hand… I’m still in my fuzzy house slippers. Because that’s just how your Chinese mom rolls.
This song here —it’s fun, a little cheeky, but also says something real
I believe women can be beautiful anywhere:
In the kitchen.
In slippers.
With garlic under your nails.
With a mushroom on your head.
Beauty isn’t about perfection.
It’s about confidence in chaos.
I cook in my pajamas too! 
Comfort in your place.
And learning to laugh at yourself—even with mushrooms on your head.
That’s also what my new cookbook is about: Traditional Chinese Wellness Recipes.
It’s not about perfect plates or fancy ingredients.
It’s about caring for yourself and your family through simple, homemade meals—using ingredients that have comfort and wisdom in every bite.
The silver ear mushroom soup my grandmother used to make for me is just one of many recipes meant to nourish, restore, and bring balance—right from your own kitchen. She always saying: Eat! Eat! eat it! It’s good for you! 😄❤️

And a big thank-you to my talented friend @iamdavidlawrence for capturing these moments.
If you remember that Reels I posted where I found a funny sign on the street—and you all helped me figure out who made it? That was David.
Now here we are, slippers and all. So grateful to create with such a thoughtful artist.
Tell me—do you wear slippers at home too?
Or are you one of those brave souls who walks around with outside shoes on in the house ? Or your slippers outside of the house? #chinesefood #chinesemom #yourchinesemom #tcm

I’m not saying any of these things are bad.
I’m saying: I took them to the extreme in my 20s without understanding the context or consequences 😂🤦🏻‍♀️

🧠 I didn’t know the impact of HIIT on female hormones — I was doing Barry’s classes on an empty stomach, chasing the “that girl” body while completely wrecking my cortisol.

🚺 I went on birth control at 19 for a few small breakouts. Stayed on it for nearly a decade. After getting off, I had no clue how my cycle worked, and my real acne journey began LOL. Studies now link hormonal contraceptives to shifts in the gut microbiome — PubMed: [PMID: 39951399] 

🥬 I thought cold green smoothies + raw kale salads = health. But now that I work with a TCM doctor, I’ve learned that too much cold/raw can damage your digestion — especially if you have conditions like SIBO. In TCM, raw and cold foods are believed to weaken Spleen Qi and impair the body’s ability to transform and transport nutrients.

💊 I stacked supplements thinking they’d fix everything — gut, skin, hormones. But healing wasn’t just about pills. It required food. Nervous system work. Emotional regulation. Slowing down.

🧬 I jumped into biohacking before mastering the basics. Red light, castor oil, rebounding, saunas… all great tools. But none of it mattered when I wasn’t sleeping well, managing stress, or eating in a way that supported my body.

🥑 And finally, I hadn’t touched a Coca Cola or Doritos in a decade — but I was binging “healthy” alternatives like avocado oil chips and stevia gummies. And I wondered why I was bloated all the time. Turns out, overeating anything (even the “healthier” version) is still stressful on your body.

This post isn’t an attack on these trends — it’s a reflection. On how wellness can become performance. Obsession. Perfectionism in disguise.

So if you’ve ever spiraled down a similar path… you’re not alone.
And if you’re still learning to find your middle ground — same.

Libido as a Reflection of Jing and Vitality in TCM

In Traditional Chinese Medicine, a healthy libido is seen as a direct reflection of one’s Jing—the foundational life essence stored in the kidneys. Jing governs growth, reproduction, and vitality, and when it is abundant, the body expresses this through vibrant health, balanced hormones, and a natural sexual desire. For women, especially, a robust libido indicates that the Kidney Yin and Yang are harmonized, supporting menstrual regularity, ovulation, and overall reproductive strength. When libido is low, it can suggest an underlying deficiency in this core essence, often exacerbated by stress, overwork, poor diet, or chronic illness. TCM doesn’t view sexual desire as a superficial indulgence, but as an important indicator of internal harmony and vitality.

Hormonal Balance and Libido in Functional Medicine
From a Functional Medicine perspective, libido is intricately linked to hormonal balance, especially estrogen, progesterone, testosterone, and DHEA. When these hormones are in optimal ranges, women often experience stable mood, good energy, restful sleep, and a healthy appetite for intimacy. A diminished libido can signal imbalances in the HPA (hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal) axis, thyroid dysfunction, or blood sugar dysregulation. Chronic stress, nutrient deficiencies, inflammation, and gut imbalances also interfere with the complex endocrine communication that supports sexual desire. In this view, a thriving libido is not isolated—it is woven into a tapestry of physical, emotional, and biochemical wellness.

The last three months… migraine free.

(Fingers crossed that I didn’t just jinx it, but honestly, I finally feel like I have the tools now if one tries to creep in.)

This is coming from someone who used to get migraines monthly, with that horrible prodrome neck pain as my warning sign, that then turned into pounding pain at the back of my neck that radiated to my eye aka  and day ruiner.

I’d had enough, and felt like as someone who treats this issue and helps other people….Why can’t I help myself? I really started paying attention, tracking when they happened, what triggered them, where I was in my cycle, even the time of day.

Here’s what’s made the biggest difference for me:
 
1. A tailored supplement protocol I figured out my migraines were tied to my cycle. I focused on specific supplements that helped balance things out. I did this for a solid 6-8 weeks before I weaned off.

 2. Monthly TCM acupuncture Every 3 weeks, timed around my cycle. Non-negotiable now. I also realized that this was much needed me time that my nervous system needs. 

3. Chiropractic care ( thank you @dr.shelleypinard )
I stay on top of my neck tension before it spirals into something bigger. Maintenance over crisis care always.
 
4. Strength training I got serious about it and outsourced my programming (thank you @kayleevmiller ). Stronger neck, upper back, and nervous system resilience all helping me stay migraine free.

5. Mind-body work I’ve been reading Mind Your Body by @nicolesachslcsw and it’s changed how I see chronic symptoms. If my neck starts acting up now, I pause and ask: what is this tension trying to tell me? Usually I’m stressed or dealing with something and once reflecting on this… it honestly dissipates 🤯. 

 6. Prioritizing sleep Nothing new here,  but consistently getting real, deep sleep has been key.

If you’re dealing with chronic migraines, don’t give up. You might just need to zoom out and look at things from more than one angle.

Family: Joint Fir (Ephedraceae)
Hardy to Zones 3 to 10
(Blue Stem Joint Fir, Mu-zei-ma-huang) Perennial, primitive subshrub native to the arid steppes of China and Russia. Rare. Extremely robust on the landscape. Traditional usage (TCM): a secondary source of Ma-huang. Germination is best in coarse, sharp sand. Mix sand 50/50 with potting soil and fill pot to 3/4 inch of rim. Lay seeds on surface and cover with 3/4 inch of sand. Water daily and keep very warm. Germination takes 1 to 2 weeks. Back off on watering after germination to avoid damping off. Allow to grow at close spacing until the seedlings are about 4 inches tall, then individuate seedlings to their own pots, using the same 50/50 mix. Grow on for a year before transplanting to landscape. Plant prefers sun and very fast draining soils. Mulch with sand or volcanic rock. Space plants 3 feet apart.

post_owner.name: AVIATION NEWS
text:
New Delhi:Air India has completed precautionary inspections of the locking mechanism of fuel control switch (FCS) in all of its Boeing 787-8 aircraft and found no issues, officials of the Tata-owned airline said.

Air India ran the checks after the civil aviation regulator (DGCA) on Monday issued a directive to inspect the FCS of specific Boeing aircraft models by July 21.

(AIIB) report into the crash of a Boeing 787-8 Dreamliner in Ahmedabad had said the fuel cutoff switches for both engines were moved to the cutoff position, one after another within a 1-second interval, at an altitude just moments after liftoff.

“All our Boeing 787-8 aircraft have undergone throttle control module (TCM) replacement as per the Boeing maintenance schedule. The FCS is part of this module,” an Air India official said.

“Over the weekend, our engineering team initiated precautionary inspections on the locking mechanism of FCS on all our Boeing 787 aircraft. The inspections have been completed and no issues were found,” the official said.

Earlier, almost the entire Boeing 737 Max fleet of Air India Express was also checked, and no issues were found, the official added.

The DGCA directive enforced compliance with the US Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA)
bulletin issued in December 2018, which warned of potential disengagement of the fuel control switch locking feature in operators of some Boeing 737 aircraft.

However, the fuel control switch design, including the locking feature, is similar on various Boeing aircraft models including part number ‘4TL837-3D’, which was fitted in the Boeing 787-8 that crashed in Ahmedabad, killing 260 people.

Air India did not carry out inspections recommended in the 2018 FAA advisory on fuel control switch safety, as the bulletin was classified as “non-mandatory”
“, the AAlB report said.

According to the chronology laid out in the
AAIB report, both fuel cutoff switches moved from ‘run’ to ‘cutoff’, one second apart, almost immediately after takeoff. The ram air turbine (RAT) pump was deployed to supply hydraulic power as both engines fell below the minimum idle rate.

text:
[Recipe] In Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), lychee is considered a “warming” fruit and can be used to dispel cold. Both cooked and fresh lychee are also believed to tonify blood and help with Qi (vital energy) circulation. Specific benefits include aiding digestion, relieving stomach pain, and potentially helping with other cold conditions such as cold limbs, lack of energy, or menstrual problems.

If you love a comforting chicken soup and the sweet flavour of lychees, you will enjoy this recipe!  You may have noticed that I had mistakenly added Solomon’s Seal (Yuzhu) instead of Dried Chinese Yam in the reel, sorry about that! Anyway, taste of the soup is not affected and you can add Yuzhu if preferred. 

Without further ado, check it out -

Ingredients (2 to 3 pax)
2 bone-in chicken thighs
10 lychees
3 large seedless red dates
6g or a small handful of dried Chinese Yam or Solomon’s Seal 
A few slices of ginger
1000ml of water
Salt to taste (optional)

1) Clean the chicken and add them into a pot, together with red dates, dried Chinese Yam and ginger.

2) Add water and bring it to a boil. Cover and simmer under medium low for 30 minutes.

3) Add lychees (with seeds removed) and cook for another 10 minutes. Add salt if desired.

Enjoy!

This was one of the most common formats of traditional Chinese medicine. These wax balls, containing “wan” or a round herbal ball inside, vary in size from as large as an egg to the size of a mustard seed.

Traditionally, honey was the binding substance in the pill-making process, layered with medicinal herb powder, and the medicine sealed on the outside with an airtight wax coating. This was considered the most durable method for storing herbal medicine without the need for preservatives.

There is evidence that this innovation dates back 2,000 years, as wax was found to be used for similar purposes in an ancient Chinese tomb. However, it has largely been replaced with all-plastic bottles in modern medicine. We still offer a few herbal medicines encased in wax, including Die Da Wan for injury healing and Baifeng Wan for women’s health.

Note: other herbal medicine formulas also comes in this ball format, called a “honey bolus.” This does not mean they are the same medicine. For example, the one shown is for emergency situations such as strokes and heart attack. However, almost every possible herbal formula in Chinese medicine has been made in this same form, including the two mentioned above that we carry.

Key Signs of Dampness
Puffy face/eyes on waking, thick, greasy tongue coat with teeth marks, low appetite, bloating, loose stools, brain fog, fatigue, emotional heaviness, phlegmy cough, sinus clogged, or achy joints (dampness drives arthritis), indigestion, GERD, and it's only the beginning.

Daily Practices to Support Spleen, Drain Damp

Cold & iced drinks, raw food (especially salads), staying in air conditioning all the time, dairy, processed sugars, greasy/fried meals, smoothies, excessive salt or heavy spices, excessive worrying, lying in bed all day

13. Support Qi: Avoid excessive worry (affects Spleen). Spend time appreciating the beauty of rain to uplift mood (nature as medicine)
14. Use warming teas with tulsi, ginger, cinnamon, or pepper to counter inner heaviness

post_owner.name: Jessica Freedman | Your Birth Bestie
text:
Some of the best postpartum advice I’ve ever received didn’t come from a doula, a mom friend, or even a book…

It came from my professor in graduate school, Dr. Sun, a Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) practitioner who had been caring for postpartum mothers in China for 40 years before he came to America to teach.

He told me:

“The postpartum period is sacred. Treat it with the same respect as the birth itself.”

In TCM, there is a tradition called zuò yuè zi, or the “lying-in” period, a 40-day window after birth where the new mother is encouraged to rest deeply, eat nourishing foods, and avoid cold exposure. This practice isn’t about confinement; it’s about rebuilding the body’s vital energy and honoring the transformation that just occurred~physically, emotionally, and spiritually.

The mother is cared for, cooked for, and held in stillness so that her body and womb can fully heal, her milk can come in with strength, and she can begin to ground herself in her new identity.

🤍 Of course, many of us don’t live in multigenerational households, and the idea of 40 days of total rest might feel unrealistic in today’s world. But we can carry the wisdom of this tradition into our modern lives by:

✅ Asking for help and receiving it without guilt
🍲 Preparing warming, nourishing meals ahead of time
🛏 Creating a soft landing space for those early days at home
🤱 Resting as much as possible, and letting go of “getting back to normal”
🫶 Allowing the slowness to be part of your healing not something to rush through

You are not expected to bounce back…you are invited to rebuild, renew, and receive.

The postpartum period is not just recovery, it’s a continuation of the birth itself. Honor it, protect it, and let others rise up to support you in it. 💛

Black beans -  this ingredient is highly valued for its ability to tonify the kidney organ system, which in TCM governs growth, development, reproduction, and overall vitality. It is also a blood tonic and can support both “qi” (energy) and blood circulation.

Apple -  cooked apples are considered beneficial for digestion and more gentle on the stomach than raw ones. They are effective for relieving constipation and supporting the spleen and stomach. It is also believed to nourish the lungs, resolve phlegm, and help with coughs.

Lotus seeds - They are used to address imbalances or deficiencies related to the spleen (which can lead to poor appetite), kidneys and heart. Lotus seeds can also help to promote better sleep.

White Rice Water - this ingredient is considered to have a neutral nature, with a mildly sweet taste and cooling property. It can benefit the spleen and lungs and is often used to increase energy and stamina, soothe skin, moisturize” Yin”, clear heat, reduce swelling, and support kidney functions.

1/2 a large apple

🩶 Regulating your nervous system
Your body won’t drop weight or inflammation if it feels threatened. Regulation is what signals, “It’s safe to let go.”

🩶 Balancing your hormones
Unbalanced hormones = stubborn fat, water retention, cravings, breakouts. Supporting your cycle helps your body release what it’s been clinging to.

🩶 Releasing limiting beliefs
If deep down you believe “it’s not safe to be seen” or “I always get bloated,” your body tends to follow the signals those beliefs create, staying in protective patterns. When you rewrite them, your body follows.

🩶 Prioritizing recovery over forcing results
More stress = more cortisol = more holding. Recovery teaches your body it doesn’t need to brace for impact.

🩶 Elevated Self work
When you embody the version of you who already feels radiant, safe, at home in your skin, your body aligns. It’s how true transformation happens.

Summer is associated with the element fire. Fire is about warmth, transformation and dynamic, sparkling movement. Summer brings fire through the heat of the sun, long days and energized bodies. ⁠
⁠
Cardiovascular exercise serves you especially well during summer, because fire rules the heart and circulation of the blood. Fire also rules the small intestine, which in traditional Chinese medicine is intricately connected with the heart. The small intestine transforms the foods we eat into usable components, which go directly into the blood. The blood moves to the heart and is circulated through the rest of the system. If you feed your body toxic food, the small intestine has little to work with when trying to pass on good nutrients. For this reason, it’s important to eat nutritious food year-round, but during the active summer season it’s especially crucial.⁠
⁠
When fire is in excess, it often results in overexcitement, too much involvement and being overcommitted. To counteract this, eat bitter foods like romaine lettuce, dandelion greens, almonds and scallions, and cooling foods like cucumber, sprouts, watermelon, apples, lemons and limes. Avoid heavy foods like meats, eggs and oils.⁠
⁠
Summer is also an ideal time for power lunches, good conversations and warm gatherings of friends, as fire is associated with midday and connectivity.⁠

* Emotion: Anger, frustration, resentment
* Element: Wood
* Season: Spring
* Function: Regulates the smooth flow of Qi and blood; stores blood.

* Element: Fire
* Season: Summer
* Function: Houses the Shen (mind/spirit); governs blood and vessels.
* Imbalance: Manifests as insomnia, restlessness, palpitations, mental disturbances.

* Emotion: Worry, overthinking, pensiveness
* Element: Earth
* Season: Late summer
* Function: Governs digestion and transformation; produces Qi and blood.
* Imbalance: Leads to fatigue, digestive issues, muscle weakness.

* Emotion: Grief, sadness
* Element: Metal
* Season: Autumn
* Function: Controls respiration and Qi; governs skin and immunity.
* Imbalance: Results in shortness of breath, skin issues, immune deficiency.

5. Kidneys

* Emotion: Fear
* Element: Water
* Season: Winter
* Function: Stores essence (Jing); governs growth, reproduction, bones, and hearing.
* Imbalance: Can cause anxiety, developmental issues, low back pain, infertility.

text:
Causónis japonica ( Thunb ) Raf. 

Family: Vitaceae
Common names: Bushkiller, Sorrel vine, Japanese cayratia herb, “ Yabu garashi” ( Japanese) 
Synonyms: Cayratia japonica ( Thunb.)
Gagnep. 

Bushkiller is  a perennial, herbaceous climbing vine that will climb up trees and other supports, grows on the edges of rainforests and considered an invasive plant. 

It is native to tropical and subtropical 
Asia, Australia and the West Pacific. 

STEM: green and has a petiolule ( stem connecting a leaflet to the main leaf stem on any the leaflets )

LEAVES: compound, alternately arranged along the stems, about 3 inches wide and 3 inches long. Each leaf has 5 leaflets ( 5 foliolate) with the middle leaflet on its own longer stem. The leaflet is ovate in shape and has serrated/ toothed margin. Young foliage is reddish in color that becomes green on maturity. 

FLOWERS: red, white, and yellow flowers developing in umbels and producing grape- like berries with 2-4 seeds. In Japan and South Korea it blooms in July and August with its fruit ripening in September and November.
While in the Southern hemisphere, in the Australian Northern Territory, it flowers and fruit in October. 

EDIBILITY: fruits, young leaves, and flowers can be eaten raw. 

USES: used as a Traditional Chinese Medicine ( TCM) to relieve swelling and heat, and to enhance diuresis and detoxification.

1 large green radish, peeled, largely cubed

3 dried honey dates
1 teaspoon of dried apricot kernals
2 tablespoons of dried barley

🌬️ Blood Stasis due to Qi Stagnation
• Symptoms: sharp stabbing pain that worsens with stress or emotions, PMS, breast tenderness, irregular cycles.
• Root: emotional tension or lifestyle-induced stagnation of Qi, especially in the Liver.

• Symptoms: cold sensation in the lower abdomen, dull pain relieved by warmth, dark clots, sluggish flow, aversion to cold, cold hands/feet.
• Root: exposure to cold (diet, weather, lifestyle), weakening the uterus.

• Symptoms: chronic pelvic pain, lower back weakness, fatigue, low libido, infertility, or irregular cycles.

🌾 Blood Stasis due to Qi Deficiency
• Symptoms: dull pain, heavy flow with pale blood, fatigue, digestive issues, shortness of breath.
• Root: Spleen Qi deficiency failing to generate or move Blood properly.

TCM doesn’t treat just the “disease” — it treats you.
That’s why two people with endometriosis may receive completely different treatments. The goal is to move Blood, nourish what’s deficient, warm where there is cold, and support the root cause.

– Acupuncture to regulate Qi and ease pain

Your pain is valid.

Three Power Acupressure Points for Eye Health (in TCM)

Use gentle pressure on these points for 60-90 seconds both sides, using circular clockwise motions with your fingertip or AcuPen. 

How to find the points:

1️⃣ Bladder 1 – Find the tiny dip at the inside corner of your eye, right next to the bridge of your nose. A light press here can wake up tired peepers, ease dryness and help them feel less “burny” after a long day of screen-time.

2️⃣ Stomach 1 – Look straight ahead and trace a line down from your pupil to the little hollow just under the eye, on top of your cheekbone.

3️⃣ Gallbladder 1 – This one sits at the outer corner of your eye where the upper and lower lids meet. A gentle hold can soothe eye strain, reduce tension around the temples. 

🕰️ Give each point 30–60 seconds of soft, steady pressure (never poke the eyeball itself!) and feel the difference.

post_owner.name: Sensei Acupuncture Beauty
text:
Insomnia characterised by difficulty falling asleep, frequent waking during the night, or waking feeling unrefreshed can have wide-ranging effects on emotional stability, cognitive function, and overall health. While modern medicine often links insomnia to stress, anxiety, or neurological imbalances, Traditional Chinese Medicine views sleep disturbances through the lens of internal disharmony. One common pattern is Hyperactivity of Liver Fire (肝火上炎), a condition in which excess Liver Yang transforms into fire and ascends to disturb the Heart and Shen (spirit).

In TCM, the Liver governs the smooth flow of Qi and is strongly influenced by emotional states particularly anger, frustration, and repressed emotions. When these emotional stressors persist, Liver Qi may become constrained and gradually transform into fire. This Liver Fire then flares upward, disturbing the Heart and preventing it from anchoring the spirit. The result is a restless mind and body, which manifest as insomnia and associated symptoms. Individuals with this pattern typically report difficulty falling asleep, restless, or dream-disturbed sleep, irritability, easily triggered anger, headaches, dizziness, tinnitus, bitter taste in the mouth, dry throat, red or bloodshot eyes, and sometimes costal (rib-side) discomfort.

Acupuncture treatment aims to clear Liver Fire, pacify the Liver, and calm the Shen. Acupoints such as LV2 (Xingjian) to clear excess fire from the Liver while HT7 (Shenmen) helps calm the spirit and regulate Heart function. To relieve symptoms such as headache, dizziness, and agitation, GB20 (Fengchi) may be used to disperse heat from the upper body. In herbal therapy, Long Dan Xie Gan Tang (龙胆泻肝汤) is the classic formula used to purge excess heat from the Liver and Gallbladder. This formula includes bitter and cold herbs like Long Dan Cao, Huang Qin, and Zhi Zi to clear heat and fire, as well as herbs such as Mu Tong and Che Qian Zi to drain dampness and promote urination, preventing fire from accumulating further.

Through a targeted approach that combines acupuncture, herbal medicine, and lifestyle adjustments such as reducing alcohol, spicy foods, and stress.

In Chinese medicine, there’s no exact mention of the lymphatic system, but the idea of moving and draining fluids is central to health. TCM views proper flow of Qi (vital energy) and Jin-Ye (body fluids) as essential to prevent swelling, puffiness, and fatigue. 

When Qi or fluids stagnate, it can create dampness or phlegm, leading to issues like water retention, digestive sluggishness, or even skin problems. 

Lymphatic massage, which helps stimulate fluid movement and circulation, fits naturally into TCM’s goal of keeping Qi and fluids flowing smoothly.

While it’s a modern technique, lymphatic massage echoes ancient principles of TCM: clearing blockages, moving fluids, and restoring harmony in the body.

I aim for 1-2 lymphatic massages per month and have found it hugely helpful following travel as well as during my luteal phase when I am feeling like my body is holding on to a bit more water.

It’s also believed to promote hair health, helping to improve conditions like hair loss and premature graying, and to benefit the skin. Black sesame powder is also associated with improved digestion and bowel movement.

Sweet fermented rice wine (Jiu Niang / 酒酿) is another ingredient with various benefits in Traditional Chinese Medicine. TCM practitioners value it for promoting blood circulation, warming the body, and helping with digestion. It is often recommended for use with menstrual irregularities as it can be used to treat blood stagnation.

Without further ado, check out this nutritious Chinese style breakfast using the above mentioned ingredients. As “Jiu Niang” is sweet, feel free to adjust the amount you use or add some water into the ingredients before steaming.

Ingredients
3 tbsp or 60 to 80g of sweet fermented rice wine (can adjust based on preference)
2 tbsp of pure black sesame powder
2 to 3 seedless red dates (cut into slices)
1 egg
Moderate amount of water (optional, can add if you don’t like your food to be too sweet)

1) Add all the ingredients into a steaming bowl.

2) Bring a pot/wok of water to a boil and steam the black sesame sweet fermented rice wine mixture for 10 minutes.

Recommended to mix together and eat. Enjoy!

✨ How does dry brushing work?

Dry brushing involves gently brushing the skin in specific directions (toward lymphatic drainage pathways) using a natural-bristle brush. The brush gently gliding across the skin gently “tugs” the skin, and with that it stimulates:
▫️Superficial lymph (70% of our lymph is superficial) to help depuff and detox
▫️Circulation for more vibrant skin
▫️Exfoliation to create buttery smooth skin and improve skin texture
▫️Nervous system via light pressure, which can feel grounding and energizing

The pressure should be light…imagine using just enough to push a coin across a table. This helps support lymph flow, which lies just below the skin’s surface.

✨ Where did dry brushing originate?

Dry brushing is an ancient healing practice that has been used for centuries in Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM). It’s been applied alongside other holistic practices like gua sha to support detoxification, lymph and recently beauty benefits.

🔮 Traditional Chinese Medicinal Tea Recipe 
Makes 2 servings (one per day)

What you’ll need
* 1 bag of raw herbs (from your herbalist)
* Stainless steel or glass pot

Instructions
1. Add 4 to 6 cups of cold water to cover the herbs
2. Let soak for 20 to 30 minutes to release the active compounds
3. Bring to a boil, then simmer uncovered for 45 minutes to 1 hour
4. Strain the liquid and this is your first batch. It should be reduced down to 1.5 to 2 cups. You can reduce it down to 1 cup so it’s easier to consume

7. Strain again. This is your second batch and it should be reduced down to 1 to 1.5 cups 
8. Mix both batches together
9. Let cool to room temperature then store in glass jars in the fridge
10. Reheat before drinking. Drink after breakfast or lunch

Learning to take care of myself so that I get stronger.
⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
I’ve always thought of myself as resilient. Stoic. Unflappable. Stress was just part of life. But I was achieving this “I can do it, just suck it up and power through it” approach to whatever life threw at me with the naive idea that my body would just roll with it indefinitely. When I struggled with my sleep, I concluded that it gave me more waking hours to get 💩 done. When the stress hit my gut, I took is as a signal that I was performing at my best — I was in my zone. I took pride in doing everything myself. It gave me control over getting things as close to perfect as I possibly could.
⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
Then, midlife happened and I discovered that my body wasn’t rolling with it anymore. Why? Because I’ve been abusing it for years thinking that I’d found a way to do it all. Since then, I’ve been trying to rethink doing me. It’s an ongoing process, but over the past couple of years, I’ve undergone a significant mental and physical overhaul. 
⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
A lot of my personal approach involves deep dives, testing (on myself) and then joining the dots where sometimes people haven’t joined them. So, when @aun_koh and I visited @rakxawellness two months ago, I loved the jam-packed daily schedules. I got to try a wide range of treatments I was already curious about — ranging from those administered by medical practitioners to traditional medicine (Ayurveda, Thai and Chinese), physiotherapy, personal training, spa, holistic wellness, nutrition etc. We studied blood work and data. The efficiency, legitimate expertise across the board, and quality of experience provided me with heaps of lasting learnings. The outcomes were a blend of active intervention with longer term lifestyle adjustments (I’ve kept up with TCM and adjusted my diet a little), plus straight up quality relaxation. Biggest lesson: Reducing cortisol isn’t about eliminating external triggers. There isn’t a simple fix and much starts with working on myself.

text:
Never add honey to boiling hot tea or food.
When honey is heated above 140°F, it begins to break down and form a compound called hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF). 

In large amounts, HMF has been shown in studies to be potentially harmful to cells and the nervous system. High heat also destroys honey’s beneficial enzymes, antioxidants, and antimicrobial properties—essentially stripping it of its healing value.

This aligns with traditional wisdom. In both Ayurveda, Traditional Chinese Medicine, and many cultures around the world, heating honey has long been discouraged. Ayurveda teaches that hot honey creates a sticky toxic residue that burdens digestion and circulation. In TCM, honey (feng mi) is used medicinally in teas and tonics, but always added to warm, not hot, liquids to preserve its qi-tonifying and moistening qualities.

If it’s too hot to comfortably sip or touch, it’s too hot for honey.

Let your tea or food cool slightly before adding it, and allow its natural medicine to do what it was meant to do.

Have you had cupping done and then noticed the marks on your back and wondered what they mean? Or are you curious about cupping and nervous about what it looks like?

Cupping is an ancient therapy that uses suction to draw out stagnation from the body. It boosts circulation, releases tension, and helps move stuck Qi and Blood. In TCM, our saying is “if there is free flow there is no pain”. The circular marks are signs that your body is clearing what it no longer needs— physically and energetically.

Cupping marks are not bruises.

Bruises come from trauma or broken blood vessels, while cupping marks are intentional and caused by suction drawing stagnant blood and toxins to the surface. There’s no tissue damage involved. They’re a sign the body is processing and releasing old buildup—think of them as a diagnostic window into how much stagnation is present.

Cupping marks can vary in color due to differences in blood stagnation and toxin levels in the area and energetic pathway being treated. Darker marks indicate more stagnant blood and toxins, while lighter marks suggest better circulation and fewer toxins. The discoloration is a result of the suction drawing blood and fluids to the surface, a truly amazing modality!

text:
Vietnamese Spring Rolls
Still trying to hold on to the memories of Vietnam and quickly whipped these up this week. 
They are amazing as taste incredible (so fresh!) but also last well in the fridge (obviously being mindful of your prawns and making sure fresh).
It’s delicious and simple and a great way to use up left over chicken.

Rice paper rolls - 
12 sheets of rice paper (can buy in any large supermarket)
2 shredded poached organic chicken breasts (or roast left overs) 
Fresh mint leaves 
Approx 150 g rice vermicelli noodles cooked (follow pack instructions)
Packet of cooked organic prawns
Shredded baby gem or crunchy lettuce

Place a sheet of rice paper on a flat surface wipe with a wet cloth or sprinkle with water to completely cover with water and it will instantly start to soften. But don’t drown it in water or is goes quite gross and flabby.
At the bottom of the circle place a tablespoon or so amount of your rice noodles, top with a layer of lettuce and then the shredded chicken. Place a couple of mint leaves on top and three pink prawns (pink side down) - place these slightly above the layered pile - so when you roll they are positioned at the top and visible. Now roll up, half way through fold in the edges. Repeat x 12 and serve with dipping sauce

Dipping sauce - 
2 tablespoon lime juice 
2 tablespoon sugar 
2 teaspoons fish sauce
4 teaspoons water 
half a teaspoon dry chilli 
1 garlic clove grated
Dash rice wine vinegar to help balance the flavours
Mix all together. Taste and adjust if needed 
Always here if you have any questions.

Eating with the seasons is more than a culinary trend—it’s a timeless principle rooted in nature, Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), Ayurveda, and modern nutrition. Here’s why it’s vital:

🌿 1. Nature’s Perfect Timing

Nature produces what the body needs at the right time. In summer, cooling fruits and hydrating vegetables help combat heat. In winter, root vegetables and warming grains provide grounding and nourishment.

🧬 2. Better Nutrient Density

Seasonal produce is harvested at peak ripeness, meaning:
☑️ Higher in vitamins, antioxidants, and flavor
☑️ Lower in transport-related nutrient degradation

🌀 3. Supports Body Rhythms (TCM Insight)

In Traditional Chinese Medicine:
〰️ Spring supports the Liver – eat green, sprouting foods
〰️ Summer nourishes the Heart – opt for light, hydrating meals
〰️ Late Summer (Earth element) balances digestion – favor sweet, earthy foods like squash
〰️ Autumn supports the Lungs – include white foods like pear, radish
〰️ Winter strengthens the Kidneys – choose warming stews, seaweeds, and black beans

Eating with the seasons balances Yin and Yang, supports organ health, and aligns with the Five Elements.

🌎 4. Environmental & Local Benefits
➰ Less transport = lower carbon footprint
➰ Supports local farmers and community economies
➰ Reduces reliance on artificial ripening and storage chemicals

💰 5. Budget-Friendly

In-season produce is often more abundant, and therefore more affordable. Out-of-season foods are typically shipped long distances or grown in artificial environments, increasing cost.

🧘‍♀️ 6. Promotes Mindful Living

Seasonal eating invites you to:
	🔺 Slow down
	🔺 Tune into natural rhythms
	🔺 Cultivate presence, gratitude, and intuitive nourishment

“Eating seasonally is how we return to harmony with the Earth and ourselves.”

[Recipe] This fragrant and creamy coconut soup is filled with the goodness of naturally sweet pumpkin and nutritious Chinese Yam. Both vegetables are believed to be beneficial for spleen and stomach health in Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM).

This soup can be eaten together with other dishes during your meals or separately as a dessert, due to its sweet and savoury flavour.

Without further ado, check out the recipe -

Ingredients
1 BeiBei Pumpkin (贝贝南瓜）
250g of of Chinese Yam (after skin is removed)
400ml of hot water
200ml of coconut cream

1) Chop BeiBei pumpkin and Chinese Yam into bite-sized pieces. Recommended to wear gloves when handling Chinese Yam as it may caused itchiness if your hands are unprotected.

2) Preheat some cooking oil in a pot or wok. Add pumpkin and stir-fry for 1 to 2 minutes. Add Chinese Yam and stir-fry everything together for around another minute.

3) Add hot water and bring it to a boil. Cover with a lid and simmer under medium heat for 10 minutes.

4) Stir in coconut cream. Add salt to taste.

Enjoy!

text:
Sore feet? Give them a cup of tea.

I always have green tea in the house - I love the Jasmine Green Tea from @thehayoumethod, but it’s not just for drinking. It’s brilliant for tired, sore feet too.

You don’t need anything fancy - a foot bath, washing-up bowl, or even a saucepan will do. Simply:

1. Brew strong green tea (I use jasmine and buy in bulk so I can be generous).

2. Fill a tub with warm water and pour the tea in slowly – careful, it’s hot!

3. Soak your feet for 10–15 minutes. Even 5 will help. Keep adding tea to keep the water warm.

4. Relax – read, breathe, meditate, or just sit.

5. Dry off with a towel (or like me, a fluffy tea towel).

It’s a lovely, ancient self-care practice that helps relax and revive sore feet – especially after a long day.
