text:
The Federal Government has adopted a National Flood Insurance Policy (NFIP) aimed at addressing the growing threat of flood-related disasters across the country.

The initiative was announced on Thursday in Abuja during the Technical Committee Meeting (TCM) on the Development of the National Flood Insurance Policy and Implementation Framework.

The Permanent Secretary of the Ministry of Environment, Mr Mahmud Kambari, said the policy would reduce the financial burden on both federal and state governments currently allocated to emergency relief and post-disaster reconstruction.

Kambari, who was represented by Mr Kunle Awojemila, Deputy Director in the Department of Flood Erosion Control and Coastal Management, said the NFIP is a proactive response to the increasing frequency and severity of flooding in Nigeria.

“The time has come to shift from reactive responses to proactive and sustainable flood risk management.

“The establishment of a National Flood Insurance Programme as outlined in Section Four of the National Erosion and Flood Control Policy (NEFCOP) is central to this strategy,” he said.

He added that the NFIP would serve as a financial safety net for individuals, businesses, and communities, enabling swift recovery from flood-induced losses and ensuring long-term resilience.

The technical committee, he noted, would define clear timelines, assign responsibilities, and develop monitoring mechanisms to ensure the policy’s effective implementation.

Also speaking, Mrs Rukayat El Rufai, Special Adviser to the President on National Economic Council and Climate Change, stressed the need to prioritise flood insurance to secure a more resilient future for Nigerians.

text:
Research on water: Did you know? 

According to Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), ice water is considered unhealthy because it disrupts the body’s natural balance of yin and yang, especially harming the digestive system (referred to as the Spleen and Stomach system in TCM). 

Here’s why:

1. It Weakens Digestive Fire (“Spleen Yang”)
 • The digestive organs in TCM are thought to function best when warm.
 • Drinking ice water is believed to extinguish the “digestive fire,” making it harder for your body to process and absorb food.
 • This can lead to bloating, fatigue after meals, loose stools, or poor appetite.

2. It Causes Qi (Energy) Stagnation
 • Cold constricts the body. When you drink cold water, it can cause internal constriction, slowing the movement of qi and blood.
 • This can result in symptoms like cramping, sluggish digestion, and even menstrual irregularities in some women.

3. It Can Aggravate Dampness
 • Cold fluids are said to contribute to internal dampness, a condition that can manifest as heaviness in the body, brain fog, or mucus buildup.
 • For those already prone to dampness (common in Western diets), ice water worsens the imbalance.

4. It Shocks the Body’s Natural Rhythm
 • TCM emphasizes harmony with nature and internal temperature regulation.
 • Ice water, especially when consumed quickly or during meals, is thought to shock the system, similar to jumping into an icy lake unexpectedly.

🚫 When Ice Water Is Especially Discouraged
 • During meals – it can interfere with digestion.
 • During menstruation – it may cause cramping or stagnation.
 • In cold weather – it increases internal cold, harming circulation.
 • For people with cold constitutions – those who tend to feel cold, tired, or sluggish.

✅ What’s Recommended Instead?
 • Warm water or room temperature water is preferred.
 • Herbal teas (like ginger, goji, or red date tea) are often used to support warmth and digestion.
 • Even in hot weather, TCM often recommends cooling foods, not cold drinks.

Always something new to learn on how our bodies were made and how to best care for ourselves…knowledge & wisdom are powerful friends…

Turmeric isn’t a magic cure-all and in Chinese Medicine, we never use single herbs in isolation like that.

🌿 In TCM, turmeric (known as Jiang Huang) is warm, acrid, and bitter. It moves blood, breaks up stasis, and unblocks Qi which is amazing for certain patterns like pain from stagnation, trauma, or early-stage inflammation.

💥 But when it’s used alone, especially in capsule form and without consideration for your pattern, it can actually worsen symptoms like:
🔥 Acid reflux
💩 Loose stools or diarrhea
🧊 Yin deficiency with heat signs
😩 Fatigue with digestive weakness 

Turmeric might be helpful in a balanced formula but blasting the body with warming herbs when your system is already inflamed or deficient is like throwing hot chili oil on a fire and wondering why it didn’t go out.

⚖️ That’s why TCM uses blends: to balance warming with cooling, tonifying with moving, drying with moistening. Every formula is customized to your body’s needs.

👉 So before you grab another golden milk latte or turmeric capsule because “it’s anti-inflammatory,” pause. Your body might need something totally different.

This jelly-like snow fungus is a TCM beauty secret! It mimics collagen, holds up to 500x its weight in water, and hydrates your skin from the inside out to help you glow from within 💫

White Fungus (Tremella) Sweet Soup

Ingredients (4 servings)
🍄 1 whole white fungus 
❤️ 8–10 red dates
🍯 honey (to taste)
💧 4 cups water 
🍒 goji berries (a small handful, optional) 

Instructions
1. Soak white fungus for 1 to 2 hours until soft and jelly-like.
2. Trim off the yellow root and cut into bite-sized pieces.
3. Rinse red dates and remove pits if you prefer.
4. In a pot, add water, white fungus, and red dates.
5. Bring to a boil, then simmer for 1 to 2 hours until the fungus turns soft and gelatinous.
6. Add goji berries in the last 5 minutes.
7. Let cool slightly then stir in honey to taste.
8. Serve warm or chilled!

text:
Your bloating isn’t just caused by gluten 👀 

That daily iced latte might be the reason you’re feeling bloated, tired and craving sugar all day.

Potential food intolerances aside, from a Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) perspective, drinking cold beverages (especially iced coffee) is one of the sneakiest ways we weaken our digestion and throw our internal balance off...

Especially in the summer.

In TCM, your digestion is powered by what’s called Spleen Yang (aka, your inner digestive fire.)

When you drink something cold, you’re essentially dumping ice on that fire, forcing your body to spend extra energy just to warm things up before it can even start digesting.

With repetition of this habit, it can lead to:
* bloating & sluggish digestion
* fatigue, brain fog, and afternoon crashes
* period pain
* water retention & puffiness
* sugar and caffeine cravings
* loose stools or irregularity
* cold hands and feet
* dampness in the body → acne, phlegm, yeast, sinus issues

It’s not about perfection. It’s about supporting your body with intention.

Instead of shocking your system with ice, try:

🌷Cooling herbal teas (like mint, rose, or chrysanthemum) served warm or at room temp

🍲 Light, hydrating meals with cooked veggies and summer fruits

🧘🏽‍♀️Cooling your body with shade, breath, and gentle movement

Wellness doesn’t always mean the trendy new iced matcha cafe.

Wellness is all about aligning with your body’s natural rhythms.

And that often starts with warmth 🫖🌿

text:
[Recipe] High quality aged dried tangerine peel is a highly prized item in Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM). It is used to regulate “Qi” (vital energy), especially in the digestive system. This can help to relieve symptoms such as indigestion, poor appetite and bloating. In addition, dried tangerine peel is also good for relieving coughs with excessive phlegm.

Apples are also believed to have beneficial properties in TCM, particularly for the lungs and digestive system. It is common for the Chinese to boil both dried tangerine peel and apple together for a healthy drink, beneficial for both digestion and “cleansing” the body of excessive fat due to overeating.

When it comes to choosing dried orange peel, it is recommended to use aged / mature ones with a darker hue and more complex, mellow aromas. They have a subtly sweet flavour, and are thinner and harder texture-wise. In contrast, the less aged version tends to be more bitter with a lighter fragrance, making them not as palatable. For reference, I am using 10 years old dried tangerine peel for this recipe.

Without further ado, check out the recipe below -

Ingredients
1 medium sized apple
5g dried aged tangerine peel
5g dried hawthorn
700ml water

1) Add aged tangerine peel (inner side down) to a pot of water and bring it to a light boil. Cook for 1 minute, then remove from pot and set aside. This process is to “clean” the tangerine peel and evoke its fragrance before the actual cooking starts. Known as “醒皮” in Mandarin.

2) Add apple slices, parboiled dried aged tangerine peel (inner side up), hawthorn and water. Bring the water to a boil, then turn the heat down to low and simmer the liquid for 25 to 30 minutes.

This beverage is naturally sweet and tangy, with a refreshing citrusy note from the aged tangerine peel. Enjoy!

text:
A magnificent Reef Manta Ray gracefully passes while feeding on plankton as another hovers in the distance at the famous German channel in Palau, Micronesia while out with our great friends @paddlingpalau 

At maturity, these spectacular reef mantas (Manta alfredi) can reach up to 5 meters across.

Unfortunately, Mantas are listed as extremely vulnerable worldwide by the IUCN from threats such as bycatch and overfishing for the harvest of their gill rakers. 
Sadly,  the demand for the gills of Manta and Mobula rays has risen dramatically over the past decade and a half for use in traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), even though they were not historically ever harvested for this purpose.

These rakers often go for up to $500 per kilogram to be used in TCM as an ingredient for soup that is claimed to boost the immune system by reducing toxins and enhancing blood circulation, curing chickenpox,  throat and skin ailments,  and male kidney issues yet none of these claims are supported by any scientific evidence nor in traditional Chinese Medicine texts.

* Women are much more prone to thyroid issues, and cold plunges can further stress the thyroid and adrenal glands, leading to fatigue and even slower metabolism if you’re already sensitive or run cold.

It is considered a medical emergency, as prompt treatment is vital to minimize brain damage and reduce the long-term effects of the condition.

From the perspective of Traditional Chinese Medicine, a stroke is not simply a blockage of blood flow but a result of an imbalance in the body’s vital substances, such as Qi (vital energy) and blood. This involves a disruption in the circulation of Qi and blood, leading to blockages or imbalances. These disruptions manifest as physical symptoms similar to those observed in Western medicine, such as numbness, paralysis, and difficulty speaking.

In Traditional Chinese Medicine, there are several key factors that contribute to a stroke, including:
•	Blood stasis
•	Qi deficiency
•	Internal wind
•	Heat and phlegm

Treatment involves:

1.	Acupuncture: Used to move stagnant blood, clear internal wind, and restore Qi flow. Specific points help unblock channels and support the recovery of function.

Treatment focuses on restoring these imbalances through methods like acupuncture, herbal medicine, and lifestyle changes to ensure smooth Qi and blood flow, reduce internal heat and wind, and strengthen the body's vitality. Have you heard of the mystery of White Flower oil? 🤔 It’s not the latest true crime novel but murkiness around the origins of this classic herbal pain reliever 💙 Invented in Penang, Malaysia by businessman Gan Geok Eng, the analgesic hit the shelves in 1927. A combination of menthol, eucalyptus, wintergreen, camphor, lavender, and peppermint oils, it actually contains no white flowers. The name comes from the inventor’s favorite bud, the white narcissus daffodil 💮

As for where the formula comes from, that remains a mystery. Stephen Gan, the son of Gan Goek Eng and executive director at his father’s company, told the South China Morning Post, “My father told me he got it from a German doctor on a cruise ship, but he told other stories to my brothers. One was that it’s a family recipe from my grandfather. Who invented it, we don’t know.”

Regardless of where it comes from, White Flower oil is an easy and fragrant way to relieve stress and pain. Just add a few drops to your bath or foot soak, and breathe deep 😌 Available at our Soho and @chelseamarketny stores, and pearlriver.com.

Jujube, Goji Berry & Ginger Tea Recipe

Ingredients (1 to 2 servings)

🍒 1 tablespoon goji berries
🫚 3 to 4 slices of fresh ginger (adjust to taste)
💧 3 cups filtered water

What to Eat in Summer According to Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) 🥗💧

Summer in TCM is ruled by the Fire element 🔥 and associated with the Heart and Small Intestine. It’s a time of yang energy—expansive, active, and hot. To stay in balance, we focus on cooling, hydrating, and heart-nourishing foods 🧘‍♀️🌿

Comment SUMMER below for my favourite summer recipes! 

Here’s what to include in your meals this season:

🍉 Cooling Foods: Think hydrating and water-rich — watermelon, cucumber, zucchini, celery, mung beans, and leafy greens. These help clear internal heat and keep you cool.

🌿 Bitter Flavors: TCM says bitter foods support the heart and help drain excess heat. Try bitter melon, dandelion greens, romaine lettuce, and chicory. @thesproutingcompany broccoli sprouts are great and I eat almost daily! 

🧊 Light & Fresh Cooking: Ditch the deep frying — go for steaming, blanching, or quick stir-frying. Cold noodle salads, spaghetti squash + lightly sautéed veggies are your best options! Be mindful not to over do it on the raw. 

💧 Herbal Teas: Sip on fresh mint tea to aid digestion.

🍑 Fruits to Favor: Peaches, plums, and lychee nourish fluids and support the heart. Just don’t overdo raw fruit—balance is everything.

⚖️ Avoid: Heavy, greasy, spicy foods and too much alcohol—they build internal heat and strain digestion.

✨Tip: Rise early, stay active (but avoid mid-day heat), and eat your biggest meal when the sun is highest — just like the energy of the season.

You may have heard that postpartum foods are supposed to be warm, soft, and easy to digest for the first 40ish days… and one pushback we often hear is, “But I am having a summer baby… there is no way I can eat hot soups.”

However, in both Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) and Ayurveda, warmth in the postpartum period isn’t about external weather—it’s about supporting and rebuilding internal balance. Birth depletes heat, blood, and fluids, leaving the body vulnerable to "cold invasion," regardless of the season. So even in summer, warm foods help replenish what was lost and protect long-term vitality (especially digestion, immunity, and hormone balance).

Warming foods aren’t about eating chili in a heatwave. They’re about healing from the inside out—gently rebuilding your strength so your body can cool itself more efficiently. Think of it like a warm hug for your digestion, your hormones, and your nervous system. You don’t need to eat hot soups in 100° weather—but the principle of “warm, soft, and easy to digest” still applies. Think gently warming spices, cooked foods, and room-temp nourishing drinks instead of icy, raw, or processed ones.

text:
What are meridians and acupoints?

During ancient time, human discovered that the stimulation of certain points on the body by using tools such as small sharp stones led to symptomatic alleviation for particular sickness. With many experimentation and observation throughout thousand years, they derived the patterns of the needle points which forms the basis of the TCM Meridian (Jing Luo) theory.

Most of the acupoints recorded were then categorised and grouped under 14 meridians and the meridians are named under the respective organs and functions. While some of the points that have specific functions were noted as extra points.

The medirian system refers to a distribution of the channels within the body which facilitates the movement of Qi, blood, essence and fluids. This is important for the nourishment, energy distribution and communication among the internal organs, limbs, joints and also the superficial skin of the body.

Acupoints are known to have respective therapeutic functions to promote body healing by triggering the body's physiological responses. The therapeutic functions of acupoints are generally categorised as:

Local therapeutic effect: For example, Zu San Li (ST36) is located at lower limb, below the knee. Obviously it could help in relieving the pain and discomfort of the knee and lower limb. 

Remote therapeutic effect: Zu San Li again belongs to Stomach Meridian is commonly used to treat gastrointestinal issue like indigestion, diarrhea or stomach bloating. Although it is located at lower limb as mentioned, it has effect of mobilizing the Qi of Stomach meridian that runs through the digestive systemn.

Special therapeutic effect: Zu San Li, also known as "point of longevity". It is believed that stimulating it can replenish the Qi and blood, improve the ability of body to have better defence against pathogenic factors and reduce body weakness in general.

There are classical 361 acupoints registered with (WHO) in year 1991. Physicians could practice acupressure, acupuncture, gua sha, cupping, blood letting or tuina on these acupoints to stimulate the function of the acupoints.

post_owner.name: LANSHIN ™
text:
As a TCM practitioner, I’m used to Chinese medicine practices getting ‘mistranslated’ when they arrive in the West. I get it—we try to understand something foreign through a lens already familiar, like defining Gua Sha as a lymphatic drainage technique.

To me, that’s like calling yoga a form of ballet where you have to point your toes or you’re doing it wrong. Skipping lymphatic prep (which I never do) isn’t a mistake, and using drainage strokes doesn’t matter. I rarely do either, and my results? Still beyond.

Western beauty and skincare seems hyper-fixated on lymphatic drainage. But in Chinese medicine—and true Gua Sha practice—the focus is broader. Gua Sha isn’t so much drainage technique as a friction technique aimed at

🩸 Boosting blood flow (face or body)
🌀 Releasing fascia adhesions
💆 Relieving muscle tension
⚡️Stimulating energy channels (经络)
♻️ Promoting toxin release
💧And yes, improving fluid circulation

So why the ‘lymphatic drainage’ mix-up? From what I understand, lymphatic drainage is best using a feather-light touch, no oil, and fingers—not exactly how Gua Sha works. Face Gua Sha, for example, uses oil and varying pressure (light to firm) to engage fascia, muscles, and circulation.

The most traditional Gua Sha produces sha—that signature red petechiae—while facial Gua Sha is a gentler adaptation that originates from those same roots.

Bottom line? If you want to combine lymphatic drainage and Gua Sha, go for it! But they’re not the same thing—and you don’t have to merge them to do Gua Sha correctly. Hope that clears things up!

Phlegm-Heat Disturbing the Mind (痰热扰心), a syndrome in which internal heat and turbid phlegm obstruct the Heart orifices and agitate the Shen (spirit). This pattern typically arises from a combination of emotional stress, improper diet and lifestyle factors. 

Excessive consumption of greasy, spicy or heavily processed foods, combined with emotional strain or suppressed anger can lead to the accumulation of internal heat and dampness. 

Over time, these transform into phlegm-heat, which blocks the orifices of the Heart thus disturbs mental clarity and emotional stability. The result is insomnia marked by restlessness, irritability, disturbed and shallow sleep. 

Patients with Phlegm-Heat disturbing the mind often present with symptoms such as difficulty falling asleep, profuse dreaming or nightmares, a sensation of heaviness in the head or body, chest oppression, dizziness, nausea, bitter taste in the mouth and possible episodes of anxiety or agitation.

Acupuncture treatment focuses on clearing heat, resolving phlegm, and calming the Shen. Commonly used points include ST40 (Fenglong) to transform phlegm, PC7 (Daling) and HT7 (Shenmen) to calm the mind and clear Heart heat, and LI11 (Quchi) to disperse excess heat from the body. GV20 (Baihui) and Yintang may also be used to settle the Shen and promote mental clarity. In herbal medicine, Wen Dan Tang (温胆汤) is frequently prescribed in cases of insomnia due to Phlegm-Heat disturbing the mind. This classic formula harmonizes the Stomach and Gallbladder, clears heat, transforms phlegm, and regulates the Qi.

In summary, insomnia due to Phlegm-Heat disturbing the mind reflects an internal obstruction pattern where turbid heat prevents the Heart from properly housing the Shen. Treatment strategies in TCM involve clearing heat, resolving phlegm, and restoring mental calm. A comprehensive approach that includes acupuncture, herbal medicine, dietary and stress management can help clear the internal obstruction, quiet the mind, and support restful, restorative sleep.

- Lack of appetite or excessive hunger

Supportive practices during Stomach time:

- Eat a warm, nourishing breakfast
- Avoid cold or raw foods that dampen digestive fire
- Sit and eat mindfully, free from distractions
- Set clear intentions for the day ahead

Why Summertime is the Best Time for Healing and Rejuvenation With the summer equinox quickly approaching with its longer days and warmer temperatures, is often considered an optimal season for healing and rejuvenation. 
•
Both Western medicine and Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) offer many reasons why summer is ideal for health and wellness.
•
Here’s why summer is perfect for optimal health:
1. Natural Vitamin D Boost: Sunlight exposure increases Vitamin D production in the skin, essential for bone health, immune function, and mood regulation. Adequate Vitamin D levels reduce the risk of various diseases, including osteoporosis and depression.

2. Increased Physical Activity: The pleasant weather encourages outdoor activities like walking, swimming, and gardening. Regular physical activity improves cardiovascular health, enhances mood through endorphin release, and supports overall physical fitness.

3. Enhanced Mental Health: Longer daylight hours reduce symptoms of Seasonal Affective Disorder (SAD) and promote a positive mental state. Sunlight exposure also boosts serotonin levels, which helps improve mood and reduce anxiety.

4. Detoxification: Warmer temperatures promote sweating, a natural detoxification process that helps expel toxins from the body. This can improve skin health and overall bodily functions.

5. Abundant Fresh Produce: Summer provides an abundance of fresh fruits and vegetables, rich in vitamins, minerals, and antioxidants. A diet high in fresh produce supports immune function, skin health, and overall well-being.

6. Connection with Nature: Spending time in nature reduces stress, lowers blood pressure, and improves mood. Activities like hiking, picnicking, and beach visits allow for relaxation and mental rejuvenation.

7. Social Connections: Summer often brings more opportunities for social interactions through vacations, barbecues, and outdoor events. Strong social connections are linked to better mental health and longevity
•
Embrace the healing power of summer by staying active, enjoying fresh foods, and connecting with nature and loved ones. Your body and mind will thank 
you!

Feeling calm & lowering stress (or cortisol = stress hormone) doesn’t have to be about buying new gear. Sometimes it definitely can help BUT there’s so many things you can do to instead that are FREE!

✨ NATURE WALKS
Shinrin-yoku AKA forest bathing. A slow, intentional walk with no destination. Time in nature can improve your mood, your energy, calms your nervous system & your soul can feel it too

✨ SHAKE IT OFF
Literally shake your body & shake it out. Tupac (& other animals) do this to release stress & guess what? So can we! Put on your favourite song, jump, shake & dance it out!

✨ SIGHING ON PURPOSE 
Deep intentional sighs can trick your body to feeling like it’s ok to let go. Huberman has some amazing podcast episodes on breath! For me I love returning to my breath

✨ MORNING SUNLIGHT
A few minutes of morning sunlight, according to Ayurveda tells your body can help your circadian rhythm & what a beautiful way to start your day!

✨ PRANAYAMA
Pranayama AKA breath work is one way to activate your parasympathetic nervous system which can help you feel more calm. There are different types of breath work you can research + do!

✨ WRITE & RELEASE ON PAPER
Write it out. The thoughts, the gratitude, the worries, write it all out. Getting your thoughts onto paper can help clear mental clutter. You can type it out onto notes on your phone but there’s magic when pen hits paper!

✨ HUMMING
In Nada Yoga, humming can help calm your vagus nerve. Sounds weird but try humming for 20-30 seconds the next time things feel heavy for you. Really feel the vibration in your chest & notice the calmness coming to surface

✨ LEGS UP THE WALL
This Viparita Karani Yoga Asana is a super simple pose I do every night for 15-20 minutes. It can help with so much including feeling relaxed & reseting your nervous system

✨ LAUGHT IT OUT
Laughter (real or forced) can help lower stress, which is where you see many laughter yoga clubs! Watch it improve your mood in minutes!

✨ TAPPING/PRESSING
In TCM tapping/pressing your sternum helps release stored tension & can help regulate energy. My dear friend @minaleelondon taught me that it’s great for emotional release!

What are a few Web App vulnerabilities pentesters need to know? There are of course many, but here are a few key ones you'll want to familiarize yourself with:

𝗖𝗿𝗼𝘀𝘀-𝗦𝗶𝘁𝗲 𝗦𝗰𝗿𝗶𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 (𝗫𝗦𝗦). This vulnerability can enable an attacker to insert malicious code into a web page that can be viewed by other users. Ultimately, XSS can result in the theft of private data, session hijacking, or even leading to the target being redirected to a malicious website. 

𝗦𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗲𝗿-𝗦𝗶𝗱𝗲 𝗥𝗲𝗾𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗙𝗼𝗿𝗴𝗲𝗿𝘆 (𝗦𝗦𝗥𝗙). SSRF can allow an attacker to induce the server-side application to make HTTP requests to an arbitrary domain of the attacker’s choosing.

text:
GUT-FRIENDLY MILLET PORRIDGE 🫚🍐 A gluten-free, high-fibre, and easily digestible breakfast : this nourishing porridge is a beautiful Qi and Blood tonic in TCM, especially supportive for the Spleen and digestion. 
Ingredients: • 1 cup hulled millet (rinsed) • 8 cups filtered water • Your favourite Chinese herbs — I used:
* Da Zao (Jujube)
* Cinnamon quills
* Cardamom pods
* Star anise 
* Chen Pi (aged tangerine peel)
* Fresh ginger slices
* Goji berries (added at the end) • 2 pears • Rhubarb • Maple syrup • Salted butter 
Method:
1. Add 1 cup of millet and 8 cups of water to your slow cooker.
2. Add herbs (I used ginger, anise, cinnamon, cardamom, Da Zao, and Chen Pi).
3. Set slow cooker to low for 4–5 hours (or overnight for a creamier consistency).
4. While it’s cooking, stew the pears separately in a small pot with ginger and cardamom until soft.
5. Stew the rhubarb with maple syrup (I added Chen Pi here too to help drain Damp) until soft. Set aside and serve with porridge when ready.
6. Once the millet is cooked, remove and discard the herbs.
7. Optionally whisk an egg or two into your bowl for extra protein and richness.
8. Top your porridge with stewed fruits, salted butter, maple syrup or honey, and any extras: yoghurt, granola, buckinis, goji berries : make it your own!
 Perfect for anyone healing their digestion, needing warmth, or wanting a grounding, gut-healing breakfast.

Asian ginseng (Panax ginseng) and American ginseng (Panax quinquefolius) are both from the Panax family but have distinct characteristics and effects.

**Asian Ginseng** is considered “warming” and more stimulating. It’s traditionally used to boost energy, enhance physical performance, and increase mental alertness. Asian ginseng is often described as more yang in Traditional Chinese Medicine - energizing and activating. It may help with physical stamina, libido, and cognitive function, but can sometimes cause restlessness or insomnia in sensitive individuals.

**American Ginseng** is considered “cooling” and more calming. It’s traditionally used for stress reduction, immune support, and gentle energy without overstimulation. In TCM terms, it’s more yin - nourishing and cooling. American ginseng is often preferred for people who find Asian ginseng too stimulating or those dealing with stress and burnout.

**Key Differences:**

- **Energy effects**: Asian is more stimulating; American is more balancing
- **Traditional use**: Asian for physical performance; American for stress and immune support
- **Ginsenoside profile**: Different ratios of active compounds
- **Side effects**: Asian more likely to cause restlessness; American generally milder
- **Cost**: American is typically more expensive due to scarcity

**Choosing**: Pick Asian ginseng for energy and performance enhancement, American ginseng for stress management and gentle support. People sensitive to stimulants often prefer American, while those needing an energy boost may prefer Asian. Both should be used cyclically rather than continuously.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

post_owner.name: Sensei Acupuncture Beauty
text:
A sour taste in the mouth can arise from various factors. Poor oral hygiene, including the buildup of bacteria, gum disease, or tooth infections, is a common cause. Certain foods, such as citrus fruits, sour candies, or vinegar-based dishes, can leave a lingering sour aftertaste. Dehydration, which leads to a dry mouth, may also affect taste perception, heightening sensitivity to sour flavours. 

Additionally, medications like antibiotics, antihistamines, or those for gastrointestinal issues can sometimes cause a sour taste as a side effect. Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) may cause stomach acid to reach the mouth, resulting in a sour taste. Infections, such as sinus infections or colds, can alter taste, while hormonal changes during pregnancy, particularly in the first trimester, are known to influence taste perception.

In Traditional Chinese Medicine, a sour taste in the mouth is often linked to imbalances in the Liver and digestive system. The main cause is Liver Qi stagnation, which disrupts the smooth flow of Qi, leading to emotional stress, digestive problems, and a sour taste. Stress, frustration, or anger can cause the Liver's energy to become stagnant or overheated, creating Liver Heat that disturbs digestion. This imbalance can affect the Stomach and Spleen, causing acid reflux, bloating, and sourness in the mouth, as the Liver’s Qi influences the Stomach’s function.

TCM focuses on harmonizing the Liver, promoting the smooth flow of Qi, and supporting the digestive organs. Acupuncture is often used to help restore balance, clear excess heat from the Liver, and relieve stagnation. Acupoints such as Tai Chong (LV3), He Gu (LI4) and Zhong Wan (CV12) are commonly targeted to ease Liver Qi stagnation, clear heat and support digestion. Herbal remedies are often prescribed to help restore balance. For example, Xiao Yao San is commonly used to smooth Liver Qi and relieve emotional stress. 

It's advised to avoid excessive sour, greasy or rich foods that can exacerbate Liver stagnation. Cooling and soothing foods such as cucumber, bitter melon, lotys root, mint, porridge and steamed vegetables are recommended to support liver function and digestion.💕

text:
Your body’s A/C button! Small Intestine 1 (SI 1, ) is a go-to point for acupuncturists to clear heat—whether it’s from a fever, overheating, or hot flashes. Keep in mind, hot flashes are usually the result of deeper imbalances (which take time to address), but SI 1 can offer temporary relief by helping to regulate heat and cool the body.

Here’s how it works: SI 1 is located at the tip of the pinky finger, where the Small Intestine energy meridian begins. In Chinese medicine, this point is known for its ability to drain excess heat from the head and face. While needling this point is stronger, you can acupressure and massage this point to help redirect heat away from the upper body (where hot flashes often manifest) and promote better energy flow. I like to apply ear seed stickers here and press on them when needed.
Remember, hot flashes are complex and often tied to hormonal shifts, stress, or other imbalances—so while SI 1 can help in the moment, long-term relief usually requires a more layered approach.

Do you have hot flashes? Tell me about what’s worked (or hasn’t worked) for you and lmk if you have questions! I am committed to cracking the code on peri/menopause and TCM has A LOT of wisdom to help you!

What Is Gua Sha?
Gua Sha (pronounced gwah-shah) is a traditional Chinese healing technique that involves scraping the skin with a smooth-edged tool to stimulate circulation and promote healing. The term “Gua” means to scrape, and “Sha” refers to the redness or petechiae that can appear on the skin after the treatment. While it is used on the body for therapeutic purposes, a gentler form of Gua Sha is used on the face for beauty and wellness.

⸻

Origins of Gua Sha

Gua Sha dates back thousands of years to Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM). Originally used to treat pain, inflammation, and stagnation in the body, it was typically performed on the back, neck, shoulders, and limbs. Over time, a more refined facial Gua Sha practice evolved, blending traditional concepts with modern skincare practices.

Benefits of Facial Gua Sha
	1.	Improves Blood Circulation
Gentle scraping stimulates microcirculation of the soft tissue, increasing blood flow and oxygen to the skin.
	2.	Reduces Puffiness
Helps drain lymphatic fluid, which can reduce facial puffiness, especially around the eyes and jawline.
	3.	Lifts and Firms the Skin
Regular use may help tone facial muscles and promote a firmer, more lifted appearance.
	4.	Eases Muscle Tension
Relieves tension in the jaw, forehead, and neck — common areas where stress accumulates.
	5.	Enhances Product Absorption
Using Gua Sha after applying facial oils or serums helps distribute the products evenly and enhances absorption.
	6.	Glowing Complexion
Improved circulation and lymphatic drainage contribute to a brighter, more radiant complexion.

Baby pangolins, AKA pangopups, hitch a ride on their mother’s tail during the few months of their life. At a moment’s notice, a mother pangolin can roll up into a protective ball, shielding her pup from danger. While the youngsters rely on their mom’s milk during this time, they also begin eating ants and termites as early as one month old.

Pangolins are considered the most trafficked wild mammals in the world, due to the demand for their meat and scales, but change is underway. Do you know about this life-saving herbal medicine? 🌿⛑️ Used for both humans and animals, Yunnan Baiyao is a best-selling product we stock in powder, capsule, and aerosol spray. It can be found in commercial kitchens, vet clinics, and even military first aid kits.

Yunnan Baiyao, also known as “Yunnan White Powder,” is a famous traditional Chinese herbal medicine developed in 1902 by Qu Huanzhang, a physician from Yunnan province. He created the formula based on local medicinal knowledge and his own clinical experience, aiming to treat traumatic bleeding and wounds. Its effectiveness quickly gained recognition, and by the early 20th century, it became a staple in Chinese medicine.

During the Second Sino-Japanese War (1937–1945), Yunnan Baiyao was extensively used by Chinese soldiers to stop bleeding and heal wounds, earning a reputation as a lifesaving remedy. It was also used by Viet Cong soldiers during the Vietnam War, with American soldiers witnessing its remarkable healing abilities. The exact recipe remains a closely guarded secret, but known herbal ingredients include Panax notoginseng (San Qi) and Ajuga forrestii, among other herbs with hemostatic, wound-healing, anti-necrotic, and anti-inflammatory properties.

Traditionally, Yunnan Baiyao has been used to treat traumatic injuries, control bleeding, reduce pain and inflammation, and aid recovery after surgery. It comes in various forms, including powder, capsules, and sprays, available on our site. In recent years, it has gained popularity around the world, with some athletes and veterinarians using it to treat injuries and bleeding (including bleeding cancers) in pets.

text:
Comment BOOK to read insights from Dr. Tan 📖 Tan Fuyuan had a dream: to open the first college of Chinese medicine in America. However, he was among the first generation of Chinese doctors in the U.S. and faced extreme challenges practicing during the late 1800s to early 1900s. He was never able to fulfill his dream.

During this era, there was widespread racial prejudice against Chinese immigrants. Laws like the Chinese Exclusion Act created a hostile environment, while violent attacks made it dangerous to operate businesses. Western doctors attacked Chinese herbalists and dismissed Chinese medicine as quackery, and Chinese doctors were denied medical licenses because medical boards refused to recognize their training, even though practitioners like Dr. Tan completed training at top institutions like the Imperial Medical College of Beijing.

White physicians also spread rumors that their herbs contained opium or other harmful substances. One physician, Charles Kirkland, even claimed that all Chinese doctors were murderers and completely ignorant.

Despite these hardships, Chinese practitioners found ways to adapt and support in unexpected places. They treated thousands of patients, including politicians and members of high society, many who were dissatisfied with harsh treatments popular in the U.S., such as extreme bloodletting, mercury, and purgatives.

Over 2100 Americans signed a petition supporting a bill so that Pang Suey, a famed Boston practitioner, could practice legally, with Rep. Joseph McGrath, whose sick father Dr. Pang treated, nearly breaking into a fistfight against Walter Bowers of the Medical State Board, who made false accusations against Dr. Pang.

The persistence of these doctors helped pave the way for the eventual acceptance of Chinese medicine in the U.S. Their struggles highlight both the discrimination faced by early Chinese immigrants and the resilience of traditional healing practices in a new and often unwelcoming land.

post_owner.name: Shellie Clark / Terminal Cancer Thriver / Root Cause Mentor
text:
Ready?

1️⃣ BELIEVED I could heal against the medical odds.

2️⃣ Ignored my oncologists telling me I had 6 months to live at best.
Researched EVERYTHING I could find about people who had healed against the medical odds, those were my teachers now.
Then:

🥦 swapped my diet to fresh and organic as my budget allowed.
I did NOT follow any radical diet, nor did I have a crazy supplement protocol and I didn't do any cleanses.
And yes, my body still healed because I....

❤️ took the mind-body connection seriously and realised my cancer diagnosis meant looking at myself as a WHOLE PERSON not just a PHYSICAL BODY.
This ☝️ is where we go wrong.

We try and fix the body without healing the person.
As if it's not all connected.
Big mistake. Huge.

Then we plop that "fixed" body back into normal life and cancer returns or just keeps progressing. 

This is the missing link.

🙏 my liver crashed after 3 infusions of immunotherapy so the treatment that was meant to help me prolong life was off the table.

😡 I pushed forward by removing any unnecessary sources of stress, including leaving my job.
The body can handle normal stress, but chronic stress?
It simply isn't designed to cope with it all the time.

I learned that I had been living in survival mode and my nervous system NEEDED to feel safe, calm, and in balance to heal.

NO diet or protocol is going to help if you are stuck living in stress, worry, fear, anxiety, regret, shame, guilt, grief, and so on.

💔 believed what Dr Gabor Mate, Louise Hay and TCM, amongst others, taught me - the root cause of dis-ease is suppressed emotional stress.
I learnt to connect to who am I and express how I feel.
Boundaries, saying no, putting me and my needs first.

Healing from what I had just been through and what I was going through.

Asking for help.
Learning to love and forgive myself.

🧘 created a daily practice for myself including practising gratitude, meditation, visualising healing to help my body rest and repair.
This was all new to me but it was helping.
My body was healing.

I coach you through every step inside my Coaching Community, doors reopen on Monday 9th - comment EMAIL, and ill add you to the invitation list.

I’ve gained so much clarity and peace after I understood this logic behind my adult acne lol. I mean it makes sense, I guess I just wasn’t super mindful or aware about these micro actions in my day to day that made a long term impact on my gut nervous system and mental (all connected).

Here’s the life audit checklist for my girlies who feel like they’ve tried everything and still can’t figure out their adult acne: 

1. Diet — you might be eating healthy but is it healthy for YOU specifically? Ie. I used to drink smoothies and eat raw salads and now I follow TCM practices (sits better with my digestion which makes sense cause I have asian genetics)

2. Micro habits around eating — do you properly chew? Do you look at your food when you eat? Are you eating distracted? Are you rushing to eat? Are you quickly going back to work after eating? Do you eat at consistent meal times? 

3. Drinks — caffeine on empty stomach? Are you having lots of iced cold drinks? Are you incorporating the right herbs in your teas for your body? Are you supplementing with electrolytes? 

4. Supplements — in our modern society, our food sources don’t give us the best minerals and nutrients (even if it’s “organic”). get some blood work done to figure out deficiencies

5. Sleep — are you actually getting enough sleep? Not 6-7, you might need 7-8. Do you properly wind down? Do you breathe deeply before bed? Do you mouth tape or clench your jaw? 

6. Relationships — are you happy with the people in your life? Is anyone draining your energy? Is there negative vibes from any friends that need to be addressed? 

7. Purpose/career/life — how are you filling this bucket right now? Is it draining you or energizing you? Are you doing something aligned with what you enjoy or care about? 

8. Finances — are you taking care of yourself in this regard? Do you have scarcity mindset? Do you have anxiety about the future? 

9. Day to day life — do you shallow breathe? Do you stretch? Do you incorporate breathing consciously? Do you exercise? Do you see the sun? Do you touch grass? Do you laugh? Do you play and be silly? 

This is a good starting point to get the ball rolling and reflecting with yourself ❤️

Despite its small size, it plays several critical roles in your body’s immune and circulatory systems! It’s pretty impressive. 

🛡️ 1. Immune System Function. Filters pathogens: The spleen helps identify and destroy bacteria, viruses, and other harmful microorganisms in the blood. Produces white blood cells: It generates lymphocytes (a type of white blood cell) that help fight infection. Immune response center: It acts like a command center, triggering the immune system to respond to invaders.

🩸 2. Blood Filtration: Removes old or damaged red blood cells: The spleen breaks down aging red blood cells and recycles components like iron. Stores platelets: It holds a reserve of platelets (important for blood clotting) and white blood cells.

In Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), dampness is considered a pathological factor - one of the key “climatic” forces that can affect the body. It can be external (from the environment) or internal (due to lifestyle, diet, or organ dysfunction). Dampness is heavy, sticky, and obstructive, and it disrupts the smooth flow of Qi (vital energy), blood, and fluids in the body.

✨Heavy: Makes the body feel sluggish or tired.
✨Sticky: Hard to get rid of, lingers in the body.
✨Slow: Causes chronic, lingering symptoms.
✨Downward-moving: Often affects the lower body first (like legs or digestion).

🌧️ Causes of Internal Dampness
- Diet: Too much sugar, dairy, fried/greasy foods, or raw/cold foods
- Lifestyle: Lack of movement, too much sitting
- Emotions: Worry and overthinking (affects the Spleen)
- Spleen Qi Deficiency: The Spleen in TCM governs transformation and transportation of fluids—if weak, it can’t manage dampness properly

🧹 How to Clear Dampness
- Diet: Eat warm, cooked foods; avoid dairy, sugar, and greasy or raw foods
- Herbs: TCM practitioners often use herbs to treat dampness in the spleen
- Exercise: Regular movement helps move Qi and fluids
- Acupuncture & Moxibustion: Used to strengthen the Spleen and resolve damp

Stress lines. They are lines that run down the lower cheek and really tell us a lot about ourselves. Having these lines is an indication that one is overworking without a reprieve. They are going too fast through life and are unable to enjoy the experience. It can also be indicative of low self-esteem as well as breathing too shallow. This area of the cheek, according to TCM is known as The Breath of Life. If there is a hollowness in this region, it shows a state of grief, or a sunken in state of being.  If you are not breathing fully, then it can lower your immune system as your Qi/life force is being inhibited.

So, what to do? First off, these lines don’t have to be permanent. I’ve seen some lines get deeper on my face when under stress and I have also seen those lines fade as I do the internal work and release what needs to go. That being said here are some things that I would do to support yourself if you have these lines..

Sleep. Aim for quality sleep. Especially women. It’s true, we do need more sleep than men. Mamas do not have a clock out. We are nursing all night long. We are attending to our children’s needs all day. It’s no wonder that these lines show on us. But we are entering the time when we’re realizing that we are not to live like men. This is key for gut health 👇🏼

Now, this might sound a bit controversial—but in Chinese medicine, raw and cold foods are believed to have a significant impact on your digestive health.

Warming and cooking food helps break it down, making it easier for your digestive system to absorb nutrients. Cold and raw foods, on the other hand, can be more taxing on your stomach—especially if your digestion is already a bit weak.

In the UK, it’s summertime, which means we tend to be more relaxed about eating cold and raw foods. But if you struggle with any of the following symptoms, I’d still recommend cutting back on them as much as you can:

👉🏼 Loose stools
👉🏼 Fatigue
👉🏼 Brain fog
👉🏼 Excess mucus
👉🏼 Gas
👉🏼 Bloating
👉🏼 A heavy feeling in the body

All I ask is this: give it five days. Try removing as many raw and cold foods as possible. Avoid ice-cold drinks, swap them for warm options like herbal teas or ginger tea, and see if you notice a difference.

Pair this with not eating too late and making breakfast your biggest meal of the day—and you’ll be well on your way to better digestive health, from a TCM perspective.

text:
In Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), the tongue map is a diagnostic microsystem that reflects the internal health of the body’s organ systems. 

👅 Tongue diagnosis is a foundational tool in the four pillars of TCM diagnosis (observation, listening/smelling, inquiry, and palpation), offering insight into the state of the Zang-Fu organs, Qi, Blood, Body Fluids, and pathogenic influences.

Tongue Map Overview 👅

Each region of the tongue corresponds to a specific organ or organ system:

	•	Tip: Heart
	•	Just behind the tip (Front): Lung
	•	Center (Middle Jiao): Spleen and Stomach
	•	Sides: Liver and Gallbladder
	•	Root (Back): Kidneys, Bladder, Small and Large Intestines ￼

This topographical division allows the practitioner to assess not just systemic health but also the location of imbalance within the body.

⸻

Purpose and Value of the Tongue Map 👅

	1.	Visual Access to Internal State:
Since the tongue is directly connected to the organs through the meridians and blood vessels, it offers visible clues to the body’s internal harmony or disharmony.

	2.	Organ-specific Clues:
Each region may show signs of imbalance such as discoloration, swelling, cracking, coating, or dryness that reflect specific organ dysfunctions. For instance:
	•	A red tip can indicate Heart Fire.
	•	A pale, swollen center with teeth marks suggests Spleen Qi deficiency.
	•	A thick yellow coat at the root may show Damp-Heat in the Lower Jiao.

	3.	Differentiation of Patterns:
Observing the body color, shape, moisture, and coating across mapped areas helps in differentiating syndromes such as excess vs. deficiency, heat vs. cold, or interior vs. exterior patterns.

This map, combined with the tongue’s physical qualities, allows for a non-invasive yet powerful diagnostic method that TCM practitioners can use regularly to track the progress of a patient’s condition and treatment efficacy.

Instructions:
1. Large Intestine 20 – “Welcome Fragrance”
Start with acupressure at LI20. Gently circle clockwise 10–30x (or longer if congestion is intense), then switch directions and circle counterclockwise. If it feels tender, that’s likely pressure from stagnation—so lean into the release.

2. Move up slowly
While massaging upward along the side of your nose, pause on any tender spots. Think of it like breaking up congestion as you work your way toward the brow.

3. Urinary Bladder 2 – “Gathered Bamboo”
Once you reach the inner brow point (UB2), apply acupressure circles here too—10–30x in each direction. This one is often tender but deeply calming once you soften it. Notice how your whole nervous system responds?

4. Gua Sha Across the Cheekbone
Using your knuckles or a Gua Sha tool, stroke from the side of your nose along the cheekbone toward the top of your ear. Do this 10–30x, or more if congestion is stubborn—or it just feels really good.

✨ How’s your sinus congestion now? 

💬 Drop a comment if you felt a shift—or if you noticed anything else. And if not, try doing each step longer or repeat this again in an hour or two.

There are so many acupoints on your body that help relieve congestion—and these two are some of the best on your face. That means you can activate them while you’re cleansing, hydrating, or moisturizing. Double whammy!

text:
If there is one thing that women can do to optimize their health and vitality is to honor the natural rhythms of their body-specifically their moon cycle aka their period. 

for so long, we bought into the lie that we had to live like men and work and grind as they do. That not only leads to physical repercussions, but also energetic repercussions. It puts us in our masculine and can wreak havoc on our relationships. When the polarity is off, things are OFF… if you catch my drift.

Some ways to step back into our feminine is to honor our bodies needs as we’re moving into our moon cycle. This is a time to slow down, rest, go inward and reflect on what needs to change in our lives to better ourselves and everything around us. It is truly a monthly reset and a deeply spiritual experience. Here are some things you can do to make this time magical.

💫Rest, rest, R E S T. Take the first two days to nap, lay in bed and read, journal, reflect. This is a time to truly hear from our inner sanctuary. 

💫Meal prep a few dinners beforehand so that you don’t have to cook dinner those first few days. Have easy, grab and go snacks for the kids and yourself. Lots of hydration, fruits, & protein sources.

💫 Slow intentional movement and stretching. Do whatever the heck you want, but my body says STOP. I don’t want to be grinding at the gym and lifting heavy. My back will slap me later for playing that game. I prefer to do bowspring or intuitive movement.

💫Spa day. Take a mineral bath, do self massage, give yourself a facial, do your nails, brush your hair or do a hot oil hair treatment. If you have daughters, show them this. Lay in bed with them and fix each other‘s hair. Let them see that this is an honorable time.

💫Prep before cycle. I like to do a coffee enema and sauna before I start as extra detoxing. I also like to do a castor oil liver pack the first few days of my cycle.

Let me know if this helps you and what you do on your cycle.

At maturity, these spectacular reef mantas (Manta alfredi) can reach up to 5 meters across.

Unfortunately, Mantas are listed as extremely vulnerable worldwide by the IUCN from threats such as bycatch and overfishing for the harvest of their gill rakers. 
Sadly,  the demand for the gills of Manta and Mobula rays has risen dramatically over the past decade and a half for use in traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), even though they were not historically ever harvested for this purpose.

These rakers often go for up to $500 per kilogram to be used in TCM as an ingredient for soup that is claimed to boost the immune system by reducing toxins and enhancing blood circulation, curing chickenpox,  throat and skin ailments,  and male kidney issues yet none of these claims are supported by any scientific evidence nor in traditional Chinese Medicine texts.

text:
Let's talk about the 9 best things you can do post transfer to support implantation ~ naturally. 🫶🏽

1. Rest… but don’t overdo it.
Gentle walks support blood flow and calm your nervous system. Lying flat all day? Not necessary! However, spin classes, running & F45 are definitely OFF the schedule. Your womb is sacred and you want all the blood flowing to your uterus not your quadriceps. 

2. Nourish your blood and yin.
Choose warm, cooked, nutrient-rich, easy to digest foods like congee, root vegetables, bone broth, and slow-cooked stews. These build energy (Qi) and blood,  which are key in Traditional Chinese Medicine to support the uterine lining. In TCM, warmth builds life, and your womb loves warmth. Avoid cold smoothies and raw salads.

3. Keep your womb warm.
In Chinese Medicine, warmth = life force. No cold feet, ice dips or ice drinks. Socks and a warm belly are your new best friends.

4. Minimise stress + overthinking.
Deep breathing, acupuncture, and guided meditation help activate your parasympathetic nervous system. Your mind, body and embryo will love you for this. 🤍

5. Viparita Karani (legs up the wall). This gentle pose is like taking a 10-minute nap. It shifts you into your parasympathetic nervous system, increases blood flow to your womb nourishing your reproductive organs and gently supporting implantation. Just 5–10 minutes daily can work wonders.

6. Boost your oxytocin. Oxytocin isn’t just the “love hormone” it supports uterine receptivity. Cultivate it through touch, hugs, laughter, calming music, or connection with your partner or pets This is medicine and it’s free.

7. Check your progesterone levels.
Progesterone is crucial for implantation and early pregnancy. I recommend checking levels on the day of transfer and again 5 days post-transfer. If they’re not high enough, your care team can support you with adjustments. This is one of the most overlooked, yet vital pieces of your IVF success.

8. Trust your body.
Your job now is to soften, to receive, and rest. Your body is your garden  and your seed of potential has been planted.

⚠️ Pro Tip: Diabetics monitor portions; cold-sensitive bodies avoid eating before meal.

3.Mulberry: Ancient Tonic for Vitality

Nourishes liver/kidney, enriches blood, darkens hair, and sharpens vision – perfect for screen fatigue or premature graying. 

Science-Backed Evidence: 
-Anthocyanin concentration: 2× blueberries (USDA), protects retinal capillaries

⚠️ Pro Tip: Those with loose stools choose dried berries; raw may worsen dampness.

Cycles Within the Five Elements

There are two main cycles that describe how the elements interact:

1. Generating (Sheng) Cycle – Creation & Nourishment
Each element nourishes the next:

Wood feeds Fire
Fire creates Earth (ash)
Earth bears Metal
Metal enriches Water (as minerals)
Water nourishes Wood

2. Controlling (Ke) Cycle – Balance & Regulation

Each element controls another to keep balance:

Wood controls Earth (roots stabilize soil)
Earth controls Water (dams/soil absorption)
Water controls Fire (extinguishes it)
Fire controls Metal (melts it)
Metal controls Wood (axe cuts tree)

Clinical Application

In TCM, this system is used to:

Diagnose imbalances between organs and emotional states

Prescribe herbal formulas or acupuncture protocols that support or regulate specific elements

Understand symptom progression (e.g., grief weakening the lungs, which then affects the kidneys)

Our body remembers. 

When we treat symptoms instead of the root, another organ will always end up compromised.

History Fact of the Day • June 1, 2025

Note: On June 1, 1926, Norma Jeane Mortenson—later known as Marilyn Monroe—was born in Los Angeles, California, destined to become an icon whose life would mirror the glitz and tragedy of Hollywood’s golden age. Raised in foster homes, her childhood was a carousel of instability, yet by 1946, she transformed into a pin-up model, her platinum curls and breathy voice captivating post-war America. As Marilyn, she starred in 30 films, from Gentlemen Prefer Blondes (1953), where her pink-dressed “Diamonds Are a Girl’s Best Friend” became a cultural touchstone, to Some Like It Hot (1959), a comedic masterpiece. Her marriages to Joe DiMaggio and Arthur Miller, plus rumored ties to JFK, fueled tabloid frenzy, while her struggles with mental health and addiction shadowed her stardom. Dead at 36 in 1962, her legacy endures—2025 sees L.A.’s TCM Festival screening her films, fans in vintage dresses mimicking her subway-grate pose, a reminder of a star who burned too bright, too fast.

post_owner.name: Manual Jakarta
text:
Notes of time and tradition run deep in Toko Obat Mutiara, one of the oldest traditional Chinese medicine shops in Glodok. 

Founded in 1944 by Yoe Sauw Kwan, a sinshe (traditional Chinese medicine practitioner) from Fujian, the shop is now helmed by his grandson, Bambang Sutejo, with his nephew continuing the role of sinshe in the family lineage.

“In Glodok, the oldest businesses are either food stalls or medicine stores,” said Bambang. “With the nature of our work, knowing Mandarin is essential to navigate the practice. That’s why it can be a challenge to find a new generation to carry it on.” 

From herbal ointments to old-wisdom ingredients, the shop draws a mix of regulars who have been coming since his grandfather’s time, and younger visitors, many of whom are just starting to embrace traditional remedies. “It’s not as integrated yet, but people are getting curious,” closed Bambang. “I think that’s the beauty of TCM, while the healing process may take longer, when it works, the results are long lasting.” 

Faces of Jakarta is a series where we feature creative figures, long-time residents and familiar faces that capture the city’s inimitable charm and diversity. #FacesofJakarta#ManualTheWeekendIssue

Did you know that stress can significantly impact your hormonal balance? Let’s break it down:

1. **Stress Triggers Cortisol Production** 😟➡️💧 
When you’re stressed, your body releases cortisol, the “stress hormone.” This response is designed to help you manage immediate challenges but can become problematic with chronic stress.

2. **Cortisol’s Effect on Progesterone** ⚖️ 
Elevated cortisol levels can lead to a decrease in progesterone production. Progesterone is vital for regulating the menstrual cycle and overall hormonal balance.

3. **Low Progesterone = High Estrogen** 🚨 
When progesterone levels drop, estrogen can become dominant, leading to a condition known as estrogen dominance. This imbalance can cause various health issues.

4. **The Link to Inflammation** 🔥 
High estrogen levels are associated with increased inflammation in the body. Chronic inflammation can lead to various diseases, including autoimmune disorders, weight gain, and more.

You can buy sulfur dioxide kits on Amazon! A small amount of it is totally okay for our body, as it is in many wine also. China sets a strict number for the most amount of sulfur dioxide that can be added to an herb, so it’s not like a life-threatening concern. However, I like to test it because if an herb contains sulfur dioxide, it generally means that the vendor doesn’t care much about the quality of their herbs and may have added other chemicals to it, mistreat it during storage, and so on. For a comprehensive understanding of the herbs you purchase, you should still ask for lab tests or a lot of questions (small growers with organically agriculture practices may not have lab tests).

When my patient with painful periods says she walks barefoot on cold floors… Chinese medicine is already raising an eyebrow. 👀❄️

According to Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), exposing your feet to cold can disrupt your internal balance—especially when it comes to hormones and your menstrual cycle.

Here’s why it matters (and what TCM has taught for centuries):
🔥 Cold can invade the uterus — The feet are a key entry point for cold energy in the body, which can lead to stagnation and painful cramps.
🌊 It blocks the flow of qi and blood — Good circulation is vital for a smooth cycle. Cold slows things down, leading to clotting, discomfort, and irregularity.

text:
The market is in Bo Zhou, Anhui. The majority of the TCM herbs / herbal tea that you can get from Chinatown and TCM pharmacies around the world come from here. 

Vendors bring herbs from all across China to here to trade. Even though their main business is wholesale, they are surprisingly nice and patient when you ask questions. However, most of them don’t know a thing about TCM. They are just here to sell. A few vendors I’ve talked to are significantly more knowledgeable with their herbs and I learnt a lot from them! Half of them take naps in the afternoons so definitely go early in the morning (in the video, it was the afternoon and many shops were closed already). 

Bo Zhou herbs were once known to be “low quality”. There were fake herbs, herbs with heavy metals etc. The good news is that the government has been really cracking down on those vendors for the past decade. Now (from what I heard and what I saw), you can trust the herbs there. You won’t be able to find organic herbs there, but you can certainly find some great quality farmed / wild herbs. All vendors let me take samples of their herbs for testing purposes before ordering their herbs. Again, you get what you ask for. If you know what you are looking for and ask the right questions, you will get great herbs here! 

Do you want to visit this market? What herb would you buy? 😊

🌾 Why Whole Grains Are Essential for Digestion (According to TCM)

In Traditional Chinese Medicine, whole grains help moisten your stomach and intestines — keeping your digestive tract from drying out and becoming stagnant.

🥣 When you skip whole grains or eat only dry foods (like crackers, processed snacks, or overly dry proteins), your organs become internally dry. That’s when food gets stuck, causing:

🚫 Bloating
🚫 Post-meal pain
🚫 A heavy, sluggish feeling

Whole grains (like rice, millet, barley, or oats) act as natural lubricants for digestion. They support the spleen and help food move smoothly through the gut.

💡 How much do you need?
It depends on the grain:
👉 Hard-to-digest grains (like wild rice or some seeds): ~5% of your meal
👉 Easy grains (like white rice or congee): up to 30%

✅ Make whole grains a regular part of your meals to balance moisture, ease digestion, and reduce bloating naturally.

text:
Traditional Acupuncture is a key practice in Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), involving inserting thin needles into specific points on the body to stimulate energy flow and balance. This technique aims to restore the natural flow of “Qi” (life force energy), travelling through pathways called meridians, and address imbalances that can lead to illness, taking a holistic view of your health.

Traditional acupuncture often looks at the tongue is seen to reflect the degree of health or imbalance of the body and feeling of the pulse quality in the wrist showing a snap shot of how the qi is responding at that point in time. 
Commonly used in traditional acupuncture are;
 ✨Moxa - Chinese mugwort herb for nourishing and warming
✨Cupping - to stimulate blood flow and alleviate pain or muscle tension.
✨Other techniques such as guasha, Chinese massage, ear acupuncture, etc.

Western Medical Acupuncture (WMA) has little or no emphasis on Chinese Medical philosophy. This model uses anatomy, physiology and current medical models in its quest to alleviate pain. 
This style of acupuncture tends to use localised needles around area that are painful in a bid to alleviate pain. 
The philosophy here is stimulating sensory nerves under the skin and in the muscles. This results in the body producing natural substances, such as pain-relieving endorphins.

🤷‍♀️Me… I use both approaches, based of the needs and expectations of the patient. 

✨I might use localised WMA for tennis elbow or lower back pain for instance, whilst my chronic widespread  pain patients I am more likely to revert to the TCM approach.

Sadly,  the demand for the gills of Manta and Mobula rays has risen dramatically over the past decade and a half for use in traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), even though they were not historically ever harvested for this purpose.

These rakers often go for up to $500 per kilogram to be used in TCM as an ingredient for soup that is claimed to boost the immune system by reducing toxins and enhancing blood circulation, curing chickenpox,  throat and skin ailments,  and male kidney issues yet none of these claims are supported by any scientific evidence nor in traditional Chinese Medicine texts.

In the clinic, explaining the concept of Jing, Shen, and Qi in Traditional Chinese Medicine can feel like trying to eat soup with a fork.

So I always try to use simple digestible ways to explain it to patients in order to make it all click.

The candle analogy makes it easier to explain these concepts and to make people see how essential they all are for life:

* The wax is your Jing. This is your essence, what you’re born with. Think of it as your body’s fundamental fuel reserve. It burns slowly over time, like the candle’s wax. When the wax runs out, the flame fades , this is the natural process of aging and mortality. In TCM, Jing is responsible for growth, fertility, and longevity.

* The flame is your Shen. Your Shen is your light, your spirit, your mind. When the flame is steady and bright, your thoughts are clear, and your emotions are grounded. If it flickers or dims, it signifies an unsettled spirit, often manifesting as anxiety, confusion, or burnout.

*The heat is your Qi. Qi is the invisible energy that moves everything. It radiates from the flame, powering every function of your body, from your breath and blood circulation to digestion and physical motion. You gain Qi from food, air, and rest, and you spend it daily to keep going.

The Heart of Vitality
So, to summarize:
* Jing is the wax.
* Qi is the heat.
* Shen is the flame.

When you balance these three vital aspects, your candle burns steady and bright. That, in essence, is the heart of vitality and well-being in TCM.

9 Things You Need to Know Right NOW, When Transitioning from Spring to Summer according to Traditional Chinese Medicine

1.The Energy Shifts from Wood to Fire. Spring is about growth and vision. Summer brings movement, warmth, and connection. It’s the most Yang season, associated with the Fire element—and with it, the Heart and Small Intestine.

2.Your Heart Needs Protection
In TCM, the Heart governs blood, emotions, and spirit. Too much heat, overstimulation, or poor sleep can lead to anxiety, restlessness, or feeling ungrounded.

3.The Sun is Strong, But So Is the Risk of Overheating. Longer days and stronger sun can easily overheat the body. This can show up as irritability, rashes, fatigue, or even digestive issues.

4.Sweating Isn’t Always Cleansing
While it’s healthy to sweat, too much sweating weakens Qi and fluids, especially if followed by cold exposure or wind. Always dry off and keep your neck and chest covered after being outside.

5.Digestion Still Needs Warmth. Raw foods and iced drinks may seem refreshing, but they weaken the Spleen. Focus on lightly cooked meals, herbal teas, and hydrating foods like cucumber or zucchini or try chrysanthemum tea. 
 
6.Sleep Grounds the Fire Element
Fire rises. Sleep and rest bring it back down. Try to wind down earlier, keep a consistent bedtime, and start your day gently to stay in balance.

In Traditional Chinese Medicine, digestion isn’t just about what you eat—it’s about how, when, and how well your body can process it. There are 3 main reasons your digestion might be off:

post_owner.name: My Mum's Flavour
text:
[Recipe] In TCM, luffa is a cooling vegetable best for removing heatiness in the body, clearing of phlegm, treating heat-type cough and relieving water retention. Apart from stir-frying it, luffa can also be used to make soup.

Nutrient-rich mushrooms are used with luffa in this vegetarian recipe, for a refreshing soup with a light umami flavour. This soup is gout-friendly when taken in moderation and rich in plant protein.

Without further ado, check out the recipe -

Ingredients
1 medium sized Luffa
130g fresh golden oyster mushrooms
15g dried black fungus
50g dried beancurd skin
160g frozen Edamame (in shells) or around 65g edamame beans
1000 to 1200ml hot water

1) Chop luffa into thick strips. Soak dried black fungus and beancurd skin till fully rehydrated.

2) Stir-fry golden oyster mushrooms till soften and fragrant in some pre-heated oil. Add luffa and cook everything together for a minute.

3) Add hot water. Bring it to a boil, then add rehydrated black fungus and beancurd skin. Bring the water to a boil again, then cover with a lid and simmer for 5 minutes.

4) Add edamame beans and mix everything together. Add salt and pepper to taste.

Enjoy!

text:
9 Things You Need to Know Right NOW, When Transitioning from Spring to Summer according to Traditional Chinese Medicine

1.The Energy Shifts from Wood to Fire. Spring is about growth and vision. Summer brings movement, warmth, and connection. It’s the most Yang season, associated with the Fire element—and with it, the Heart and Small Intestine.

2.Your Heart Needs Protection
In TCM, the Heart governs blood, emotions, and spirit. Too much heat, overstimulation, or poor sleep can lead to anxiety, restlessness, or feeling ungrounded.

3.The Sun is Strong, But So Is the Risk of Overheating. Longer days and stronger sun can easily overheat the body. This can show up as irritability, rashes, fatigue, or even digestive issues.

4.Sweating Isn’t Always Cleansing
While it’s healthy to sweat, too much sweating weakens Qi and fluids, especially if followed by cold exposure or wind. Always dry off and keep your neck and chest covered after being outside.

5.Digestion Still Needs Warmth. Raw foods and iced drinks may seem refreshing, but they weaken the Spleen. Focus on lightly cooked meals, herbal teas, and hydrating foods like cucumber or zucchini or try chrysanthemum tea. 
 
6.Sleep Grounds the Fire Element
Fire rises. Sleep and rest bring it back down. Try to wind down earlier, keep a consistent bedtime, and start your day gently to stay in balance.

7.Emotions Can Run High. Joy is the emotion of summer, but too much heat can turn joy into anxiety, overstimulation, or emotional exhaustion. Make time for quiet and nervous system regulation.

8.Support the Skin and Circulation
The Heart and Small Intestine influence circulation and skin clarity. If you’re seeing more breakouts or hives, or feel flushed and warm, it may be internal heat. Bitter greens, mint, and cooked chrysanthemum can help.

9.Transition Slowly. Don’t rush into summer. Let your body acclimate. Wake earlier, eat lighter, move with intention. The choices you make now shape how you feel in fall.

Save this if you tend to feel scattered or off during seasonal shifts. Transitions deserve attention too.🌞

The hairline in ancient Chinese face reading has to do with the water element, though it is a minor feature. This element has an association with fear. The ancient Chinese saw the hairline as the mother’s influence. This could be influence from the actual mother, but could also be a caretaker or someone in a religious leadership position, or even a father. But it has to do with the main caretaker of the individual. The idea here is that the person who took care of the child instilled a sense of fear with rules and regulations, standards and expectations. Sometimes parents will use fear as a tactic to instill a belief system into their children.

So a child can develop this hairline that is lower and somewhat oval across the forehead. The lower the hairline, the stronger the mothers influence, the repression and the installation of fear. These people tend to be quite mannerly and polite, because of the fear looming in the back of their minds. The higher the hairline, the more unfazed a person is by the rules and regulation. There is more of a freedom in their spirit and there was more than likely more freedom growing up. Not that they aren’t polite but they just don’t get too concerned about what society has to say they have to be like.

In Taoist philosophy, we come to understand that the highs are born from the lows — that joy and elevation are not separate from sorrow, but rather shaped and deepened by it. 

The valley gives rise to the mountain; the stillness gives shape to the song. 

In the low points, when life feels quiet, uncertain, or heavy, we are offered a sacred invitation to listen more closely, to learn more deeply, and to meet parts of ourselves often hidden in the thrill of the high.

If you find yourself in a low moment now, may you be well held — by your own breath, by the people and practices that nourish you, and by the slow wisdom that reveals itself only in the quiet. These spaces, though uncomfortable, are fertile ground. They ask us not to fix or force, but to soften and allow.

Just as the stars can only be seen against the darkness of night, our inner light is sometimes most visible when everything else falls away. 

Trust that you are not broken — what if you are becoming? The Tao teaches us that life moves in cycles, and this too will turn. 

There is meaning here, even if it is not yet fully visible.

May you rest in the knowledge that this phase has purpose, and that you are not alone.

text:
5 things I WOULDN’T do as a Traditional Chinese Medicine Practitioner 

In TCM, true health isn’t just about avoiding sickness; it’s about balance, harmony, and deep nourishment. These practices might seem small, but they have a MAJOR impact on your Qi, digestion, and overall vitality. 

In clinic, these are some of the first things I share with patients, and they often see very quick results!

1. Skip Breakfast
Between 7–9 AM, your Spleen (the organ responsible for digestion in TCM) is most active. Skipping breakfast weakens this vital system, draining your energy and compromising your immunity. Even something small and always warm helps fire up your metabolism and nourish your body for the day ahead.

2. Eat Raw Foods
Your Spleen hates cold and dampness. Raw foods, like that cold yogurt, overnight oats, or smoothies, force your body to expend extra energy to “cook” them internally. This slows digestion, leads to bloating, and creates dampness. I always choose warm, cooked meals to keep my digestive fire strong.

3. Drink Iced or Cold Drinks
Just like raw foods, cold liquids make your body work overtime to warm them up to body temperature. This drains your energy, slows your metabolism, and can leave you feeling fatigued. I stick to room-temperature or warm drinks so my body doesn’t have to expend precious energy, ensuring my blood and Qi are always nourished.

4. Walk Around with Wet Hair
This might surprise you, but wet hair allows cold and damp to enter your body through key points on your head and neck, according to TCM. Over time, this weakens your immunity and disrupts the flow of Qi and blood. It can lead to tremendous fatigue, feeling cold constantly, and even water retention. Always dry your hair!

5. Burn Myself Out
Your Kidney energy is your life’s battery, and overexertion drains it fast. Depleting this vital essence is no joke; it can manifest as low back pain, premature greying, poor memory, tinnitus, night sweats, hot flashes, low libido, and hormonal imbalances. I prioritize protecting mine with boundaries (still a work in progress, honestly!), because even trees need winter to recharge.

This midday window is about sorting through input — food, information, emotions, and interactions — and keeping only what nourishes.

In TCM, the flavor associated with the Small Intestine is bitter — a taste that helps clear heat, dry dampness, and bring precision to the body and mind. Think of bitter greens, dark chocolate, or strong tea. Bitterness refines — just like this time of day. It reminds us that not everything we take in needs to stay.

Supporting the Small Intestine during its peak hours can look like:
• Drinking warm water or bitter herbal tea
• Limiting decision-making and stimulation
• Taking a short walk to process and reset
• Sitting quietly to integrate the first half of your day

To discern without judgment.
To let go of what clutters the body and mind.

The medicine of 1–3 PM is subtle but profound: knowing what to keep — and what to release.

I don’t see a ton of press and hold tutorials, so share your favorite TCM expert accounts with me.

Savannah’s work is impactful and inspiring because she’s teaching us to find what’s true in our own body. It’s a creative body of work that draws from the deep wisdom of different cultures, modalities, and schools of thought.
