☯️ Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), dietary rules are slightly different than in the western system. TCM focuses on nourishing the body’s energy (Qi) and organs through a variety of foods, flavors, and cooking methods. It’s about eating foods that complement each persons constitution as well as eating with the season.

☯️ Here are some key factors to consider in TCM dietary therapy;

🥘Five Flavors: TCM associates five flavors (sweet, sour, bitter, pungent, salty) with specific organs and energy flows. Having a mix of these is important 
🌞Seasonal Eating: Consuming foods in season is considered beneficial, as it aligns with the natural rhythms of the body and environment.  
🔥Food properties  Foods are categorised based on energetic temperature not macronutrients. For example some foods are Yin (cooling, moist) and some are Yang (warming,dry). Certain types of foods help treat different conditions and support different constitutions. 
🍎Avoid Cold and Raw foods (and drinks): TCM generally discourages excessive consumption of cold, raw foods. Raw foods can be difficult to digest and therefore cause bloating, diarrhoea and fatigue. Lightly cooking vegetables and stewing fruit is preferable to raw foods.  🌈 Eat the rainbow: There are 5 elements that are associated with different flavours AND colours in Chinese Medicine. It’s important to try and consume as many colours as possible to support each organ. Red, yellow, green, white and blue/black are the colours that connect to each organ in TCM

Your period is your monthly report card!

In both conventional medicine and Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), the color of your menstrual blood can actually give you some clues about your hormone health, fertility, and overall wellness- It’s a pretty good indicator of how happy your reproductive system is... 

🟤 Brown or dark blood:
This can often appear at the start or end of your period, and may not flow properly like normal blood does. 
This usually indicates old, stale blood that has taken longer to leave the uterus- a sign of stagnation and possibly a cold uterus in TCM. It can also be linked to poor circulation and in terms of hormones we would be suspicious of low progesterone... 
If the blood is very dark AND clotted, once the blood flow is coming through, then you’re dealing with some significant Qi stagnation (small clots) or Blood stagnation (large clots), and you probably experience pain too 😣

🌸 Diluted/ Pink blood: 
This weak colour suggests low estrogen levels, especially if the flow is light, as well as some potential iron deficiency, nutrient deficiencies or anaemia. In TCM, this is an indicator of Qi + Blood Deficiency and tends to go hand-in-hand with low energy and poor digestion 😴

🩸 Healthy Red Blood: 
A medium, vibrant red color is ideal and reflects good circulation, and strong Kidney + Spleen Qi (energy) in TCM 🙂

🔥 Bright red blood: 
The blood will be very bright when there is excess heat in the body, which can be the result of stress, inflammation, or certain diet/lifestyle habit. In TCM, this heat needs addressing as it can disrupt ovulation and affect fertility 🥚

So, if you’re trying to conceive, struggling with irregular cycles, or just want a deeper understanding of what your body is trying to tell you- this is where we start ✔️

Wishing @chinesetheatres a 98th Birthday today! 🍰🍰💖 Built by a partnership headed by Sid Grauman, the theater opened May 18, 1927, with the premiere of Cecil B. DeMille’s “The King of Kings.”

It has since been home to many premieres, including the 1977 debut of “Star Wars”, as well as many private events and three Academy Awards ceremonies. 

Among the theater’s features are the concrete blocks set in the forecourt, which bear the signatures, footprints, and handprints of popular motion picture personalities from the 1920s to the present day.

THE NAME: 

Originally named Grauman’s Chinese Theatre, it was renamed Mann’s Chinese Theatre in 1973, and reverted to its original name in 2001. In 2013, Chinese electronics manufacturer TCL Corporation purchased the facility’s naming rights for $5 million.

THE ARCHITECTURE:

The exterior’s most notable feature is the 90 foot tall pagoda centered in the middle of the forecourt. The design features numerous traditional Chinese ornamentations, including a 30 foot tall stone-carved mural of a dragon on the central wall between the columns. Two Ming dynasty-era guardian lion statues flank the venue’s entrance. 

The U.S. government granted permission for the statues, as well as temple bells and other artifacts, to be imported from China. Moon Quon, a Chinese poet and filmmaker, traveled to the United States to oversee a team of Chinese artisans tasked with creating the theater’s traditional decoration.

Goji berries 枸杞子 have been widely used in traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), for thousands of years, and because of their neutral nature, they can be used by those with either a Yin or Yang deficiency. Goji berries are regarded for their ability to support the Liver, Kidneys, eyes, and Lungs. They are especially known for their Liver support.

📍 Comment Goji below and I will send you a link to my wildcrafted Goji Extract! Be well :) 

Goji berries are a major source of zeaxanthin dipalmitate (ZD), a xanthophyll carotenoid shown to benefit the liver. Liver disease is one of the most prevalent diseases in the world. Some conditions, such as chronic hepatitis B virus, liver cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma, remain incurable. Managing them can constitute an economic burden for patients and healthcare systems. Hence, development of more effective pharmacological drugs is warranted. Studies have shown the hepatoprotective, antifibrotic, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antiapoptotic, antitumor, and chemopreventive properties of ZD [1].

Goji berries have been used to treat liver disease in traditional Chinese medicine for a very long time. I recommend it to anyone suffering from Liver imbalances as well as any eye issues as the eyes are governed by the Liver in TCM. Goji berries contain taurine. Taurine is an amino acid, which is a building block of human proteins found in the brain, spinal cord, heart and muscle cells, skeletal muscle tissue, and retinas. Taurine is also present in leukocytes or white blood cells that reside in the immune system and play an essential role in protecting cells from damage [2]. Taurine has anti-oxidative, anti-inflammatory and immuno-modulating properties which can protect the retina [3].

Research on animal models indicates goji berries can help with managing liver health and preventing the progression of alcohol-induced fatty liver disease [PMID: 25552899].

Research on human liver cancer cells has also found the goji berry can inhibit tumor growth [PMID: 25552899].

Gentle pressure and deep breathing focused on the lower abdomen can stimulate the vagus nerve, which modulates the parasympathetic nervous system—promoting relaxation, digestion, and emotional regulation.

This has real implications for reducing anxiety, improving gut function, and lowering inflammation.

Known as the “second brain”, the gut has its own network of neurons (ENS) that communicate with the brain.

Acupressure in this area may enhance gut-brain signaling, helping with motility, digestion, and emotional regulation, especially because of serotonin production in the gut.

3. Fascia and Interoception:

The lower abdominal area contains dense fascia, which is connected to the body’s network of internal sensation (interoception).

Pressing gently on this area may increase body awareness, calm the nervous system, and support trauma healing, particularly in somatic practices.

text:
Elderflower, Rhubarb and Rose Petal Cordial 
Elderflowers are just coming out at the moment (their berries which come later in the year - make a wonderful winter immune boosting syrup). Combined with seasonal rhubarb and foraged rose petals they make a delicious sweet and sour, refreshing cordial. Perfect for this time of year and tonifying the liver and gallbladder of spring time, as well as the stomach and spleen of the earth element according to TCM.
✅ Remember to save the post so you can come back to it.
It’s SO easy to make - simply just a sugar syrup with the flavours essentially infused. The citric acid preserves it for longer and add more of the zingy ness which I love.
I love adding in seasonal botanicals to boost the cordial more and tie in with the seasons. This time of year is a heady mix of fragrances and colours which wake up the senses and create such visual excitement. One of my favourite times of year.

This makes x 2 large bottles 
1.5 kg caster or granulated sugar
2 pints warm water 
2 1/2 lemons peeled and sliced
50g citric acid
30-35 heads elderflower

Simple place your sugar into a large saucepan and add in your warm water - stir to gently melt on a low heat. When dissolved turn the heat up and allow to boil for a few minutes to make a syrup.
Next add in your lemon peel and sliced lemons as well as elderflower heads. Stir all together. Heat off. Add in your citric acid and leave all to sit and “stew” together over night or for 12/24hrs.
Strain everything through a sieve and bottle up. I’m not entirely sure how long this keeps.. but it’s a long time (as it’s mainly sugar syrup) I’ve still got mine from last year but I store mine in the fridge and you can easily freeze in plastic or glass safe bottles.

I came to Singapore with a suitcase and good intentions. I left with a damp passport, six mosquito bites, and a new spiritual guardian named Uncle Raymond who sells noodles in Chinatown.

In Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), the concept of emotional energy centers is closely tied to the flow of Qi (life force energy) through the meridians. Each major organ in TCM is associated not just with a physiological function but also with an emotional aspect. These emotional energies are seen as both influencing and being influenced by the health and balance of the corresponding organ.

Here’s a breakdown of the primary emotional energy centers in TCM:

1. Liver 

* Emotion: Anger, frustration, resentment
* Element: Wood
* Season: Spring
* Function: Regulates the smooth flow of Qi and blood; stores blood.

2. Heart 

* Emotion:Joy (excessive joy can be harmful), anxiety
* Element: Fire
* Season: Summer
* Function: Houses the Shen (mind/spirit); governs blood and vessels.
* Imbalance: Manifests as insomnia, restlessness, palpitations, mental disturbances.

3. Spleen

* Emotion: Worry, overthinking, pensiveness
* Element: Earth
* Season: Late summer
* Function: Governs digestion and transformation; produces Qi and blood.
* Imbalance: Leads to fatigue, digestive issues, muscle weakness.

4. Lungs 

* Emotion: Grief, sadness
* Element: Metal
* Season: Autumn
* Function: Controls respiration and Qi; governs skin and immunity.
* Imbalance: Results in shortness of breath, skin issues, immune deficiency.

5. Kidneys

* Emotion: Fear
* Element: Water
* Season: Winter
* Function: Stores essence (Jing); governs growth, reproduction, bones, and hearing.
* Imbalance: Can cause anxiety, developmental issues, low back pain, infertility.
